articles.title: Examining the Prevalence and Persistence of Data Implicated in Article Retractions
articles.authors: Ashvin Narayan; A.J. Million; John T Kubale
articles.abstract: Sharing study data has become a regular aspect of the research process, often required by journals, funding agencies, and other stakeholders to facilitate study replication and collaboration among researchers. However, while post-publication remedies—retractions, corrections, and expressions of concern—have long been used to flag ethical issues in scientific literature, their application to corresponding data is inconsistent, potentially contributing to the spread of dis- and misinformation. A lack of standardized corrective mechanisms to address problematic data hinders the identification of problematic datasets, researcher assessments of their impact, and associated determinations of data reliability. Using the Inter-University Consortium for Social and Political Research (ICPSR) and its catalog of social-scientific data as a case study, we seek to identify problematic datasets and establish workflows for evaluating the reliability of archived data. In this paper, we identify ICPSR datasets associated with publications requiring post-publication remedies. We examine editorial notices of post-publication remedies and data documentation to identify errors and/or ethical concerns affecting ICPSR datasets. Our work highlights how inconsistent documentation and communication about post-publication remedies inhibit the use of traditional corrective publishing mechanisms extended to the research data space. This work also seeks to identify resources and practices that may better facilitate processes of data re-evaluation and remediation, helping to mitigate the downstream impacts of data-related issues on scientific research.

articles.title: Scientific Misconduct and the Neo-Feudalisation of Knowledge: A Conceptual Analysis of a Mutually Reinforcing Relationship
articles.authors: Kris A. Willems; Wynand van der Walt
articles.abstract: Scientific misconduct is conventionally understood as an individual ethical failure: a deviation from the norms of honest inquiry by researchers acting in bad faith or under excessive pressure. This paper argues that each such framing, while not incorrect, is analytically insufficient. Drawing on the sociology of science, political economy, and research integrity literatures, it proposes a conceptual framework in which scientific misconduct and neo-feudal knowledge structures co-form a mutually reinforcing feedback system. The framework is grounded in the concept of the modern clerisy–the credentialed scientific class whose authority shapes policy, technology, and public narratives–and examines what happens when members of that class, under systemic pressure, begin to mirror the power structures they are nominally tasked with transcending. The paper identifies two reinforcing pathways: misconduct erodes the epistemic legitimacy on which democratic knowledge systems depend, while neo-feudal structures–characterised by gatekeeping, the privatisation of knowledge, and metric-driven hierarchies–incentivise the very practices that generate misconduct. Together, these pathways suppress epistemic diversity, concentrate knowledge authority within elite networks, and produce global inequities in knowledge production. The paper concludes that reform must be both structural and cultural: better systems and better stewards of knowledge are not alternatives but prerequisites for one another.

articles.title: Can grant evaluation still distinguish scientific excellence?
articles.authors: Martin Bulla; James Wilsdon; Peter Mikula
articles.abstract: Grant peer review increasingly depends on fine-grained numerical scores to rank many formally excellent proposals. In the era of generative and agentic AI, this architecture may be losing resolution. We analyse score-distribution data from EU Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Postdoctoral Fellowships and show sharp compression of evaluation scores in the 2025 call. Compared to 2024, there was a 64.6% increase in the volume of applications received, low-scoring proposals became rare, and ~20% of proposals reached a score of ≥95%. The timing is consistent with AI-assisted optimization, but alternative structural explanations remain possible. Nonetheless, the score compression exposes a structural vulnerability of highly standardized evaluation systems: evaluation precision near the top of the scale may be more apparent than real. We use this pattern to derive a cross-funder diagnostic framework: compression should be strongest in schemes with explicit scoring rubrics, become more visible after broad diffusion of advanced AI drafting and reasoning tools, and intensify as these tools gain capabilities. Data from Human Frontier Science Program (HFSP) Postdoctoral Fellowships and Research Grants, which first screen short Letters of Intent before inviting selected applicants to submit Full Proposals, show broadly similar score distributions across years, with no comparable compression. Cross-funder score tracking can therefore distinguish scheme-specific disruptions from broader temporal shifts and identify designs that preserve evaluative resolution. If compression is becoming more widespread, funders should reconsider whether fine-grained ranking remains an efficient and fair way to select among many excellent proposals.

articles.title: Analyzing the Consistency of Retraction Indexing
articles.authors: Malik Oyewale Salami; Corinne McCumber; Jodi Schneider
articles.abstract: Post-retraction citation may be partly due to authors’ and publishers’ challenges in systematically identifying retracted publications. Previous research has repeatedly highlighted inconsistencies in the metadata and display of retracted publications. Yet limited work has investigated the indexing of retracted papers. To assess retraction indexing quality, we investigate the agreement in indexing retracted publications between 11 database sources, restricting to their coverage, resulting in a union list of 83,317 unique items. We also discuss common errors in indexing retracted publications. A researcher might assume that, if a database has some mechanism to identify retracted publications, then the database will correctly identify what is retracted. This is not the case: there is inconsistency in which publications are identified as retracted, across the 11 database sources we queried. Our results reveal low retraction indexing agreement scores, indicating that databases widely disagree about which publications within their coverage are retracted. Our findings highlight the need for increased adherence to standard retraction metadata practices and, where possible, increased open sharing of retracted publication metadata, in order to reduce inadvertent post-retraction citation.

articles.title: Where Reproducibility Policy Actually Lives: A Stratified Audit of 150 Clinical Journals and the Limits of Automated Policy Retrieval
articles.authors: Adrian C Demidont; Andrea J. Farina
articles.abstract:
Background: Computational research is reaching clinical journals faster than the infrastructure to evaluate it, while meta-research reads journal policy through automated agents assuming it is legible. We audit what journals document to evaluate such work and whether that policy is machine-legible.

Methods: From a SNIP-stratified random sample of 150 MEDLINE-indexed clinical journals in six specialties, we hand-coded five editorial-capacity indicators, separating disclosure, deposit, and verification. Coding was checked against a timestamped archive, with blind automated cross-checks and independent second coding on indicator subsets (pooled κ = 0.69).

Results: Requirements clustered into 50 policy units across the 150-journal frame. A data-availability statement was mandated by 32% by publication but only 6% at submission; none mandated code deposit or a runnable artifact. A statistics/methods editor appeared on 28% of boards, an AI editor on 5%. Half the author-instruction pages (75/150) were refused by all three standard HTTP clients, and one automated pass recovered 3 of 48 data mandates.

Conclusions: Clinical journals document abundant means to disclose where data are but almost none to verify a computation runs—and that policy is barely legible to an automated audit. One problem seen twice: infrastructure not built to be read. Data and code are openly released.

articles.title: Psychiatric Symptom Severity and Performance Monitoring:  Intraindividual Variability in Neural Responses and Behavioral Adjustments to Errors
articles.authors: Bohyun Park; Scott Baldwin; Michael J. Larson; Peter E Clayson
articles.abstract: Performance monitoring involves evaluating actions and adjusting behavior accordingly. Atypical neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are commonly observed in individuals with psychopathology, raising the possibility that psychiatric symptoms may disrupt the link between error-related neural activity and subsequent behavioral adjustment. However, neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are often examined separately, leaving trial-level event-related brain potential (ERP) coupling with behavior poorly understood. The present study examined whether previous-trial error-related ERP components predicted current-trial behavior (i.e., response time [RT], accuracy) and whether these relationships varied by self-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms. In a college student sample (N=247), larger previous-trial error-related negativity (ERN), an index of early error monitoring, predicted longer RTs. In contrast, larger previous-trial error positivity (Pe), an index of later error awareness, predicted higher current-trial accuracy. Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores did not robustly moderate these ERP-behavior relationships or consistently predict behavioral adjustments. These findings suggest that trial-level coupling between error-related ERP components and behavioral adjustment showed no robust evidence of differing across levels of self-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms within the observed range. More broadly, the results highlight the value of examining performance monitoring as an integrated neural-behavioral process rather than as isolated neural or behavioral indices.

articles.title: Why Are You Slowing Down? Performance-Monitoring ERPs Predict Drift Diffusion Model Parameters of Post-Error Adjustment
articles.authors: Bohyun Park; Chad Dubé; Michael J. Larson; Peter E Clayson
articles.abstract: Post-error slowing is usually attributed to the prioritization of accurate responding. However, neural and behavioral measures of performance monitoring are typically examined in isolation, failing to capture how individuals’ responses to an error relate to changes in subsequent decision making. The role of performance monitoring in the context of the speed-accuracy tradeoff can be understood by examining within-person changes in the relationship between error-monitoring event-related brain potentials (ERPs) and drift-diffusion model (DDM) parameters. In the neural domain, we examined the error-related negativity (ERN) and error positivity (Pe), the two error-monitoring ERPs that reflect different stages of error processing. In the behavioral domain, we used a DDM to characterize the cognitive operations involved in the task. We used Hierarchical DDM regressor models to relate the two domains using data collected from 177 healthy participants during a flanker task. We found that larger previous-trial ERN predicted a less cautious response style (i.e., lower decision boundary) and slower visual encoding and motor execution on the current trial. Robust relationships were observed between heightened early-stage error processing and changes in both attentional and non-attentional processes in subsequent decision-making, even after accounting for current-trial characteristics. Importantly, heightened error detection and the subsequent increase in non-decision time provided strong support for the bottleneck theory of post-error slowing, such that sustained error monitoring interferes with efficient visual encoding on the subsequent trial.

articles.title: Becoming a climate activist:  A qualitative investigation of movement participation
articles.authors: Anna Aretha Sach; Cameron Brick; Roos Herings; Disa Sauter; Nils Jostmann
articles.abstract: Activists are mobilizing worldwide to address the climate crisis. In the past years, climate movements have attracted many newcomers. Yet, even among motivated individuals who contacted a movement, becoming an actively engaged member remains rare. Previous studies have focused on non-engaged people’s intentions and barriers to joining or have surveyed long-term activists, yet little is known about newcomers. We studied how newcomers join different climate movements. In co-creation with activist organizers, we aimed to identify the phases of joining a climate movement and what facilitates and hinders engagement. We interviewed 23 individuals who had joined Extinction Rebellion (XR) United Kingdom, XR Netherlands, or the International Climate Students Movement. Five months later, the interviewees completed a short follow-up survey. Using inductive thematic analysis, we identified three phases associated with specific facilitators and barriers. The first phase was often initiated based on previous experience and a strong motivation to make a change. The second phase was marked by becoming active and socially integrated. In the final phase, activists transitioned from newcomers to active members. In the medium term, feeling effective and positive within the movement was associated with sustained engagement. Based on these findings, we recommend tailoring support for interested potential activists, newcomers, and experienced activists. Providing clear information, dedicated integrator roles, and emotional check-ins can help build broad, welcoming, and persistent activist movements. We suggest future longitudinal research starting from the moment of entry, as well as quasi-experiments testing socialization tactics.

articles.title: From Acute Attack to Prolonged War: A Scoping Review of Mental Health Burden in Israel After October 7
articles.authors: Yossi Levi-Belz; Adrian Mendelson; Yael Segal Elbak; Dalia Moallem; Ziv Ben-Zion
articles.abstract:
Background: The October 7, 2023, attack in Israel was followed by a prolonged war marked by repeated threat, displacement, reserve mobilization, and hostage-related uncertainty. This context generated a rapidly expanding yet heterogeneous empirical literature on psychological distress. This scoping review mapped the scope, temporal patterning, distribution, and evidence gaps of peer-reviewed publications among individuals residing in Israel after October 7, foregrounding prolonged war as the central context.
Methods: This prospectively registered review followed PRISMA-ScR guidance. Searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, APA PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection for publications from October 7, 2023, to April 2026. Eligible publications reported quantitative findings on mental health symptoms, functioning, risk or protective factors, or service use. Findings were synthesized narratively by publication characteristics, temporal patterns, exposure contexts, population groups, and evidence gaps.
Findings: Searches yielded 11,285 records; screening identified 240 eligible publications, of which 205 reported distress-related outcomes and were retained here. Cross-sectional publications predominated (120/205; 58.5%), followed by longitudinal or repeated-assessment publications (80/205; 39.0%); intervention or experimental publications were rare (5/205; 2.4%). Findings documented acute increases in PTSD/PTSS, depression, anxiety, acute stress, sleep disturbance, and general distress, followed by partial but uneven symptom reduction during the first year. Evidence beyond the first year was limited but suggested persistent or possible cumulative burden under prolonged-war conditions. Burden was concentrated in groups marked by direct trauma, displacement, bereavement or hostage-related uncertainty, military or caregiving burden, minority or age-related vulnerability, and moral injury or betrayal.
Interpretation: Post-October 7 mental health burden is best understood not as a bounded post-event aftermath, but as distress evolving within a prolonged crisis. Future research should move beyond early symptom documentation toward longitudinal, functional, service-oriented, and intervention-informed evidence.

articles.title: Motivational Framing Shapes Effort Judgments in Individuals with Depressive Symptoms
articles.authors: Thomas Meyer; Rebecca Kochtokrax; Hannah Sautmann; Nexhmedin Morina
articles.abstract: Effort-related motivational deficits in depression are often studied through effort-reward decisions, yet everyday effort also depends on the reference standards against which it is judged. In a preregistered laboratory crossover study, 51 participants with at least mild depressive symptoms received two opposing effort framings: self-initiated allocation toward goals and need frustration emphasizing burden and affective demand. After reconstructing previous-day activities, participants evaluated upward and downward social, temporal-past, criteria-based, and counterfactual standards for their two most effortful activities per session, yielding 1,632 standard-endorsement judgments followed by intensity and discrepancy ratings for endorsed standards. As predicted, need-frustration framing increased endorsement of upward criteria-based standards (“this should feel less effortful”). However, this effect did not generalize across upward comparisons. Instead, need frustration decreased upward temporal standards (“this used to feel easier”) and increased downward counterfactual standards (“it could have been harder under worse circumstances”). Intensity ratings among endorsed standards were not reliably affected, although an exploratory relevance score supported the specific role of upward criteria-based standards. Perceived effort was higher under allocation but correlated more positively with depressive symptoms under need frustration. These findings suggest that motivational framing changes the comparison standards people identify as relevant to everyday effort judgments and highlight the need to assess the appraised meaning of effort-related comparisons directly.

articles.title: Student Adoption of an AI Tutor for Statistical Programming: A Longitudinal Study
articles.authors: Clément Préau; Matthias Burke; Tjark Müller; Tobias R. Rebholz; Frank Papenmeier
articles.abstract: Background: The rise in AI use among students has raised questions about the integration of AI tools into higher education. This longitudinal study examined the adoption of an AI tutor and its consequences during a semester-long university course on R programming. Methods: We analyzed the relationships between AI tutor usage, academic performance, students’ attitudes toward R programming, self-efficacy, and their attitudes toward and trust in AI. Results: We found that 76-84% of students used the AI tutor during the exam-relevant phase of the semester and that, on average, students used alternative AI tools only 8% of the time. Surprisingly, trust in and attitudes toward AI did not predict AI tutor usage, raising questions about the interplay between personal dispositions and situational demands. AI tutor usage was positively associated with academic performance, and no adverse effects of usage were observed. In this context, we discuss the potential to mitigate negative consequences of cognitive offloading by embedding AI tools within an appropriate instructional framework. The AI tutor was positively evaluated by students, and adaptations made during the semester provide further insights into user-friendly design features. Conclusion: This study offers an example of how AI tools can be integrated into a university course setting in a way that may help mitigate adverse effects of AI overreliance. We encourage future research to explore the implementation of AI tools in domains beyond programming.

articles.title: Explicit knowledge enables allocentric target but not distractor learning
articles.authors: Litian Chen; Freek van Ede; Heleen A Slagter
articles.abstract: Humans can learn to attend to and to ignore specific locations based on statistical regularities. Such statistical learning effects may arise through both implicit and explicit mechanisms and may be expressed in egocentric (viewer-centered) or allocentric (world-centered) reference frames. In the absence of explicit knowledge, statistical learning is typically egocentric, but explicit knowledge can promote allocentric target-location learning. Yet, whether explicit knowledge can similarly promote allocentric distractor-location learning remains unclear. Here, we addressed this question across six experiments. Study 1 (Experiments 1-4; n=95) examined whether explicit knowledge can enable allocentric distractor-location learning using an additional-singleton visual-search task in which participants continuously changed their viewpoint following full-body movements. Participants were either informed (explicit) or uninformed (implicit) about a high-probability distractor location, which was defined relative to their perspective (egocentric) or the environment (allocentric). Unlike what has been reported for target regularities, even with explicit knowledge of the regularity, no evidence for allocentric location learning was found for distractor regularities. Study 2 (Experiments 5-6, n=54) confirmed that explicit knowledge can support allocentric target-location learning in our set-up. Together, these findings indicate that explicit knowledge about world-centered spatial regularities can be exploited when it concerns task-relevant but not task-irrelevant information. This dissociation suggests that learning what to ignore is not simply the inverse of learning where to attend, with important implications for theories of statistical learning and attentional control.

articles.title: Neural correlates of individual differences in cognition: a behavioral performance, EEG, and MRI dataset
articles.authors: Mareike Hülsemann; Henrike Maria Jungeblut; Maximilian Lueckel; Benjamin Meyer; Anna-Lena Schubert
articles.abstract: The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability. The multi-indicator design supports latent-variable modeling of all major constructs alongside their structural, functional, and electrophysiological neural correlates. Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). Electroencephalography (EEG) data was collected during four resting-state blocks and during task performance (cognitive control and processing speed). High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging using the SANDI protocol, and multi-band multi-echo functional MRI during rest and task-switching were acquired in a subset. Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data are accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository. All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.

articles.title: Media portrayals of youth self-harm and suicide: An examination social determinants and inequalities
articles.authors: Leigh Huggard; Daisy Wiggin; Eve Griffin; Elaine McMahon
articles.abstract: Increasing evidence shows that social inequalities are central determinants of youth self harm and suicide. Media coverage shapes public understanding of these risk factors, yet little is known how Irish news outlets portray them. The study examined the representation of determinants in popular Irish print and online news between 2023 and 2025. Following a systematic keyword search of eight major outlets, 918 articles were examined, of which 25% contained at least one causal explanation. Using abductive content analysis guided by the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health framework, articles were coded for type of causal explanation, source of the explanation, and social characteristics of described individuals. Frequency counts and chi square tests assessed differences by year, publication, source, gender of described individuals, and whether the explanation referred to suicide, self harm, or both. Psychosocial explanations dominated (71% of mentions), driven by abuse/trauma (37%) relational factors (23%), and technology and social media use (17%). Macro-level structural determinants such as wider political, socioeconomic, or cultural contexts were less frequently mentioned, and no biological factors were reported. Female experiences were over represented (62% of profiles), and explanations were most commonly supplied by lived-experience accounts (20%) and non-expert professionals, such as politicians or teachers (17%). No temporal trend was observed, and there were limited differences in explanations for self-harm vs suicide. The findings reveal a media landscape that foregrounds individual level narratives and under represents systemic risk factors. Extending Irish suicide reporting guidelines to require inclusion of structural determinants and expert perspectives could improve public awareness, reduce stigma, and bolster evidence based prevention strategies.

articles.title: Actions speak louder than words: Towards measuring real-world behaviour change in psychedelic research
articles.authors: Sarah Roche; Kim PC Kuypers; Joana Wensing; Natasha Mason
articles.abstract: The therapeutic and societal promise often attributed to psychedelic drugs implies meaningful change in real-world behaviour, yet such change is rarely measured directly. Across psychedelic research, outcomes are typically assessed using symptom scales, self-reported psychological states, or retrospective judgments of change, which may capture subjective improvement but do not by themselves demonstrate altered behaviour. Reviewing evidence across health, prosocial, and pro-environmental domains, we show that outside addiction, claims about behavioural transformation remain methodologically ahead of the data. We outline methodological approaches that could help bring the field’s strongest claims into closer alignment with more rigorous tests of real-world change.

articles.title: Perceived Artificiality Markedly Reduces Trustworthiness but Only Minimally Affects Attractiveness in AI-Synthetic Faces
articles.authors: Jiaxin Wang; Satoshi Nishida
articles.abstract: With the spread of artificial intelligence (AI)-synthesized human faces in digital communication, researchers have begun to investigate the associations of the perceived artificiality of such faces with their social evaluations, finding that artificial faces tend to be perceived as less trustworthy and attractive. However, as facial trustworthiness and attractiveness are strongly correlated, it is unclear which dimension is more strongly influenced by perceived artificiality once the correlation between trustworthiness and attractiveness is controlled. Accordingly, we collected the manual ratings by 100 participants of the perceived artificiality, trustworthiness, and attractiveness of 500 AI-synthesized faces and analyzed the unique pairwise associations among these variables using participant-wise partial correlation and generalized estimating equation analyses. Perceived artificiality showed a robust negative association with trustworthiness even after controlling for attractiveness, whereas the association between artificiality and attractiveness was much weaker and negligible in magnitude after controlling for trustworthiness. These results suggest that artificial cues predominantly influence social trust rather than aesthetic evaluation. Our findings offer important insights into the distinct psychological role of perceived artificiality in social face perception.

articles.title: Autobiographical Recollective Style in Grapheme–Color Synesthesia: Overlap with Fantasy Proneness and Multisensory Imagery
articles.authors: Eiko Matsuda; Eiko Matsuda
articles.abstract:
Although more vivid mental imagery and subjectively richer individual autobiographical memories have been reported in
synesthetes, whether synesthesia is associated with a trait-like autobiographical recollective style governing how individuals
typically recollect their personal past remains unclear. We compared 27 participants operationally classified into a grapheme–
color synesthesia group through large-scale screening with 30 controls selected through individual matching on age and sex.
Autobiographical recollective style was assessed using the Japanese version of the Autobiographical Recollection Test (ART-
J), and we examined the extent to which group differences overlapped with Big Five personality traits, fantasy proneness,
and multisensory imagery vividness. The synesthesia group scored higher than the control group on the ART-J total score
and all seven subscales. The group coefficient was not substantially attenuated in a model that included the five Big Five
traits. By contrast, adding fantasy proneness and multisensory imagery significantly increased the explained variance and
substantially attenuated the point estimate of the group coefficient. These findings suggest that the characteristics of the
grapheme–color synesthesia group extend beyond visual imagery to a broad subjective autobiographical recollective style
encompassing scene construction, reliving, rehearsal, and integration into a life story, and that this group difference partly
overlaps with broader characteristics of inner experience.

articles.title: Trajectory elevation in reach-to-grasp movements under increased arm weight and repeated trials
articles.authors: Yoshihiro Itaguchi; Luna Ando
articles.abstract: This study examined how three-dimensional upper-limb movement trajectories are modulated by changes in gravitational load. We hypothesized that individuals adopt a trajectory elevation strategy in reach-to-grasp movements performed on a desk to compensate for increased movement variability arising from motor noise. To increase motor demands and create conditions under which trial-related fatigue effects could emerge, we manipulated arm weight and used an extended repeated-trial protocol. Participants completed 400 reach-to-grasp trials under three weight conditions (0 g, 200 g, and 400 g), with weights applied to the forearm during the middle 300 trials in the 200 g and 400 g conditions. From the first weighted block—when substantial muscle fatigue was unlikely to have developed—maximum trajectory height was greater in the weighted conditions than in the 0 g condition. Across trials, trajectory height gradually decreased in the 0 g and 200 g conditions, whereas a slight increase was observed in the 400 g condition. In the 400 g condition, trajectory elevation across trials was positively correlated with trajectory variability in later trials. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that trajectory elevation may serve as a strategy to mitigate detrimental effects on task performance caused by fluctuations in motor output, whether arising from added weight or trial-related fatigue effects. Additionally, exploratory analyses examined the effects of within-day repeated practice on aperture control during reach-to-grasp movements.

articles.title: Validating local open-weight LLMs against expert raters for graded deductive coding of open-ended responses in Russian
articles.authors: Artem S. Yashin; Shchennikova Maria V.; Darisy G. Zhao; Anna A. Zinina; Nikita Arinkin; Eugeny V. Melnichuk; Artemiy A. Kotov
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to code open-ended survey responses, but their validity against expert annotation remains uncertain, especially outside English. We evaluated four open-weight LLMs for deductive coding of Russian responses from a psychological human-robot interaction experiment (N = 33): DeepSeek-R1-32B, Qwen3-32B, Gemma3-27B, and Mistral-Small-3.2-24B. Ten psychology-trained coders provided a graded expert reference for seven predefined codes. Each model was run under singular-code prompts, an exploratory conservative variant, and fixed-sequence prompts mirroring the expert memo, with ten repeated runs aggregated into graded code-presence estimates. Agreement was assessed with graded concordance, calibration, human-equivalence, and threshold-sensitivity diagnostics. The strongest configurations by concordance — DeepSeek-R1-32B with singular-code prompting (CCC = 0.71) and Qwen3-32B with fixed-sequence prompting (CCC = 0.69) — reached agreement with the expert aggregate comparable to the disagreement among individual experts, although both relied on reasoning mode, which was confounded with model identity. Several models over-attributed codes relative to experts, and prompt format and aggregation strategy materially affected agreement. We recommend validating LLM coding as a measurement procedure, with reported calibration and uncertainty, rather than as automatic expert replacement in small applied psychological datasets.

articles.title: Revealing implicit social bias through EEG-informed generative AI.
articles.authors: Aotong Li; Tuukka Ruotsalo; Christian Montag; Michiel Marten Spape
articles.abstract: Social biases can shape rapid judgements of others, but social desirability and limited self-awareness make these biases difficult to measure. We tested whether electroencephalographic (EEG) responses to faces could provide implicit feedback for generating visual prototypes of political leadership. Forty adults were recruited, of whom 38 provided analysable EEG data. Participants viewed 300 AI-generated faces during rapid serial visual presentation while attending to faces they would vote for, and subsequently provided explicit yes/no votes that were used to label image-locked EEG epochs. An EEGNet ensemble classified later-voted versus non-voted faces, and its predictions guided a pretrained StyleGAN3 model to generate participant-specific and multi-participant BrainVote faces. Twenty returning participants evaluated these faces and label-shuffled matched controls in a mock election two months later. Classification exceeded permutation baselines for 36 of 38 participants. BrainVote faces were preferred to matched controls, and 80% of returning participants voted for the face generated from their own EEG responses. Aggregation across participants produced increasingly homogeneous prototypes characterised by senior and masculine features, with stronger patterns among participants with larger gender-career Implicit Association Test scores. EEG-informed generative AI can therefore visualise sample-level implicit leadership associations while revealing how aggregation may amplify demographic stereotypes.

articles.title: Personality Prediction from Moments to Lifetimes
articles.authors: Emorie D Beck; Adam Taylor Nissen; Eileen Kranz Graham; Dan Mroczek
articles.abstract: Personality is robustly linked to long-term outcomes, yet predicting momentary behavior (i.e., who does what, when, and where) remains challenging. We argue that personality and its outcomes can be understood at multiple levels within an emergent hierarchy, and that prediction requires identifying what level(s) is most informative for a given target. Broad traits reliably predict distal outcomes such as cognitive aging and mortality but reveal little about underlying processes. Within-person patterns capture shorter-term regularities, though heterogeneity is often overlooked. Momentary processes unfold as complex, multivariate systems that support personalized prediction but challenge generalization. We therefore propose a bottom-up integrative framework that derives comparable features from person-specific dynamics and tests whether they predict outcomes at other levels. Emerging evidence suggests that such features can bridge levels and support more integrative, explainable prediction.

articles.title: Building Science Identity Through University-High School Partnerships: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of a Graduate Student-Led Science Expo
articles.authors: Freya Joëssel; Abbie Clapp; Laura Jett; Kelci Cox; Nicholas Allan Vest
articles.abstract: Research-practice partnerships provide a promising framework for designing and evaluating STEM outreach, yet the role of graduate student organizations as sustained research partners remains underexplored. We examined a graduate-student-led partnership (a science exposition) between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and a local high school aimed at fostering science identity in highschoolers from historically underrepresented backgrounds. Quantitative analyses (N = 48) showed pre-to-post-expo increases in overall science identity, with significant gains in perceived representation and recognition as a science person. Qualitative analyses (N = 64) of open-ended post-reflection questions highlighted the importance of interacting with relatable researchers, authentic scientific engagement, and representation. These findings illustrate how graduate student organizations can function as research-practice partners by integrating outreach, evaluation, and continuous improvement.

articles.title: Spontaneous thought as attentional competition
articles.authors: Sneha K. S. Sheth; Rebecca M. Todd; Lawrence Ward
articles.abstract: Spontaneous thought appears to be free-flowing, but is not random, often comprising personally relevant content. We present a novel framework, Attentional Competition in Thought (ACT), that characterizes spontaneous thought as a result of priority-weighted competition, similar to visual selective attention. ACT comprises three interacting systems: generation presents candidate thoughts for selection, valuation integrates implicit sources—motivation, affect, current concerns, and memory accessibility—into priority weights, and regulation adds goal-based weights. Valuation and regulation also modulate overall competitive gain. By varying weight strength, spread, and leading system, ACT presents a common underlying mechanism for thoughts as different as freely moving thought, rumination, and deliberate problem-solving, placing the latter two on the same priority-weighted structure. On this view, even the freest-feeling thought remains implicitly shaped by priority. ACT generates testable behavioural, neuroimaging, and clinical predictions, and reframes maladaptive repetitive thought as reflecting excessive priority assigned to particular contents, placing valuation alongside cognitive control as a target for intervention.

articles.title: Social sages: Popularity as a distinct form of social status emerging in middle childhood
articles.authors: Katherine Grace Vasquez; Alex Shaw
articles.abstract: Status hierarchies begin pervading social life early in development. In children’s schools, popular kids sit atop the social hierarchy constructed by their peers. Is popularity a distinct form of social status, and if so, what are its central features? One potential answer is peer copying: popular kids are copied by their peers. But popular kids often possess other positive characteristics (e.g., attractiveness, wealth), raising the possibility that this copying is a byproduct of these other traits. To address this, we introduced children to novel characters who differed in popularity and other traits. In five preregistered studies (N = 502 5- to 10-year-olds), children predicted who was “copied” by their peers. In Study 1, children chose the popular character over an unpopular character, but assumed the popular character was rich. In Studies 2-4, children said popular kids are copied more than rich kids (as young as 7 and reliably by 9). They believe this copying is specific to certain matters, like style, not academics. This pattern did not reflect a general preference for popularity: children were divided about whether they would prefer to be popular or rich themselves. Study 5 solidifies that popularity is not merely being well-liked: by age 9, children said a popular, not-liked, kid was copied more than a well-liked, not popular, kid. These findings demonstrate that children treat popularity as its own form of social status that involves being copied. We discuss the implications of these results for current theories regarding the development of social status concepts.

articles.title: The developmental dynamics of bilingual spelling:  Longitudinal and intervention evidence for language-specific orthographic differentiation
articles.authors: Manon Jones; Catherine Alice Clark; Gwennant Evans; Joseph Benjamin Russell Smith; Carly Deluca; James Hodgetts; Ferrida Ponce; Cadi Sion; Samuel David Jones; Cameron Downing
articles.abstract: Spelling in bilingual children requires navigating two orthographic systems that may compete as well as cooperate. Although bilingual language research demonstrates extensive cross-language co-activation, far less is known about how such dynamics shape spelling development. We investigated whether cross-linguistic influence in spelling – indexed by the extent to which children’s misspellings conformed to English-consistent versus Welsh-consistent phoneme–grapheme mappings – predicted literacy development in Welsh–English bilingual children. Across three studies involving 524 children aged approximately 7–11 years, we quantified the extent to which misspellings reflected sublexical mappings characteristic of English or Welsh orthography. In Study 1, longitudinal analyses of children in control groups showed that greater phonological plausibility under English-consistent mappings at baseline predicted greater growth in English spelling accuracy, whereas greater plausibility under Welsh-consistent mappings predicted slower growth. In Study 2, a Welsh-medium literacy intervention did not affect English spelling accuracy but strengthened Welsh-consistent mappings and improved English-consistent mappings among children with the weakest baseline skills. In Study 3, an English-medium intervention strengthened English-consistent mappings but did not alter Welsh-consistent mappings. Together, these findings suggest that bilingual spelling development involves increasing differentiation of language-specific sublexical mappings through experience. This differentiation appears to be shaped by instructional context and orthographic depth, such that increasing sensitivity to target-language mappings supports spelling growth, whereas persistent influence of non-target mappings may constrain it.

articles.title: Functional Brain Activation during Statistical Learning is Related to Rapid Automatized Naming of Digits and Objects (but not Letters): An fMRI Study
articles.authors: Praveen Prem; Adwoa Boadu; Sarah Saju; Kelly Nisbet; Jacqueline Cummine
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Statistical learning (SL) is the implicit process of extracting statistical regularities from the environment and has been found to be strongly linked with language ability in both children and adults. Notably, SL has been shown to activate brain regions that are implicated in language/reading; however, the extent to which this brain activity is related to reading-related tasks is unknown. Here, we used fMRI to explore the brain-behavior relationships between SL and reading processes.
Methods: 48 Adult participants (28 Female, mean age 21 years old) completed a Visual SL (VSL) task inside the MRI that included two phases: 1) familiarization, wherein participants were presented with novel triplets of shapes varying in transitional probabilities, and 2) testing, which involved selecting best-fitting triplets that assessed their learning of these probabilities. Outside the scanner, participants completed three Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN) tasks consisting of quickly naming strings of digits, letters, and objects as a measure of basic reading ability.
Results: Using a whole-brain correlational approach with RAN performance as covariates, significant brain-behavior clusters were identified between VSL task-evoked neural activity with RAN digits and objects, but not letters. The regions were predominantly left-lateralized in visuospatial-motor network as well as the parietal regions, caudate, and cerebellum, with the precuneus as a common hub.
Conclusion: These findings link to a more multimodal understanding of the neurocognitive processes, indicating that SL-related neural activity in skilled readers is preferentially linked to naming of symbol sets with inherent semantic content (digits, objects) rather than arbitrary orthographic forms (letters).

articles.title: Neuropsychological assessment of executive functions in Argentina: a systematic review of locally validated instruments
articles.authors: Camila Ailen Morgenstern; Dinka Piromalli Girado; Sofia Abrevaya
articles.abstract: Neuropsychology in Argentina faces challenges due to the scarcity of culturally validated tests. Executive functions (EF) are essential for daily functioning; however, no systematic review of instruments for assessing EF in adults currently exists in the country. Following PRISMA guidelines and registered in OSF, three independent reviewers searched PubMed, SciELO, LILACS, and Scopus. Performance and self-report studies on executive domains in Argentine adults were included, without date restrictions. From 2,734 screened records (35,748 imported; 33,014 duplicates removed), 25 studies reporting psychometric properties of 16 instruments were included. Normative data, reliability, and validity of tests evaluating inhibition, cognitive flexibility, verbal fluency, working memory, processing speed, and ecological functioning are detailed, along with self-report scales. Results show local advances with limitations in federal representation, age coverage, and normative methodology. This systematization represents an indispensable preliminary step for the development of digital versions in the national context.

articles.title: The Role of Temperament and Personality Traits in the Development of ADHD from Late Childhood through Adolescence
articles.authors: Katherine M. Lawson; Jocelyn I. Meza; Richard Robins
articles.abstract: Individual differences in temperament and personality traits may shed light on the presentation and development of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) across adolescence. The present study used multi-method, longitudinal data from a large sample of Mexican-origin youth (N = 674; 50% girls) to examine associations between ADHD symptoms (including combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive subtypes) and a wide range of temperament and personality traits assessed via self-, mother-, and father-reports and coded observational data. First, we found moderate one-year rank-order stabilities of combined, hyperactive-impulsive, and inattentive ADHD symptoms (r’s ranging from .27 to .51), but relatively low eight-year rank-order stability from age 10 to 17 (r = .19 for combined); eight-year stability was higher for boys than girls. Second, hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive symptoms were both negatively correlated with concurrent effortful control and conscientiousness, and positively correlated with impulsivity, negative emotionality, and neuroticism; in addition, hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were positively associated with surgency and extraversion. Third, bivariate latent growth curve models showed that the levels and slopes of effortful control (and its facets) and negative emotionality (particularly the frustration, aggression, and depressed mood facets) were significantly related to the levels and slopes of ADHD symptom trajectories. Findings from random-intercept cross-lagged panel models showed that temperament domains and ADHD symptoms had meaningful between- and within-person associations, but no significant cross-lagged associations. Associations were stronger for adolescent self-reports of temperament/personality than for mother reports. Overall, findings highlight connections between temperament and personality traits with ADHD symptoms across adolescence.

articles.title: Testing the Alliance and Cognitive Change as Simultaneous Processes of Change in Cognitive Therapy for Anxiety
articles.authors: Alexandra Kaelin Barnhill; Madeline Kushner; Doug Terrill; Matthew W. Southward
articles.abstract: Researchers have proposed that both a strong working alliance and cognitive change are key processes of change in cognitive therapy for emotional disorders. Schmidt et al. (2019) demonstrated that within-person cognitive change occurring between sessions mediated the relation between within-person cognitive change in the previous session and subsequent depression improvement. We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of Schmidt et al. (2019) in a sample of adults with elevated anxiety (N = 200; Mage = 32.1; 78% female, 80% White, 73% heterosexual) who completed self-report measures before and after four sessions of cognitive therapy. Using dynamic structural equation modeling, we replicated Schmidt et al.’s (2019) results that between-session cognitive change (CC-S) mediated the relation between in-session cognitive change (CC-I) and depression improvement (ODSIS; B = –.16, p < .01) and extended them to improvements in anxiety (OASIS; B = –.18, p < .01). We also found that between-session cognitive change mediated the relation between the working alliance (WAI-SR) and anxiety and depression improvement (Bs: –.12-–.11, ps < .01). The indirect effects involving cognitive change did not significantly differ from those involving the total alliance and agreement on the tasks of therapy, ps > .15, but were stronger than those involving agreement on the goals of therapy and the therapeutic bond, ps < .03. Both the alliance and cognitive change may be key processes of change, albeit at different steps in the overall pathway, in cognitive therapy for emotional disorders.

articles.title: Seeing Events in 3D Enhances Scene Memory and Vividness
articles.authors: Peggy L. St. Jacques; Júlia Feminella Duarte da Costa; Shikang Peng
articles.abstract: Episodic memories arise from perceptually rich, spatially structured experiences, yet most laboratory studies rely on two-dimensional (2D) stimuli that omit key features of naturalistic perception. We tested whether one such feature—binocular depth—alters how events are later remembered. Participants viewed immersive, first-person 360° videos presented in either 2D (monoscopic) or 3D (stereoscopic) virtual reality while the display, field of view, and context were held constant. Events experienced in 3D were rated as having stronger scene-related qualities and greater vividness than events experienced in 2D. These differences remained after accounting for both within-person and between-person variation in subjective presence, indicating that presence alone did not explain the effects of depth. Depth did not systematically alter emotional intensity or pleasantness. These findings show that binocular depth selectively influences the spatial and visual qualities of later remembering and that conventional 2D presentation may omit perceptual information that shapes how episodic memories are formed.

articles.title: Two temporally distinct prediction stages overlap under moderately faster speech
articles.authors: Naomi Nota; Ruth Corps; Muzna Shehzad; Lauren Hadley; Graham Naylor; Martin John Pickering
articles.abstract: Prediction is a core mechanism in language comprehension, and evidence suggests it involves separate stages. The associative stage involves fast, automatic predictions driven by semantic associations (e.g., a verb cueing likely referents), while the strategic stage involves slower, deliberate predictions incorporating broader contextual cues (e.g., agent gender). Although faster speech has been shown to decrease prediction, no research has investigated how these stages are individually impacted. We conducted a preregistered visual-world eye-tracking experiment in which English speakers listened to non-speeded (4 syllables/second) or speeded (5.5 syllables/second) sentences while viewing four-object arrays. Stimuli included a female or male agent (Kate or James) and a verb (e.g., wear) that primed two target images (e.g., dress and tie) alongside two unrelated distractor images (e.g., hairdryer and drill). Verb-related targets included one stereotypically compatible with the agent’s gender and one incompatible. One distractor was gender-compatible and one gender-incompatible. Participants showed associative predictions (more fixations to verb-related targets than distractors) and strategic predictions (more fixations to agent-compatible targets than incompatible targets). In non-speeded speech, the stages were temporally distinct, with associative prediction occurring before strategic prediction. In speeded speech, however, these stages overlapped. These results suggest that changes in speech rate can influence predictive timing.

articles.title: Increased pupil dilation in autistic adults during a naturalistic audiobook-in-noise paradigm
articles.authors: Ryan J Oakeson; Allison C Nugent; Amaia Benitez-Andonegui; Sarah Joanne White; Sophie K Scott
articles.abstract:
Autistic people experience disproportionate challenges in noisy environments than non-autistic people. To capture a naturalistic representation of listening effort in adverse condition, an autistic (n=27) and non-autistic group (n=22) were presented with an audiobook and different speech masking noises while their pupils were measured with an eye tracker. The audiobook task consisted of a target-only condition and three noise conditions: 1-speaker, 2-speaker, and speech-shaped noise. The task was entirely passive with no behavioral or subjective measures. We measured the mean and variance of the evoked pupillary response—a reliable measure of cognitive effort. 
Primary findings revealed effects of the speech-masking conditions and condition occurrence on temporal dynamics of pupillary behavior. Specifically, the autistic group exhibited a general increase of mean pupil dilation over time, whereas the non-autistic group showed no difference in pupil size over time. Both groups showed increased variance in pupil size over time in all conditions throughout the task. These findings demonstrate that an audiobook-in-noise task can provide insight into temporal dynamics of pupil behavior during naturalistic speech perception in noise (SPiN). These results also suggest increased listening effort required in the autistic sample compared to the non-autistic controls.

articles.title: Authoritarianism in American Conservatives and Liberals Before and After January 6th
articles.authors: Lucian Gideon Conway
articles.abstract: January 6th narratives often center around authoritarianism, but little empirical data has directly evaluated the overlap between authoritarianism in the American populace and January 6th. In the present study, we evaluate authoritarianism in conservative and liberal participants (total n = 2264) across five time frames from November 2020 until after the events of January 6, 2021. Three primary findings emerged. (1) Authoritarian asymmetry: Conservatives wanted more authoritarianism than liberals across all time frames. (2) Authoritarian contextualism: Both conservatives and liberals wanted more authoritarianism from the government when their party was in power. (3) Targeted authoritarian adjustment: Conservatives’ authoritarianism towards Trump and Biden changed after January 6. However, contrary to expectations, conservatives desired less authoritarianism from Trump and more authoritarianism from Biden after January 6. Taken together, these findings help us better understand the contextual and ideological factors related to authoritarian attitudes surrounding unprecedented authoritarian behavior in the United States.

articles.title: Developing an open multi-domain assessment battery using laboratory tasks for children in low- and middle-income countries
articles.authors: Joseph Coffey; Elizabeth Spelke
articles.abstract: Recent years have seen growing interest in field research using randomized designs to evaluate the impacts of interventions on early child development in low- and middle-income countries. Measuring these impacts requires assessments that can track development prior to school entry in settings that are often noisy and outdoors. Drawing from research in developmental cognitive science, we created an open multi-domain assessment battery for testing children in low- and middle-income countries consisting of tasks based on experimental paradigms used in laboratory settings. These tasks were designed to target abilities that emerge across cultures early in life and predict later performance on related skills in adulthood. This battery was administered to 1435 Ghanaian children whose parent previously took part in a randomized controlled field experiment on the impacts of parent secondary education on their children, measuring performance on tasks at ages 1.5, 3.5, 5.5, and 7.5 years. Starting at age 3.5, children’s responses to the tasks were internally consistent and above chance, with overall test results predictive of later performance. There was strong evidence of validity both for tasks in numeracy and spatial reasoning, which were designed to tap into culturally invariant cognitive capacities, as well as those in language and executive functioning, which required more context-specific adaptation. In contrast, there was little evidence of validity in infant tasks or tasks focused on intuitive physics or mental state reasoning. Nevertheless, our results suggest that our approach to assessment design is effective at producing tasks that are internally consistent and sensitive to individual differences within cohort. By making our testing materials and data freely accessible, we hope to provide a foundation for the development of tools for studying cognitive development in field settings.

articles.title: Digital (self-)nudging: A framework for a continuum of user agency
articles.authors: David Joachim Grüning; Friederike Stock; Vincent Beermann; Jan Enkmann; Philipp Lorenz-Spreen; Stefan Michael Herzog; Paul Schmiedmayer; Amy Orben; Ralph Hertwig
articles.abstract: Digital environments increasingly steer behavior through nudging, which alters choices without necessarily foreclosing any option. Digital nudges demand little effort from users but have been criticized for their opacity, limited adaptability, and potential to undermine autonomy, and their effects vary considerably across users and contexts. Self-nudging has emerged as an alternative emphasizing user agency, by which we mean the extent to which users themselves define the set of environmental changes available to them and select among those changes. We propose a framework that arranges (self-)nudging interventions along a continuum of user agency, with traditional nudging and standard self-nudging at its end points. Along it we distinguish four forms, namely other-directed, guided, recommended, and self-directed choice, differing in who defines the set of options for changing the environment and who selects among them. We argue that the appropriate level of agency depends on the heterogeneity of an intervention's treatment effects, on what researchers know about that heterogeneity, and on what users know about their intervention responses. The framework makes explicit the trade-offs between effectiveness, autonomy, and long-term maintenance of behavior change, guides the design and evaluation of digital interventions, and extends beyond digital settings.

articles.title: Free will: Theory and Practice
articles.authors: Joachim Krueger; Ariella T Reynolds
articles.abstract: This is a book review of ‘The Science of Free Will: How Determinism Affects Everything from the Future of AI to Traffic to God to Bees’ by Samir Varma. The review has been submitted to The American Journal of Psychology.

articles.title: Intention to Participate in Wheelchair Sports Groups Among Individuals With Physical Disabilities
articles.authors: Florence Epiney; Linus Hany; siegfried Nagel; Mirka Henninger; Christoffer Klenk
articles.abstract: Club-based wheelchair sports offer crucial avenues for adapted physical activity for individ-uals with physical disabilities. Yet, research examining participation intention in these set-tings is missing. Addressing this critical gap, we introduced an integration of behaviour change theories within a social-ecological framework to explore predictors of participation intention in adapted physical activity. Employing a cross-sectional exploratory design, survey data were collected from inactive members of the Swiss Paraplegic Association reporting physical disabilities. To capture complex, non-linear, and higher-order interactions, a condi-tional random forest was combined with interpretable machine learning techniques. Results revealed that exercise motivation, loneliness, social support, restrictions due to disability, and exercise self-efficacy are relevant predictors. These findings indicate that while intention represents an individual cognitive state, its formation is also driven by psychosocial factors and the desire to overcome isolation. These insights provide guidance for sports clubs and federations to design interventions to increase APA intention and participation.

articles.title: Statistical learning and rhythmic ability in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Individual differences outweigh group effects
articles.authors: Iris Maria van der Wulp; Marijn Eefje Struiksma; Frank Wijnen
articles.abstract:
Speech segmentation is fundamental to language acquisition and supported by statistical learning (SL). Research on SL is inconclusive as to whether it can occur outside the scope of attention and whether SL is impaired in individuals with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Furthermore, individual differences in SL are hypothesized to be influenced by other cognitive abilities such as musical rhythmic ability (RA) and phonological working memory (WM), which previous literature indicated may be impaired in ADHD. 
	The current study investigated SL in participants diagnosed with ADHD (N = 41) and neurotypical (N = 118) peers, exposing them to an artificial language and assessing SL both during exposure using EEG-measures of neural entrainment, as well as behaviorally after exposure. Furthermore, we explored whether multiple tasks assessing RA and WM were related to SL ability, and how SL related to vocabulary size. 
	Bayesian statistical evidence indicated absence of group differences on SL, RA, WM, and vocabulary. Instead, individual variability outweighed group effects. Combining the groups yielded anecdotal evidence for a positive correlation between SL and vocabulary size, but not between SL and RA or WM. These results suggest that SL operates comparably in our samples of neurotypical individuals and individuals with ADHD, and was not found to be related to tasks assessing RA or WM. Notably, our sample consisted of mostly female participants in both groups. Future studies may want to further examine gender differences in ADHD symptoms and take a dimensional approach to ADHD symptomatology in relation to individual differences in SL ability.

articles.title: Multilevel Reward Prediction Errors Drive Emotional Valence During Perceptual Decision-Making
articles.authors: Thalia Vrantsidis; Alan Voodla; Kimia Sabbagh
articles.abstract: What role do expectations, outcomes, and their mismatches—i.e., reward prediction errors (RPEs)—play in generating emotions? Existing theories make competing predictions, with value-based perspectives suggesting that emotional valence tracks the value of outcomes and expectations, value-updating perspectives suggesting that it instead tracks RPEs, a common value-learning signal, and mixed views suggesting a role for all three factors. Yet empirical tests of these predictions have produced mixed results. Here, we demonstrate how these conflicting results could be explained within a value-updating perspective, as resulting from multiple simultaneous RPEs operating at different levels and timescales. In particular, we build off recent work which suggested that affect in a perceptual decision-making task was influenced by both expectations and outcomes, but not by RPEs. The current study re-evaluates this conclusion, by modifying the original task and analyses to dissociate trial-level and block-level RPEs through their unique temporal dynamics. Results showed that both forms of RPEs drove affect in this task, with no clear effect of expectations or outcomes beyond this, contrary to previous conclusions. These results thus support value-updating perspectives, while highlighting the importance of considering multiple forms of RPEs when accounting for affective valence. Moreover, demonstrating key links between value-updating signals and emotions has broad implications for affective science.

articles.title: Disentangling sociality and communicative meaning in EEG correlates of feedback processing
articles.authors: Corinna Lorenz; Lioba Johanna Catharina Schmücker; Jana Isabelle Braunwarth; Nicola Kristina Ferdinand; Daniela M Pfabigan
articles.abstract:
Previous research has reported a processing advantage for social over non-social stimuli when using culturally overlearned social gestures such as thumbs up/down as feedback stimuli. However, these stimuli confounded sociality with a known communicative meaning and its inherent familiarity, hence it is not clear whether the processing advantage arose from the social nature or the communicative meaning of the stimuli or a combination of both. This pre-registered EEG study aimed to disentangle these two characteristics and investigated whether a processing advantage is also observable for social gestures without previously known communicative meaning. 
Forty-two healthy volunteers (31 women) conducted a time estimation task and received feedback via social-unfamiliar (unknown hand gestures) and nonsocial-unfamiliar (abstract shapes) stimuli, as well as social-familiar stimuli (thumbs up/down) while EEG was recorded. Single-trial Feedback-Related Negativity (FRN) and P300 amplitudes and frontal midline theta (FMΘ) power were extracted to assess early feedback evaluation, cognitive control, and more elaborate processing stages such as working memory updating.
Task performance did not differ between social-unfamiliar and nonsocial-unfamiliar stimuli, but was slightly better for social-familiar stimuli. The FRN differentiating between positive and negative feedback was largest for nonsocial-unfamiliar stimuli, while comparable for both social conditions. In contrast, FMΘ power differentiated between positive and negative feedback only for social-familiar stimuli. For P300 amplitudes, the difference between negative and positive feedback was more pronounced for social-unfamiliar than social-familiar feedback, which was mostly driven by smallest P300 amplitudes after negative social-unfamiliar feedback.
The current results speak against a processing advantage purely driven by the social nature of the stimuli. It seems to be the combined effect of well-known communicative meaning and social stimulus characteristics that leads to the previously proposed processing advantage observed on the behavioral and neural level.

articles.title: Conversational AI Should Fill the White Space in Mental Health Care, Not Replace Humans
articles.authors: Nick Kabrel; Elizabeth Stade; Shannon Wiltsey Stirman; Jaan Aru; Johannes Eichstaedt
articles.abstract: Conversational AI (CAI) is being rapidly deployed in mental healthcare settings, with much of the attention focused on using chatbots to deliver therapy directly to patients. However, we argue that this vision is too narrow and overlooks broader opportunities for CAI to extend existing systems of care. Mental health care systems have struggled for decades with structural gaps outside of immediate therapy delivery. Specifically, we identify opportunities for CAI to support (1) prevention and screening, (2) patients on waitlists, (3) between-session processes during ongoing therapy, and (4) post-treatment aftercare. Patients spend most of their time in these stages where human support is currently the least available. Rather than focusing on replacing clinicians in therapy, we argue that CAI should be strategically integrated into the broader care infrastructure to make the care system more seamless, less burdensome, and increase its capacity, thereby enhancing its effectiveness. We review preliminary studies that suggest that this is plausible. Across stages of healthcare delivery, we highlight specific opportunities and candidate mechanisms for effective and ethical implementation of such blended human-AI care.

articles.title: The balance corpus: An audiovisual collection of 30 adult pairs playing an interactive word-guessing game
articles.authors: Jiahao Eric Yang; Mingtong Li; Susanne Fuchs; Suzanne Aussems
articles.abstract: This paper reports on the development of the balance corpus, a multimodal dataset of adults interacting with either a friend or a stranger under varying postural stability constraints induced via a wobble board manipulation. The dataset comprises 60 adults (30 pairs) who played a word-guessing game (Taboo). The task consisted of four rounds in which participants alternated between the roles of clue-giver and guesser. Each round included 10 trials, resulting in 40 trials per pair and 1,200 in total. In each trial, the clue-giver described a target word while avoiding five semantically related taboo words, and the guesser attempted to identify the target word within a 60-second time limit. The dataset includes fully synchronized audiovisual recordings from two cameras per participant, separately capturing the clue-giver and guesser, alongside speech transcripts, gyroscope recordings from the wobble board, and participant metadata. The metadata includes participants’ demographic characteristics, height, weight, and handedness and footedness. The dataset enables analyses of speech, gesture, body movement, and postural control in face-to-face interaction under varying stability constraints.

articles.title: Coping With Complexity: A Selective Sampling Account of Consideration Set Formation for Product Bundles
articles.authors: Yonatan Vanunu; Oleg Urminsky; Daniel Bartels
articles.abstract: Consumers frequently encounter a variety of products to choose from, and these products are often complex bundles of multiple components. To simplify decisions, consumers sometimes consider only a subset of the products on offer—the consideration set. We propose a selective sampling account of consideration set formation, according to which consumers probabilistically sample information from within each bundle when deciding which alternatives to consider. Converging evidence from six studies and computational modeling shows that consideration set inclusion is shaped by the distribution of values across bundle components, even when total value is similar. Consumers favored bundles with attractive values on highly relevant components, but they also favored bundles with attractive values on less relevant components when those components were made salient by their spatial position in the display, with downstream consequences for the final choice. Importantly, traditional compensatory and non-compensatory models cannot fully capture this behavior. We conclude that consumers cope with complexity by disregarding seemingly less relevant or less salient information, thereby biasing consideration toward bundles with attractive features on the items most likely to be attended to. This suggests a counterintuitive managerial implication: highlighting high-value but less relevant components in the bundle may be especially effective because consumers may otherwise overlook them while selectively paying attention to more relevant components.

articles.title: When Does Cognitive Ability Matter for Vote Choice? Ideological Orientation as a Moderator in the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Till Lubczyk; André Kretzschmar
articles.abstract: Cognitive ability predicts vote choice, but does it do so equally across the ideological spectrum? In a preregistered longitudinal study, U.S. young adults (N = 594) completed a broad cognitive ability assessment and five ideology measures (right-wing authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, social and economic conservatism, political self-placement) before the 2024 presidential election and reported their vote afterwards. Lower cognitive ability and stronger right-wing orientations each predicted voting for Trump, replicating prior findings; these associations held when controlling for demographics, including education and household income. Critically, Local Structural Equation Modeling revealed that ideology moderated the cognitive ability-vote choice association: it was robust among liberal and moderate voters but faded to near zero at high levels of right-wing commitment for four of five measures. The findings are consistent with motivated cognition accounts and challenge the assumption that reasoning ability plays a uniform role in electoral decision-making.

articles.title: What makes preventative psychosocial interventions acceptable to young people exposed to Adverse Childhood Experiences? A scoping review
articles.authors: Tom A. Jenkins; Jeffrey Lambert; Chloe Hampshire; Tom Freeman; Sarah Halligan; Lisa Price`; Caledonia Swindells-Macleod; Pamela Charlotte Jacobsen
articles.abstract:
Background: Exposure to Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) is a risk factor for the development of both common and severe mental health problems. Interventions delivered before a person has developed a need for care from services could help prevent onset of mental health difficulties. Understanding what makes an intervention acceptable to a young person is key to designing interventions likely to achieve good real-world uptake. This review aimed to synthesise what is known about factors which make psychosocial interventions acceptable to young people exposed to ACEs. 

Methods: We conducted a scoping review by searching electronic databases (Pubmed, APA PsychNET, Scopus) for studies reporting quantitative and/or qualitative data on acceptability of psychosocial interventions delivered to young people (aged 12-25) with a history of ACEs, outside of clinical services. Quantitative data on acceptability were synthesised using descriptive statistics, and qualitative data were synthesised using thematic synthesis. Recommendations based on findings were co-produced with a youth advisory group to inform effective implementation of such interventions. 

Results: Twenty-four studies from 16 countries describing a range of psychosocial interventions were included. Factors associated with acceptability were: ‘Personal relevance and readiness: the right intervention at the right time’, ‘Accessibility and inclusivity: removing barriers to participation’, ‘Empathic and therapeutic relationships’, and ‘Person-centred intervention content’. Co-produced recommendations for practice included: taking time to understand accessibility needs, investing time in relationship-building, and providing opportunity for participant choice. 

Conclusion: Findings highlight that interventions which are relevant, accessible, person-centred, and foster positive therapeutic relationships are more likely to be acceptable to young people with ACEs.  

Review Registration: The review was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework on 12th June 2025 before searches were ran: https://osf.io/ypbd9/registrations

articles.title: The emotional experience of time: Effects of anxiety and interoceptive ability on temporal perception
articles.authors: Gaia Lapomarda; Alessio Fracasso; Carmen Morawetz; Alessandro Grecucci; David Melcher
articles.abstract: Our experience of time is deeply shaped by emotional and bodily states. Anxiety is known to distort our temporal perception, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we tested whether interoception links anxiety to variability in timing. Thirty participants underwent fMRI while performing a temporal reproduction task within a modified Threat of Scream paradigm. Safe and Threat blocks alternated, with aversive screams unpredictably delivered during Threat blocks. Screams reliably increased subjective anxiety and engaged salience and limbic regions, including the amygdala, hippocampus, and insula. Despite these affective and neural responses, Threat did not produce systematic changes in temporal accuracy. Instead, individuals with higher interoceptive accuracy tended to preserve reproduction accuracy under elevated anxiety, implicating an interoceptive contribution to anxiety-related variability in timing. At the neural level, reproduction compared with the encoding phase increased activity in sensorimotor and parietal regions, with engagement of the insula, cingulate, and striato-thalamic regions in the Safe context. Under Threat, the same contrast encompassed a more circumscribed set of sensorimotor and parietal regions, and screams robustly recruited a salience–limbic–temporal network relative to both non-emotional tones. Together, these findings suggest that individual differences in interoceptive accuracy may moderate the relationship between anxiety and temporal reproduction, and characterise the neural response to threat during a timing task.

articles.title: The vegetative state is not a state of mind
articles.authors: Martin M Monti; Caroline Schnakers; Nicholas D. Schiff; Yelena G Bodien
articles.abstract: The discovery of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) has revealed a conceptual inconsistency at the heart of disorders of consciousness (DoC) nosology. Advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that behavioral unresponsiveness does not necessarily imply the absence of consciousness or cognitive capacity, yet contemporary diagnostic categories continue conflating responsiveness with consciousness itself. This conflation is embedded throughout DoC nomenclature, where behavioral syndromes such as the vegetative state (VS) and minimally conscious state (MCS) transform observations of what patients do (or do not do) into inferences about what they experience (i.e., their state of mind). We argue that this category error now impedes the translation of over two decades of scientific advances into a coherent clinical framework.
