First, it has fostered the widespread but incorrect conflation of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD), despite the fact that the two concepts identify different patient populations and may carry distinct implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. Second, it renders contemporary DoC nosology incapable of coherently incorporating modern neuroimaging and electrophysiological findings. Because the absence of consciousness is an entrenched, definitional component of the vegetative state (VS), its behavioral phenotype cannot be reconciled with covert neurophysiological phenotypes such as CC and CMD. As a result, current nomenclature impedes the development of a phenotype-endotype framework in which bedside behavioral classifications are complemented by biologically informed categories derived from advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological assessments. We trace the origins of this problem to a historical shift whereby the definitions of vegetative state and minimally conscious state evolved from descriptions of observable behavior into claims about a patient's mental state. Disentangling responsiveness from consciousness, we argue, is essential if the field is to incorporate contemporary evidence and develop a coherent, biologically informed nosology of disorders of consciousness.

articles.title: Varieties of generalization inspired by Pavlov’s legacy
articles.authors: Gonzalo Pablo Urcelay; Courteney Tiegan Louise Fisher; José A. Alcalá
articles.abstract: In this selective review, we summarise recent studies from our laboratory in which we have assessed the effect of different variables (such as contiguity and contingency) on the generalization of prior learning. Much of this work was inspired by Pavlov’s work in which it was first documented that trace conditioning can broaden generalization, a finding that we have replicated in human participants. We then describe studies in which we have assessed whether the affective valence of stimuli and outcomes can affect generalization, and we find that indeed human participants can generalize across the valence of stimuli and this can interact with different outcomes. Finally, we review a study in which we assessed whether changes in a response-produced safety signal can influence avoidance and conclude that it does. We also observed that this generalizes and this depends on the similarity between trained and tested safety signals (i.e., outcomes). Overall, we conclude that generalization is a much more complex phenomenon than previously thoughts, and that more research is needed to understand this phenomenon and make it amenable to current theorising.

articles.title: Perceived Artificiality Markedly Reduces Trustworthiness but Only Minimally Affects Attractiveness in AI-Synthetic Faces
articles.authors: Jiaxin Wang; Satoshi Nishida
articles.abstract: With the spread of artificial intelligence (AI)-synthesized human faces in digital communication, researchers have begun to investigate the associations of the perceived artificiality of such faces with their social evaluations, finding that artificial faces tend to be perceived as less trustworthy and attractive. However, as facial trustworthiness and attractiveness are strongly correlated, it is unclear which dimension is more strongly influenced by perceived artificiality once the correlation between trustworthiness and attractiveness is controlled. Accordingly, we collected the manual ratings by 100 participants of the perceived artificiality, trustworthiness, and attractiveness of 500 AI-synthesized faces and analyzed the unique pairwise associations among these variables using participant-wise partial correlation and generalized estimating equation analyses. Perceived artificiality showed a robust negative association with trustworthiness even after controlling for attractiveness, whereas the association between artificiality and attractiveness was much weaker and negligible in magnitude after controlling for trustworthiness. These results suggest that artificial cues predominantly influence social trust rather than aesthetic evaluation. Our findings offer important insights into the distinct psychological role of perceived artificiality in social face perception.

articles.title: Historical Stereotype Change is Tied to the Entry and Exit of Distributed Group Concepts
articles.authors: Shiyao Wang; Joshua Conrad Jackson; Xuechunzi Bai
articles.abstract: Stereotype change is usually characterized using broad dimensions such as warmth and competence. We argue that these evaluative stereotypes rest on a richer web of group-related associations that we call distributional stereotypes. Using decade-specific word embeddings trained on 385 million words of historical American English, we trace the distributional stereotypes of 12 national groups across a century. Three findings emerge. First, distributional and evaluative stereotypes are correlated, but distributional stereotypes preserve historically specific content that evaluative stereotypes do not capture. Second, distributional stereotypes change primarily as group-related concepts enter and exit the cultural record, rather than because persistent concepts become more positive or negative. Third, distributional stereotypes are more strongly associated with groups’ occupational outcomes, whereas evaluative stereotypes are more strongly associated with their treatment in political discourse. Stereotypes are evolving networks of culturally available ideas that ebb and flow with historical events.

articles.title: Autistic children and adolescents have difficulty perceiving speech in social and non-social noise
articles.authors: Yurika Tsuji; Shu Imaizumi
articles.abstract: Difficulty perceiving speech in noisy environments is common in autistic individuals and may be associated with an attentional bias toward non-social stimuli. Our previous study found no interactive effect of social and non-social noise on the relationship between autistic traits and difficulties perceiving speech in noise. However, this effect may be observed in autistic children and adolescents, who have a greater attentional bias than individuals with high autistic traits in the general population. In this context, this study tested two hypotheses: (1) autistic children and adolescents show greater difficulty perceiving speech in noisy environments than their non-autistic peers, and (2) they experience greater difficulty perceiving speech in non-vocal noise than in vocal noise. Participants detected words embedded in vocal and non-vocal background noise. Autistic participants had greater difficulty with speech perception in noisy environments than their non-autistic peers, thus supporting the first hypothesis. This difference is not explained by speech perception in silence or by a preference for noise. Our second hypothesis was not supported, which is consistent with the results of our previous study. Autistic children experienced difficulty perceiving speech in both vocal and non-vocal noise. These results suggest that difficulty perceiving speech in noise may be explained by autistic traits other than an attentional bias toward non-vocal sounds.

articles.title: Recontextualizing Cultural Humility in the Japanese Counseling Context: Development and Validation of the MCHS-J
articles.authors: Yuni Eeh; Miho Tahakashi
articles.abstract: Cultural humility offers a framework for counselors to examine their cultural assumptions and attend to intercultural dimensions of practice. In Japan, however, research has focused on clients’ adjustment, with less attention to counselors’ reflective development. This study developed the Japanese Multidimensional Cultural Humility Scale (MCHS-J) and examined cultural humility among 126 Japanese mental health practitioners and trainees. Target-rotated exploratory structural equation modeling supported an 11-item, four-factor structure comprising Openness, Self-Awareness, Egolessness, and Self-Reflection and Critique; one Openness item and the Supportive Interactions dimension were not retained. Reliability was acceptable, and associations with intercultural sensitivity and working alliance held after controlling for socially desirable responding. The retained dimensions all represent an internally oriented, reflective stance, whereas the dimension defined by explicitly negotiating relational conflict was not reproduced, paralleling its weakness in the original and Korean versions. This suggests that the inward, reflective side of cultural humility may hold across cultures, whereas how counselors are expected to handle relational conflict may depend more on local norms. The MCHS-J offers a preliminary foundation for research and reflective practice.

articles.title: When and why stimulus repetition does not lead to learning
articles.authors: Chaoxiong Ye; Liu Qiang; Robert H Logie
articles.abstract: Three experiments investigated absence and presence of learning from multiple repeated presentations. Typically, recall of a verbal list or visual array improves with as few as six repetitions of the same stimulus. However, recognition paradigms have shown no learning with 60 or more repetitions of the same stimulus. Ye et al. (2026) reported no performance improvements and no awareness of repetition across 120 repetition trials with a 500 ms study-test interval for change detection. With longer study-test intervals only some participants improved performance. We explored whether lack of learning arose from short study-test intervals, or forgetting during longer inter-trial intervals. General working memory capacity (OSPAN) was assessed for each participant. Study-test, not inter-trial, intervals modulated absence or presence of learning and repetition awareness. OSPAN correlated with performance only when learning was observed. These new results highlight the importance of strategy differences in how participants perform cognitive tasks, that are not apparent in aggregate group data. Results also are consistent with the Ye et al. (2026; Logie, 1995; Shimi & Logie, 2019) proposal that lack of learning across repetitions reflects a temporary visual cache memory within a trial, the contents of which are over-written by the array on the next trial, even if arrays are identical. A weak episodic memory is formed but cannot support performance unless cumulative strengthening across trials reaches a threshold for observable learning. General working memory capacity for encoding and retrieval is engaged only if participants show learning and awareness of the array repetition.

articles.title: Moving On Up: Momentary Physical Activity Predicts Proximal Affect and Emotion Regulation in Remitted Depression
articles.authors: Sean Minns; Sarah Zapetis; Srinidhi Jayakumar; Ellie P. Xu; Margarid R. Turnamian; Jiani Li; Mengzhe Wei; Archita Tharanipathy; Desiree E. Webb; Genevieve Fridlund Dunton
articles.abstract: Reduced physical activity is a persistent feature of major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its momentary emotional and regulatory consequences remain poorly understood, especially after remission. Across one week, young adults with remitted depression (rMDD; n = 49) and never-depressed controls (n = 40) reported affect and emotion regulation three times daily while wearing a Hexoskin torso-mounted accelerometer. Mean activity level and activity variability were derived from the continuous accelerometer signal in the 30 minutes preceding each assessment. Within individuals, increases in physical activity predicted more high-arousal positive affect and less low-arousal negative affect, while activity variability predicted emotion regulation strategy use. Depression history and current symptoms moderated these associations, with the rMDD group exhibiting a stronger physical activity–positive affect link. These findings provide the first evidence that momentary physical activity patterns predict both adaptive and maladaptive emotion regulation, highlighting activity variability as an overlooked dimension relevant to depression risk.

articles.title: Confirmatory Matrix Factorization
articles.authors: Changsheng Chen; Robbe D’hondt; Alireza Gharahighehi; Sameh Metwaly; Celine Vens; Wim Van Den Noortgate
articles.abstract: Recent advances in assessments have challenged traditional psychometric methods in analyzing high-dimensional sparse data and achieving accurate predictions. Meanwhile, machine learning methods, such as Matrix Factorization (MF) sharing similarities with the common factor model, show promising potential for addressing those challenges but lack interpretability. To fill this gap, we propose Confirmatory Matrix Factorization (CMF) as a computational psychometric method based on MF and compare it to Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and Confirmatory Penalized Factor Analysis (CPFA). The comparison is based on 48,600 data sets generated by the common factor model under various characteristics, alongside two real data sets. The results show that CFA and CPFA struggles with non-convergence in high-dimensional sparse data, whereas CMF performs effectively with high computation efficiency. CMF generally outperforms CFA and CPFA regarding prediction performance in most cases. CMF can successfully recover factor loadings and the estimated factor scores from three methods are comparable. Additionally, missing values negatively affect the performance of the three methods. Overall, CMF can be an interpretable and robust alternative to CFA and CPFA, particularly in emerging assessments where CFA and CPFA is less effective.

articles.title: Seeing Beyond Replication Success: A Framework for Evaluating Multi-Lab Replication Outcomes Using Meta-Analytic Bayes Factors
articles.authors: Naike Wang
articles.abstract: This study introduces a new replication success classification framework for multi-lab replication studies that goes beyond the traditional binary distinction of replication success and failure. The framework distinguishes between true and false replication successes and failures, revealing the underlying composition of observed replication results and how they are shaped by study-level factors in both the original and replication studies. Using a large-scale simulation, we evaluated four meta-analytic Bayes factor (MABF) methods as tools for determining replication success within this framework. Results showed that the MABF methods were generally more effective at ruling out spurious effects than at confirming small true effects. The one-sided fixed-effect meta-analytic Bayes factor and the inclusion Bayes factor methods most reliably identified genuine replication success. The framework illustrates how bias and methodological choices influence the underlying composition of replication outcomes. These findings provide a more nuanced understanding of replication results and offer practical guidance for designing and evaluating future large-scale replication projects to strengthen research reproducibility.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Self-Consciousness Across Offline and Social Media Contexts
articles.authors: Phoebe Loew; Cameron James Bunker
articles.abstract: Women tend to be more self-conscious than men. Drawing on Whole Trait Theory, we show, however, that gender differences in self-consciousness manifest differently between offline and social media contexts. Participants (Studies 1 and 2; N = 2,770; 58% women) completed context-framed measures of self-consciousness specified to indicate a) offline and b) social media contexts in c) private (i.e., concerning internal states) and d) public (i.e., concerning external appearance) senses. Findings showed that both women and men were more privately and publicly self-conscious offline than on social media. However, public self-consciousness was pronounced on social media in women relative to men (Study 1). Greater femininity also predicted greater public self-consciousness, which, in turn, was more pronounced than private self-consciousness on social media (Study 2), suggesting effects beyond gender categories. We corroborated these findings with women’s qualitative experiences, which further suggested the prominent role of image-based platforms and attempts to manage self-consciousness online (Study 3; N = 37, 76% women). Our findings imply unique gender dynamics in self-consciousness, centering women’s public self-consciousness on social media.

articles.title: Subjective effects of flicker light do not differ between open- and closed-eye viewing
articles.authors: James Thurbon; Annabelle Mitchell; Jordan J Wehrman; Vince Polito
articles.abstract: Flicker light stimulation shows promise for inducing visual imagery, altered states of consciousness, and changes in arousal, with potential applications in relaxation and imagery-based therapeutic interventions. However, optimal utility depends on identifying how viewing conditions shape subjective and physiological outcomes. We examined whether eye condition (open, closed) modulates subjective and autonomic responses to 15 Hz audiovisual flicker. Methods. In a preregistered mixed-design experiment, 68 participants were assigned to eyes-open or eyes-closed conditions and completed two 10-minute tasks: a 15 Hz visual flicker with white noise and a passive rest control. Measures included visual imagery, altered consciousness, relaxation, and skin conductance level (SCL) as an index of physiological arousal. Results. Bayesian analyses supported no difference between eye conditions in ratings of visual imagery, altered consciousness and relaxation. Flicker increased SCL and decreased ratings of relaxation compared to control, however free reports indicated variable tension and relaxation responses. Across tasks and eye conditions, SCL exhibited a logarithmic habituation pattern. Greater reductions in SCL over time occurred for eyes closed compared to eyes open, however, SCL was not related to any subjective measures. Implications. Eye condition impacted the physiological but not phenomenological effects of flicker. Flicker protocols may be implemented flexibly across eye conditions without meaningfully altering subjective outcomes, supporting use in both experimental and applied settings. Relaxation during flicker may depend on individual characteristics. The logarithmic habituation of SCL suggests that autonomic responses to flicker diminish with continued exposure, which may inform stimulation duration in experimental and therapeutic applications.

articles.title: Sonority-driven stress: codas in Brazilian Portuguese
articles.authors: Guilherme D. Garcia; Kevin Ryan
articles.abstract: This study provides experimental evidence for sonority-driven stress in Brazilian Portuguese (BP). We show that speakers systematically prefer final stress when the ultima contains a sonorant coda {N, l, r} rather than the obstruent coda {s}. The effect is specific to the ultima, the position where weight is otherwise most relevant to BP stress. A lexical analysis of monomorphemic words corroborates the experimental pattern: /s/-final words receive final stress less often than sonorant-final words. We further show that this asymmetry cannot be reduced to morphological factors (the plural suffix /-s/ is invisible to stress), nor to a sonority-free account on which final /s/ is a prosodic appendix. These findings bear on a contested question in metrical phonology (whether, and how, segmental sonority conditions stress placement), on which experimental evidence has so far been scarce.

articles.title: Tracking Attribute Mastery Change among Individuals: Multilevel Longitudinal Diagnostic Classification Model with Random Intercepts
articles.authors: Kazuhiro Yamaguchi; Haruhiko Mitsunaga; Shun Saso; Yuri Uesaka
articles.abstract: Tracking an individual’s learning status is important to ensure improvement. reviously developed multilevel or longitudinal diagnostic classification models (LDCMs) incorporated group-level structures or modeled longitudinal change through continuous latent traits underlying attribute mastery probabilities. However, the interpretation of attribute mastery transitions as within-individual processes has not been fully considered. Therefore, the RI-LDCM was developed by considering such group- and individual-level variations as random intercepts (RI) in the measurement model. A Bayesian estimation method for the RI-LDCM was also developed. A simulation study revealed that ignoring multilevel structures causes biased parameter estimates and serious under-coverage of posterior credible intervals. A real data example provided attribute mastery transitions from the four-year longitudinal data of mathematics tests in the third to sixth grades of Japanese elementary schools. The extensibility and limitation of the RI-LDCM were also discussed.

articles.title: Social inference in an empty room: children use indirect evidence to infer an agent’s past actions
articles.authors: Colin Jacobs; Mack Briscoe; Rosie Aboody; Julian Jara-Ettinger
articles.abstract: People’s actions often leave physical traces (e.g., footprints in the mud, a dirty mug) that adults can use to reconstruct what another person was doing, what their goals were, and what they knew. Here we test whether children can make these inferences in cases that require going beyond a direct mapping from traces to actions, focusing on reasoning about a conspicuous absence of evidence, and relying on an agent’s preferences to interpret physical traces that are otherwise ambiguous. In Experiment 1, five- and six-year-olds inferred that an agent had lifted a rock-filled bowl or a rice-filled bowl when they saw the corresponding physical trace (i.e., rocks or rice spilled on the table). Critically, when no traces were left behind, children also inferred that the agent had lifted the rock-filled bowl, suggesting they understood that this action was less likely to produce observable evidence. Experiments 2 and 3 then show that children can integrate the agent’s preferences when the physical evidence alone does not reveal what happened. Our results suggest that, by age five, children begin to draw social inferences from indirect evidence by integrating physical and social reasoning.

articles.title: Statistical learning generalizes across phonological context and transfers to vowel production
articles.authors: Lin Zhou; Nazbanou Nozari; Lori L. Holt
articles.abstract: Recent experience rapidly shapes speech perception, but whether this learning influences speech production remains a central question for sensorimotor theories of speech. Prior work has shown that dimension-based statistical learning can transfer from perception to production for consonants. The present research tested whether this transfer extends to vowels and to vowel duration, a temporal dimension whose role in speech motor control is not fully specified in current models. Across four experiments, listeners were passively exposed to short-term distributional regularities that either preserved or reversed the typical English relationship between spectral quality and duration for /æ/–/ɛ/ vowels. Exposure to the reversed regularity reduced listeners’ reliance on duration in vowel categorization and reduced durational differentiation in their own vowel productions. These perception–production effects replicated across four experiments. Experiments 2–4 further showed that learning generalized beyond the exposure context to novel phonological environments that varied in coda, onset–coda context, and segmental structure, and that this generalized learning also transferred to production. The findings indicate that statistical regularities in others’ speech can dynamically reshape the weighting of temporal information in both vowel perception and production, placing new constraints on sensorimotor accounts of speech learning and control.

articles.title: Reimagining Care for Community Members Who Use Substances:  An Application of the Indigenist Ecological Systems Model
articles.authors: Jillian Fish; Andrea Medley; Monica M. Desjardin; Miigis Gonzalez; Rachel E. Wilbur; Melissa L. Walls; Emily E Haroz
articles.abstract:
Background. Indigenous communities experience disproportionate substance use-related harms. Eurocentric approaches often inadequately address these inequities because of their fragmented focus, limited cultural responsiveness, and erasure of Indigenous Knowledges. Consequently, interventions frequently overlook the relational nature of Indigenous well-being. We reimagine care for community members who use substances through the Indigenist Ecological Systems Model, a socioecological framework that centers Indigenous histories, Knowledges, and interdependent-relational ethics.
Methods. The Indigenist model centers history and culture, rather than the individual, as the foundation of well-being. Following history and culture are the remaining ecological levels: Indigenous Peoples, then immediate, surrounding, and distant environments. This framework reflects an Indigenous understanding of wellness as emerging through relationships with ancestors, families, communities, lands, and more-than-human relatives.
Conclusions. The Indigenist model advances a paradigm shift in substance use research by moving from individualistic to relational, community-centered approaches; from deficit- to strengths-based perspectives; and from Eurocentric epistemologies to Indigenous Knowledges as sources of scientific innovation. We conclude by outlining core tenets of an Indigenist approach to substance use care that acknowledges the relational nature of healing while addressing root causes.

articles.title: Queer Individuals Perception of Heteronormativity in Literature and the Development of a Conceptual Model: Model of Heteronormative Impact on Social Representation and Emotion (HIRSE)
articles.authors: Brontë Rapps; Genavee Brown
articles.abstract: Heteronormativity reinforces and encourages the gender binary and heterosexuality, resulting in discrimination and marginalization; particularly towards women and queer minorities. We utilized a design probe booklet with quotes from literature that was completed by eight LGBTQIA+ participants. Thematic analysis was conducted. Two primary themes were produced: Societal Representation (Perpetuated, Hierarchical, Restrictive, and Coerced), and Emotional Impact (Demeaning, Resistant, and Resilient). From these themes, we produced a conceptual model, Model of Heteronormative Impact on Social Representation and Emotion (HISRE) that examines heteronormativity’s impact on queer individuals. In sum, our work advances understanding of how queer people recognize and respond to heteronormativity in literature.

articles.title: Measuring Psychotic Experiences at Scale: An Item Response Theory Analysis of the Adolescent Psychotic-like Symptom Screener (APSS)
articles.authors: Joshua B Gilbert; Zachary Himmelsbach; Nicole R. DeTore; Randi M. Schuster
articles.abstract: The Adolescent Psychotic-like Symptom Screener (APSS) is widely used to screen adolescents for psychotic experiences (PEs), but there are few rigorous psychometric analyses of the instrument. In this study, we apply Item Response Theory (IRT) to APSS responses from a large sample of middle and high school students in Massachusetts (N = 37,359, 49% male, mean age 14.9 years). We compare polytomous IRT models, evaluate item and test functioning, test for differential item functioning (DIF), and examine demographic predictors of PEs. We find that the data are consistent with unidimensionality and a graded response model fits the data well. Reliability is maximized about 1.5 standard deviations above the mean and is poor at low trait levels. We identify two practically significant DIF terms by sex, but they operate in opposite directions and are unlikely to generate large biases in overall scores. Latent regression analyses show that older students and male students report slightly lower levels of PEs, with a modest sex-by-age interaction. Our results support the use of the APSS as an efficient screener for identifying adolescents with elevated PEs who may benefit from further assessment, while cautioning that it is not well suited to distinguish participants with low PEs.

articles.title: Reinforcement learning underlies social connection and memory in a friendship decision-making task
articles.authors: Courtney A. Jimenez; Meghan L Meyer
articles.abstract: Who we choose to befriend can impact many of our own life outcomes, from social capital to wellbeing. Here we find that reinforcement learning principles can characterize friendship decision-making and predict social connection and memory for a potential friend. Participants completed a novel friendship decision-making paradigm in which they observed video clips from the reality TV show, The Valley, depicting a clique of friends navigating friendship with a specific character, Kristen. The clips were normed to vary in the reward value of friendship with Kristen. For each scene, participants decided whether they would want to be friends with Kristen and how connected they felt to her. One day later, they completed surprise memory tests and individual-difference measures. The reward, expected value, and prediction error of a scene about Kristen predicted participants’ feelings of connection to her. Individual differences relevant to friendship formation—concern over relationship acceptance and social support receipt—corresponded with differences in exploratory versus exploitative friendship decision-making (inverse temperature) and flexibility in learning about Kristen (learning rate). Finally, memory showed a negativity bias. Participants more accurately recalled scenes characterized by lower friendship reward and larger negative friendship prediction errors. Together, these findings suggest that friendship formation can be viewed as a learning problem: people continuously update expectations about friendship with others, and those updates shape both social connection and memory. Computational principles that help us learn about rewards in the world may also help shape who we fold into our social world.

articles.title: Editorial Perspective: Connecting Transdiagnostic Mechanisms Targeted in Cognitive Behavioral Therapies with Empirically-Based Symptom Dimensions
articles.authors: Kasey Stanton; Jack D Burke; Helena Towne; Isabella Whitesides
articles.abstract: Various avenues of transdiagnostic research hold promise for improving diagnosis and treatment but remain fragmented in some ways. We provide recommendations for integrating dimensional assessment guided by the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology framework (HiTOP) into clinical practice by more effectively connecting the HiTOP with social-cognitive vulnerability (SCV) mechanisms targeted in cognitive behavioral and third-wave therapies. Specifically, we present concrete ideas for (a) more comprehensively understanding HiTOP symptom dimension-SCV associations, (b) integrating measure development efforts spanning the HiTOP and SCV literatures, and (c) sharpening terminology for improving construct description and clinical communication. We draw on studies from this special issue on Transdiagnostic Approaches to Child and Adolescent Mental Health that provide helpful examples illustrating these points, and we use these study examples to demonstrate how HiTOP-based assessment connects with personalized treatment planning.

articles.title: No evidence for attentional prioritization in visual working memory through statistical learning
articles.authors: Chris Jungerius; Freek van Ede; Heleen A Slagter
articles.abstract: It is well-established that learning grounded in statistical regularities in the world can implicitly bias selective attention when oriented externally to the contents of perception. However, it remains an open question whether statistical learning can similarly bias internally oriented selective attention within working memory. To answer this question, across multiple experiments, we tested participants’ performance on established visual working memory tasks in which the relevance of two items for an upcoming behavioral task was implicitly predicted by the combination of the two items held in working memory (Exp 1 and 2a-b), an implicit retro-cue (Exp 3), or implicit temporal cueing (Exp 4). Across experiments, we found no robust evidence that statistical learning can bias internal attentional prioritization of contents held in working memory. We interpret these findings from the perspective that internal and external attention involve qualitatively different information selection mechanisms, operating to solve different goals.

articles.title: Large Language Models Reveal the Content and Consistency of Suicidal Thoughts: A Two- Study Longitudinal Investigation Among Adolescents and Young Adults
articles.authors: Leily Marieh Behbehani; Ruben van Genugten; Frances Grace Hart; Sharina Hamm; Kathryn Fox; Shirley B Wang
articles.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of death. Measurement of suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs) relies on self-report (e.g., “How strong is your urge to kill yourself right now?”), yet little is known about how individuals translate internal experiences into numerical ratings. We used large language models (LLMs) to examine the content and consistency of suicide urges across severity ratings, between people, and over time. Participants with past-year STBs (Study 1: N=158 adolescents, Study 2: N=202 young adults) completed open-ended questions at baseline and follow-ups. We developed a two-stage topic-modeling pipeline and identified 13 (Study 1) and 14 (Study 2) topics reflecting suicidal thought content (e.g., Family/Friends Reactions, Depressed & Exhausted). Within- and between-person consistency were U-shaped, with highest agreement at endpoints of the scale. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs for advancing measurement of suicide risk and our understanding of how people interpret and respond to self-report rating scales.

articles.title: A Test of the 2 × 2 Model of Perfectionism in Predicting Distress among Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles.abstract: Perfectionism has been consistently linked to psychological distress, yet most evidence in the Philippine context relies on cross-sectional designs, limiting temporal conclusions. Licensure examinations in the Philippines, such as the Psychometrician Licensure Examination mandated by Republic Act No. 10029 (2009), represent a high-stakes evaluative context that may amplify perfectionistic tendencies. The present study tested the 2 × 2 model of perfectionism among 315 licensure examination reviewees, examining how Evaluative Concerns Perfectionism (ECP) and Personal Standards Perfectionism (PSP) predicted Time 2 overall distress, anxiety, and depression after a one-month interval. ECP was a significant positive predictor of all three outcomes, whereas PSP was not. Consistent with the 2 × 2 model, Pure PSP did not differ from Non-perfectionism, while Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism are associated significantly greater distress, anxiety, and depression than Non-perfectionism and Pure PSP. Notably, Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism did not significantly differ, lending support to the aggravating factor hypothesis. These findings underscore that ECP, rather than PSP, drive psychological distress in high-stakes evaluative contexts.

articles.title: Cracking the multidimensionality of cognition with cross-domain transfer
articles.authors: Soroush Mirjalili; Dobromir Rahnev; Audrey Duarte
articles.abstract: Higher-order cognition emerges from the interaction of multiple cognitive processes, yet these processes remain difficult to measure during ongoing task performance. Recent work across humans, non-human animals, and artificial neural networks suggests that cognition is compositional and that cognitive processes are represented by abstract, reusable neural representations that generalize across tasks. These findings show that it is possible to decode neural signatures of a specific cognitive process in one task and covertly track its engagement in another, an approach we term cross-domain transfer. Here, we argue that cross-domain transfer provides a unifying framework for studying cognition as a system of reusable cognitive processes. We place cross-domain transfer within the broader evolution of cognitive decoding methods, discuss its theoretical foundations, and synthesize emerging evidence across cognitive domains. This framework provides new opportunities to test mechanistic theories of cognition and develop more interpretable, process-level approaches for real-time cognitive monitoring and intervention.

articles.title: A Mixed Methods Study Clarifying Clinicians’ Definitions of Harm Reduction and Related Clinician Characteristics
articles.authors: Jennifer T. Grant Weinandy; Peter D. Soyster; Brooke G. Rogers; Sammi Bowers; Linda Nellis; Cassandra L. Boness
articles.abstract: Background: Harm reduction is a vital, evidence-based approach to reducing substance-related harm, yet its clinical implementation remains inconsistent. Prior research examining clinicians' attitudes toward harm reduction has ignored a foundational conceptual gap: the lack of a shared, operational definition. This mixed-methods study aimed to clarify how clinicians define harm reduction and identify the individual provider characteristics associated with these definitions. Methods: A sample of practicing clinicians (N=174; Mean age=38, SD=13; 79% White, 60% women) completed a cross-sectional online survey. Using qualitative thematic analysis, we explored clinicians' open-ended definitions of harm reduction. Concurrently, exploratory quantitative analysis assessed the breadth of specific harm reduction strategies clinicians endorsed and the provider characteristics associated with endorsement. Results: Clinicians generally conceptualized harm reduction as a personalized, broad approach to limit harm (11 subthemes identified). However, a persistent, underlying preference for abstinence that functionally constrained this broad definition also appeared. Endorsing a broader range of strategies was positively associated with years of clinical experience and reporting personal or familial experience with addiction. Endorsing a narrower range of strategies was positively associated with holding a non-doctoral degree and identifying with a more conservative political ideology. Conclusions: The operational definition of harm reduction varies significantly among clinicians, with a bias toward abstinence that may undermine harm reduction implementation fidelity. Narrower conceptualizations reflect not only clinical knowledge deficits but also ideological frameworks, professional training, and potential semantic "label aversion." Future efforts to standardize care must move beyond skills acquisition and investigate conceptually rigorous, values-based training.

articles.title: Investigating the effect of text appearance on visual search for typos
articles.authors: Emily Heffernan; Anna Kosovicheva; Benjamin Wolfe
articles.abstract:
We engage in visual search in many daily activities, from hunting for keys to scanning
a grocery list for missed items. A subset of these search tasks (e.g., looking through a grocery
list) additionally intersect with the process of reading, requiring the observer to recognize text as
they search for a target. In these settings, how do manipulations of text appearance, which
normally affect reading performance, affect the visual search process? The present study uses a
modified version of a real-world visual search task, typo detection, to examine how stimulus font
impacts performance. One possibility is that hard-to-read fonts could hinder typo detection by
either impeding word identification or shifting quitting thresholds. Alternatively, hard-to-read
fonts could, counterintuitively, facilitate typo detection by slowing the reader down and requiring
more effortful processing. Across two different experiments, participants searched for typos in
blocks of text that varied in stroke contrast (Experiment 1) and letter width (Experiment 2).
Across both experiments, font did not impact accuracy, but participants were slower to respond
after fixating typos written in hard- versus easy-to-read fonts. Hierarchical drift diffusion
modelling isolated the mechanism underlying this difference: in Experiment 2, the rate of
evidence accumulation was significantly lower for hard- versus easy-to-read trials, while non-
decision time and decision threshold were unimpacted. These findings reveal that, though one’s
typo detection performance may be robust to changes in text appearance, there are subtle
differences in the rate of processing stimuli that impact the time course of target identification.

articles.title: “I Had to Figure It Out Alone”: A Qualitative Exploration of Fathers’ Experiences, Unmet Support Needs, and Digital Intervention Preferences during Early Fatherhood in Canada
articles.authors: Emily E Cameron; Kaeley M. Simpson; Kailey Elena Penner; Lianne Tomfohr-Madsen; Kristin Reynolds; James M. Bolton; Jon McGavock; Corey S. Mackenzie; Joshua Madsen; Ryan Jeffrey Giuliano
articles.abstract: Background: Fathers experience elevated rates of mental health concerns during the transition to parenthood, putting children at risk for adverse outcomes. Yet father-specific mental health supports are limited. Efforts to provide tailored supports are needed, including patient-oriented approaches that can improve future treatment adherence, better meet fathers’ needs, and support clinical uptake. Methods: This qualitative study examined the unmet mental health and parenting needs of Canadian fathers with young children (0-3 years old). Eligible participants had past or current lived experience of mental health challenges and/or parenting stress since becoming a parent. Fathers (N=17) from across Canada participated in one of three cohorts. Each cohort completed a six-session virtual focus group series to explore fathers’ experiences of mental health, service use, barriers to support, and preferences for tailored eHealth interventions. Focus groups were audio-recorded and transcribed; written surveys after each session were incorporated into the qualitative analysis. All data was analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Six main themes included limited access and barriers to services, primary unmet support needs, fathers’ mental health, father involvement in the family, mental health service/information experiences, and eHealth intervention needs. Key unmet needs included feeling prepared for fatherhood, managing emotion dysregulation and physical well-being, connecting with peers, accessing tailored mental health and parenting support, and finding affordable childcare. Fathers reported a strong interest in eHealth (app-based) supports with opportunities for peer connection, flexible delivery formats, and access to expert guidance. Conclusions: Findings highlight a significant gap between fathers’ support needs and available services for mental health. This study contributes to ongoing efforts to enhance men’s mental health, reduce stigma, and strengthen early intervention efforts during the transition to fatherhood.

articles.title: Dissociating retina- and face-centered reference frames of human face recognition.
articles.authors: Hélène Dumont; Valerie Goffaux
articles.abstract: Face identity recognition is a core function of the human brain, predominantly driven by horizontally oriented facial cues. While face processing largely operates in a face-centered reference frame, it is not devoid of retinotopic sensitivity. Addressing whether face rotation influences the orientation tuning profile of identity recognition enables a direct empirical test of the reference frame of human face identification. Forty-two young adults performed identity recognition of famous faces filtered to restrict content to narrow orientation bands (i.e., from 0° to 150°, in 30°-steps), and presented either upright, rotated by ±45°, or by ±90° away from upright. If the horizontal face identity information is defined along face-centered coordinates, identity recognition performance should stay tuned to the horizontal irrespective of rotation angle. Any contribution of the retina-centered reference frame should cause the peak of orientation tuning to shift away from the horizontal, in the same direction as the stimulus rotation. While overall identity recognition performance decreased when faces were rotated by ±90° compared to upright and ±45° rotation, it kept broadly tuned to the horizontal range of the face stimulus regardless of rotation angle. However, the advantage of the horizontal over the vertical range decreased significantly for ±90° compared to upright and ±45° rotations. Through the systematic investigation of the orientation tuning parameters across stimulus rotation, the present work provides quantitative evidence that the visual information driving human face-specialized identity recognition is defined within the reference frame of the face-image.

articles.title: Rethinking the depression narrative in menopause research: Delineating the role of depression versus anxiety symptoms in menopausal hot flashes
articles.authors: Evelyn Behar; Natalia Provolo; Jennifer Meigs; Kathleen Gunthert
articles.abstract: Objective: Studies show a clear link between depression and vasomotor symptoms (VMS), such as hot flashes, during menopause. However, many studies suffer from a key methodological limitation in assessing depression via the CES-D scale, which is better conceptualized as a measure of general distress that contains elements of both anxiety and depression. Thus, studies might in fact have found links between VMS and depression, anxiety, or both phenomena. Method: We investigated the unique role of depressive versus anxious symptoms in VMS in perimenopause and early postmenopause in a nationwide sample of 227 women (Study 1) and in 116 women from the nationwide longitudinal MIDUS-2 study (Study 2). Results: We found that after controlling for general distress, symptoms unique to anxiety (anxious arousal) were strongly related to VMS severity; symptoms unique to depression (anhedonia) were not. We replicated this finding using data from the nationwide MIDUS-2 study. Conclusions: Symptoms unique to anxiety, rather than those unique to depression, may be particularly relevant to hot flashes in menopause.

articles.title: “The Real Nature” of impulsive choice: Recent exposure to natural environments, not images depicting nature, reduces delay discounting in a systematic replication of Berry et al. (2014)
articles.authors: Camilo Hurtado-Parrado; Pablo Andrés Ledesma Castro; Julian Cifuentes; Mónica Arias Highera; FangLei Gao; Ellee Fillmore; Emy Ardila-Charry; César Acevedo-Triana
articles.abstract: Delay discounting (DD) has been widely studied as a behavioral process relevant to unhealthy behavior and psychiatric disorders. As a result, DD has been proposed as an underlying trans-disease process of several maladaptive behaviors, such as smoking and risky sexual behaviors, and there is a growing interest in identifying factors that reduce it. Among the interventions examined in humans, exposure to nature cues has appeared especially promising. Berry et al. (2014, 2015, 2019) reported that brief exposure to images depicting nature scenes, such as forests and mountains, reduces impulsive choice in hypothetical monetary DD tasks. Despite these promising findings, subsequent replication attempts in other laboratories have failed to reproduce this effect consistently. One possible reason is that the mechanism through which nature images may reduce DD remain unclear. Although attention has been proposed as a candidate mechanism, it has not been directly tested. The present study extended prior replication efforts by examining whether increased observing responses moderated the effects of exposure to images of nature versus built environments on DD of college students (n = 148). We replicated Berry et al. (2014) as closely as possible and incorporated a matching-to-sample task developed by Hurtado-Parrado et al. (2023) to manipulate participants’ observing responses. We found that delay discounting rates were not affected by the attentional manipulation (matching photographs or not), image content (natural or built environments), sex, or employment status, and rates in our sample were significantly higher than those reported in the participants exposed to the Natural condition in Berry et al.’s (2014) original study. In contrast, self-reported exposure to actual natural environments during the week prior to participation was associated with lower delay-discounting rates, attenuating the discounting of participants with higher exposure to nature. Further, higher exposure to natural environments was associated with reduced discounting only among participants who also reported greater exposure to built environments and working indoors. Overall, our findings do not support the notion that attention may be responsible for the inconsistencies in previously reported reduction of DD by brief exposure to nature images. Instead, they suggest that recent real contact with natural environments may be more relevant to impulsive choice than exposure to depictions of nature.

articles.title: Accounts Balanced: The Contingent Role of Rhetoric in Who Survives Political Scandal
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Marti Hope Gonzales; Allison Williams; Elliot Weiner; Rafael Aguilera
articles.abstract: When accused of misconduct in their private or public lives, people choose whether to apologize or to defend their character or reputation. Previous experiments have found that when misconduct is severe or offends outgroup members, transgressors may benefit by defending themselves and denying culpability for wrongdoing. In this study, we explore whether these tendencies can successfully reduce politicians’ accountability for wrongdoing in the context of a U.S. congressional election. We constructed a novel dataset documenting Representatives’ public remarks in response the 1992 House Bank Scandal, during which Representatives from both major parties were accused of misusing funds. Contrary to predictions, conciliatory remarks were not associated with electoral failure among more severe House Bank “offenders.” Consistent with predictions, defensive remarks (refusals) lost their typical association with electoral failure when the incumbent’s party controlled the district. Results suggest that groups may allow their leaders to escape blame for wrongdoing and retain power.

articles.title: Future-oriented action interventions promote personal and civic climate action
articles.authors: Kirsten Lydic; Alyssa Hannah Sinclair; Danielle Cosme; Jose Carreras Tartak; Omaya Torres-Grillo; Emily B. Falk
articles.abstract: A majority of people are concerned about climate change but under-engaged in climate action, especially civic or collective action. We integrated insights from multiple traditions of future-oriented psychological interventions focused on imagination and action planning, and we tested the resulting psychological intervention through three experimental conditions that targeted either a personal (e.g., driving less) or civic climate action (e.g., contacting elected officials about climate change), or neither. Participants then reported their intention to engage in personal and civic pro-environmental behaviors. Preregistered analyses (on N = 1,586 participants) showed that both personal and civic action interventions increased the targeted pro-environmental behavior. Furthermore, these effects extended to other other (non-targeted) pro-environmental behaviors, though only to the same category of action (personal vs. civic). In a second preregistered study, we replicated the intention effects of the civic action intervention. This study extends prior theory about the psychology of behavior change and provides practical insights to bridge the gap between climate concern and engagement in coordinated climate initiatives.

articles.title: Visuospatial features influencing the evaluation of two-body interactions
articles.authors: Andrea Orlandi; Mohammad Soleyman Nejad; Matteo Candidi
articles.abstract: Visual evaluation of aesthetic, semantic, and emotional aspects of two-body interactions is fundamental for social cognition, yet the contribution of objective stimulus features to these evaluations remains largely unexplored. This study investigated how different visuospatial features of two-body implied interactions influence their evaluations in terms of aesthetic pleasure, symmetry, emotional valence, meaning, and interest. Across four studies involving 200 participants, we found that visually ‘entangled’ two-body interactions, defined by the extent of shared interpersonal space, were rated as more aesthetically pleasing, interesting, and meaningful than their disentangled versions. Using Representational Similarity Analysis and hierarchical multiple regressions, we identified the contribution of each stimulus feature to these evaluations. These findings suggest that two-body entanglement enhances the perceived dyads’ aesthetic and semantic value, possibly facilitating their configural processing. The study expands prior literature and highlights a dissociation between visuospatial features and mechanisms underlying pleasure and interest in dancing bodies.

articles.title: Work-focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for patients on sick leave due to stress-related disorders: a feasibility study in primary health care
articles.authors: Anastasiya Zakrevska; Magnus Johansson; Robin Bernhardtz; Lars-Göran Öst; Erik Andersson; Elisabeth Björk Brämberg; Hanna Malmberg Gavelin; Sandra af Winklerfelt Hammarberg; Anna Finnes
articles.abstract:
Background: Stress-related disorders are the leading cause of long-term sickness absence (>90 days) in Sweden, and most patients are treated within primary health care. However, few treatments effectively address both symptoms and return to work. Work-focused Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (W-CBT) is a newly developed treatment approach combining conventional CBT techniques with a module focusing on return to work. This study aims to test the feasibility and acceptability of a new W-CBT treatment manual for patients on sick leave due to stress-related disorders in primary health care, and to explore changes in work functioning and symptoms.

Methods: The study was conducted at two primary health care centres in the Stockholm Region, Sweden. Adult patients on sick leave due to long-term stress-related disorders received treatment with W-CBT. The primary outcome measures concerned the feasibility and acceptability of the treatment, including the recruitment process and patients' perceptions of the treatment. The secondary outcome measures concerned work functioning and symptoms. Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes were used for all secondary outcome measures.

Results: Recruitment proceeded largely as planned. A total of 31 patients were included, of whom 30 completed treatment (median age 38 years, 63% women). All participants except one were recruited from one of the two primary health care centres. All participants perceived the treatment as effective and rated it as highly acceptable. Post-treatment, 81% (21/26) of participants were no longer on sick leave. Self-rated work functioning and symptoms showed high between-individual variability, but all measures improved post-treatment and were maintained at 6-months follow-up.

Conclusions: The results indicate that W-CBT for patients on sick leave due to stress-related disorders is feasible and acceptable to deliver in a primary health care setting. In addition, work functioning and symptoms improved following treatment and were maintained at 6 months, while the observed between-individual variability suggests that treatment trajectories may differ considerably across patients. These findings warrant a full-scale controlled trial to evaluate treatment effects.

Trial registration: The study was retrospectively registered on 3 November 2025 at the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3QE9J) before data analyses were performed.

articles.title: Music was my first love: Biographic resonance makes everyday music listening meaningful
articles.authors: Felix Dietrich; Alicia Ernst; Benedikt Rohr; Michael Scharkow; Leonard Reinecke
articles.abstract: Despite much research on eudaimonic media experiences, little is known about how and why certain content is perceived as meaningful by certain users in certain situations. We therefore examine biographic resonance — connections between entertainment content and users’ biographic memories — during everyday music listening on Spotify and propose that memory recall, as well as its emotional valence, relate to meaningfulness via distinct patterns of intrinsic need satisfaction. Results from a preregistered, intensive-longitudinal study (144 persons; 6,920 situations) reveal that biographic resonance relates to both high- and low-effort modes of eudaimonic entertainment. Moreover, by linking users’ self-reports with their tracked digital music use (2,786 sessions; 107,147 songs), we find that the occurrence and quality of biographic resonance vary across situations and are shaped by both content and contextual factors within algorithmically curated environments. Our results highlight how resonances between media users’ selves and entertainment content foster situational meaningfulness in everyday life.

articles.title: Surprised–Curious–Confused, Empathetic, and Entertained? The Role of Epistemic Emotions and Empathy in Eudaimonic Entertainment Experiences and Political News Processing
articles.authors: Felix Dietrich; Tanja Kugler; Sarah Lucia Hennings; Celine Conrad; Frank M. Schneider; Peter Vorderer
articles.abstract: Based on the dual-process model of entertainment experiences and motivated cognition, we propose that specific affective states such as surprise, curiosity, and confusion (so-called epistemic emotions), as well as empathy, are involved in eudaimonic entertainment experiences while reading political news. We further assume that these emotions are related to normatively desirable outcomes such as deliberation within, information seeking, and knowledge acquisition about political topics. To test the hypothesized model, we conducted a between-subjects online experiment (N = 407) that used different stimuli to induce the emotions of interest while simultaneously varying news topics. Structural equation modeling revealed that the data mostly supported our hypotheses. Overall, we find that through these affective states, even soft news can enable normatively desirable outcomes. All data and materials can be accessed from https://osf.io/82gqu/.

articles.title: Time-Based Cognition and Working Memory Explain Changes in Delay Discounting Through Adolescence
articles.authors: Camille Phaneuf-Hadd; Leah Somerville
articles.abstract: Individuals of all ages face choices between immediate but smaller and delayed but larger rewards. In a decision process known as delay discounting, people tend to devalue options that are realized farther into the future. Several candidate cognitive mechanisms have been proposed to underpin such choices: inhibition (overriding a prepotent response), prospection (orienting to the future), working memory (manipulating information held in mind), reward motivation (activating behavior for reward), and time perception (subjectively judging time horizons). These mechanisms change through adolescence, in tandem with delay discounting decisions becoming more patient from childhood to adulthood. However, the cognitive mechanisms principally responsible for developmental increases in patience remain contested. By measuring delay discounting alongside indices of inhibition, prospection, working memory, reward motivation, and time perception in the same participants (N = 159, 10-20 years, collected in the United States), the present study examined whether these mechanisms – alone or in combination – explained age variability in reward- and time-based choice in different stakes contexts. Mixed- effects modeling revealed that patience indeed increased with age, especially for higher- than lower-magnitude decisions. Dependency modeling identified dissociable and overlapping drivers of age-related changes in delay discounting: prospection mediated patience in lower-magnitude decisions whereas working memory mediated patience in higher-magnitude decisions; time perception mediated patience in both. Although compressed time perception supported older participants’ more patient choices overall, distinct cognitive mechanisms may become available during adolescence to underscore willingness to wait for larger later rewards, depending on decision stakes. These findings advance understanding of how multiple constituent processes scaffold the development of value-based choice.

articles.title: Linguistic diversity as a two-step process: Grounding polysemy in universal neural networks and expanding it by cultural learning
articles.authors: Marit Lobben; Laura Bakke; Tor Endestad
articles.abstract:
This paper advances a new account of linguistic typology grounded in the hypothesis of neural reuse, namely that languages selectively recruit pre-existing neurocognitive systems for grammatical purposes. The proposal is tested through a case study of the Mandarin classifier zuò (座), combining cognitive semantic analysis with fMRI evidence. The semantic analysis shows that zuò forms a highly structured polysemy network organized around scene-based construal, progressing from anchored entities and perceptual salience to bounded environments, landmarks, navigable spaces, and goal-directed schemas.
To examine whether this organization reflects underlying neural systems, an fMRI experiment contrasted zuò with a non-scene classifier. Processing zuò alone—prior to any scene-denoting noun—activated regions associated with scene perception and navigation, including the parahippocampal place area, retrosplenial cortex, and occipital place area. This indicates that a grammatical morpheme can recruit a scene-selective cortical system, supporting the view that polysemy may be constrained by shared neural architecture.
At the same time, the full semantic range of the classifier cannot be derived from neural structure alone. Several extensions depend on lived experience and culture-specific knowledge, suggesting that neural reuse provides a scaffold that is subsequently elaborated through usage and cultural models. The findings support a typological perspective in which languages differ in whether and how they recruit available neural systems, thereby shaping the emergence of grammatical categories and polysemy networks.

articles.title: Complex systems approach to social science
articles.authors: Merlijn Olthof
articles.abstract: The complex systems approach is an alternative paradigm for studying human behavior. In this paradigm, the study of human behavior centers around complex systems principles that are applied across various subfields. This entry provides an introduction to the complex systems approach focusing on the study of transitions, networks and multifractal scaling. A brief reflection on the field concludes the entry.

articles.title: A crosslinguistic corpus phonetic analysis of intrinsic vowel duration
articles.authors: Eleanor Chodroff; Miao Zhang
articles.abstract: This study investigated the crosslinguistic distribution of intrinsic vowel duration, the observation that high vowels tend to be shorter than low vowels, using a large-scale corpus phonetic approach. Previous studies have reported a durational difference but have been limited by small speaker samples and narrow language coverage. Nevertheless, this observation has been debated to reflect an automatic consequence of the vowel height difference, or to be under speaker control. We reconsider this dichotomy in terms of competing pressures of target uniformity and enhancement in phonetic realization. Target uniformity would be consistent with a systematically shorter duration for high than low vowels and no systematic asymmetry between front and back vowels. In contrast, enhancement would predict larger, more variable durational differences between high and low vowels. To address the empirical gap, we analyzed duration contrasts among /i/, /u/, and /a/ in inter-obstruent contexts from over 60 languages, 80 language–length contrasts, and 16 language families in the VoxCommunis Corpus using automatic and manual vowel segmentations. Linear mixed-effects models assessed duration differences across vowel height and backness, incorporating rate-normalized and raw measures, while by-speaker analyses probed individual consistency. High vowels were shorter than low vowels in approximately 90% of language contrasts and significantly so for almost 80%. Crucially, no consistent durational bias emerged between high front and high back vowels. These findings suggest that intrinsic vowel duration is better understood as a statistical universal emerging from the balance between uniformity and enhancement in phonetic realization, rather than as a purely automatic universal.

articles.title: Recycling Rivalry: Social Identity Appeals Increase Recycling When Combined with Intergroup Comparison
articles.authors: Hege Landsvik; Jareef Martuza; Sveinung Jørgensen; Lars Jacob Pedersen; Siv Skard
articles.abstract: While many people recycle at home, they are less likely to do so in public, where high waste production meets a diffusion of individual responsibility. We examine whether social identity can close this gap. Across two preregistered season-long field experiments at a Norwegian Premier Division football stadium, we test the separate and combined effects of ingroup identity appeals and intergroup comparison on the recycling behavior of football supporters. In Study 1 (N = 5,712), an ingroup identity appeal did not increase recycling relative to an outgroup appeal, suggesting that standalone identity appeals are insufficient to shift behavior. When the ingroup appeal was combined with a ranking of clubs by their recycling rate, recycling rates were more than two times higher than in any other condition. Study 2 (N = 6,598) replicated this effect against a no-intervention control. Study 3 (N = 761), a post-game survey among Study 2’s participants, showed that supporters exposed to the combined intervention reported greater motivation to recycle and greater perceived importance of contributing to the ingroup’s success. These findings extend social identity theory by showing that identity appeals increase recycling when group performance is tied to a concrete metric of success, which an intergroup comparison can supply, making the behavior a way to pursue positive group distinctiveness.

articles.title: Effect-Based Assessments of Intergroup Comparability  – The Practical Impact of Measurement Non-Invariance & Differential Item Functioning on Psychological Tests and Scales
articles.authors: Tizian Maria Benedikt Schuhbeck; Melanie Viola Partsch; Philipp Sterner; David Goretzko
articles.abstract: To assess psychological tests and scales for violations of intergroup comparability – termed Measurement Non-Invariance (MNI) in factor analysis and Differential Item Functioning (DIF) in item response theory – statistical testing has emerged as the dominating approach, but inherently fails to differentiate between major and negligible violations. To address this, upwards of 27 effect size measures for both MNI and DIF have been proposed over the last decades, using vastly different conventions in naming and notation, with no clear consensus on interpretation. This arguably constitutes a severe hindrance for the much needed popularization of a non-dichotomous assessments of intergroup comparability. We address this limitation by introducing a unifying taxonomy that encompasses all previous measures as instances of just four fundamental types: Expected Difference (ED), Expected Absolute Difference (EAD), Total Expected Difference (TED) and Total Expected Absolute Difference (TEAD), which are universally applicable, irrespective of the underlying measurement model. Furthermore, we construct corresponding effect directions and derive formulas to calulate MNI/DIF-induced biases in commonly used mean difference effects, such as Cohen’s d & Cohen’s f. We provide a dual illustration using both FA and IRT models on real-world data.

articles.title: Unified Definition of Psychological Stress and the Cognitive Integration Model
articles.authors: Haixia Gu; Yangyang Lei; Yun Zhang; Chao Chen; Chunyu Liu
articles.abstract: Psychological stress is central to health and diseases. Yet heterogeneous definitions and insufficient theoretical integration lead to findings that are difficult to replicate or compare, ultimately hindering their translation into practice. To address this problem, we aimed to identify the fundamental and conceptually distinct components of psychological stress and integrate them into a unified definition and model. We systematically reviewed 67 existing definitions of psychological stress from previous publications and identified their core components. We quantified both the use frequency of each component and patterns of co-occurrence across the literature. We also reviewed major theoretical models to evaluate how comprehensively each model captured those core stress-related components. Existing definitions and theories were found to capture only partial aspects of the stress process, resulting in a fragmented conceptualization. To reconcile these fragmented perspectives and establish a cohesive foundation, we synthesize these core components into a novel framework. We redefine psychological stress as a perceived imbalance between stressors and available resources, with stressors arising from internal needs or external demands and corresponding internal and external resources. Cognitive appraisal is central to the stress process. Notably, internal needs represent an important class of stressors, yet they have received less attention than external demands in the past. To situate this definition within the broader stress process, we propose a Cognitive Integration Model (CIM). The CIM specifies how stressors and resources are dynamically integrated through cognition to generate psychological stress, whereas coping and responses are positioned as downstream components that provide feedback regulation and link stress to health outcomes. These components across the entire stress process may be jointly shaped by genetic and environmental factors. Together, this unified definition and model provide a common framework for integrating stress research across diverse theories, terminologies, and methods. This framework reframes psychological stress not as a purely environmental exposure, but as a product of gene–environment interaction.

articles.title: Parenting Behavior in Relation to Children's Socio-Emotional Skills: A Latent Profile Analysis
articles.authors: Sonja Kälin; Nora Tilda Kunz; Niamh Oeri
articles.abstract: Parenting is closely linked to children’s social-emotional development, including externalizing behavior, peer relationships, and emotion regulation. However, most existing research has examined these associations using single parenting behaviors or predefined parenting styles, thereby neglecting the complex co-occurrence of different parenting practices. To address this limitation, the present study applied a person-centered approach using Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) to identify distinct parenting profiles and explore their associations with child socioemotional skills. Based on reports of parenting behavior from parents of N = 254 kindergarten children (51.2% female, M = 6.0 years, SD = 0.62), three parenting profiles emerged: supportive (66%), engaged-disciplinary (22%), and harsh (12%). Associations with teacher-rated outcomes showed that children exposed to engaged-disciplinary parenting displayed more peer problems. In comparison, children assigned to the harsh parenting group showed more behavioral problems and, unexpectedly, stronger emotion regulation skills. The findings underscore the need to tailor support to specific subgroups of parents with distinct parenting behaviors, to strengthen positive parenting behaviors, and, in turn, promote the development of children.

articles.title: Effects of a Neuroticism Intervention Over One Year
articles.authors: Peter Haehner; Amanda Jo Wright; Rosalie Andrae; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Personality interventions recently gained increasing interest as promising tools to improve people’s lives. Although initial evidence on the effects of these interventions is promising, their longer-term effectiveness has yet to be established. 
Methods: Using data form the Changing How I Live Life (CHILL) Study, we examined the effects of a digital neuroticism intervention over 1 year. In this study, participants (N = 475) were randomized to an active control group or intervention groups targeting different levels of neuroticism. Furthermore, participants reported on different aspects of perceived intervention utility at the 1-year follow-up. 
Results: Participants significantly decreased in their neuroticism from pre-intervention to the 1-year follow-up regardless of whether they were randomized to the intervention groups (d = -0.40 to -0.53) or the active control group (d = -0.41). Intervention effects did also not differ among groups targeting different levels of neuroticism. Nonetheless, participants were relatively happy with the intervention and reported a high willingness to pay money to get access to a similar app. 
Conclusion: This study provides novel insights into the durability of intervention-induced neuroticism changes, but future research is needed to better understand the mechanisms and boundary conditions of volitional personality changes with and without interventions.

articles.title: Self-regulation shapes who benefits from large language models
articles.authors: Xiangbin Teng; Sirui Ren
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) promise to broaden access to expertise, yet their benefits are uneven: the same model can scaffold a novice, accelerate an expert, or produce polished work that masks shallow understanding. We apply the established framework of self-regulated learning to human–LLM interaction and argue that loop quality emerges from the user–task–interface system rather than residing in the user alone. Productive loops involve three observable moves: steering sets goals and standards; monitoring evaluates fluent but fallible output; and repair tests, critiques, and revises it. Weak loops can create a synthesis trap in which users offload comparison and integration, producing false mastery—better assisted performance without corresponding transfer, confidence calibration, or error detection—and accumulating verification debt. The framework predicts that LLMs will widen differences between users when verification burden is high and regulatory support is weak, but narrow them when tasks are verifiable and interfaces externalize standards, evidence, and checks. We propose constraint density, monitoring calibration, and repair depth as process markers linking interaction traces to independent outcomes. This account turns divergent findings into testable predictions and motivates cognitive workbenches designed to preserve verification, agency, and transfer.

articles.title: An integrative framework for the human sense of control
articles.authors: Alireza Modirshanechi; Peter Dayan; Eric Schulz
articles.abstract: From managing daily schedules to making major life decisions, how much we feel in control of our lives is central to our behavior and well-being. Yet, there is currently no precise, unifying account of what it means to feel in control. Here, we propose that humans feel in control when they are prepared to tackle future tasks. We formalize this perspective via a precise yet interpretable measure of controllability that quantifies three key factors: (i) the range of available actions, (ii) the certainty or (iii) the possibility of achieving desired outcomes. This measure unifies previous conceptions of control and successfully predicts human preferences in three experiments in which participants either rate their sense of control or prepare themselves to seek rewards or avoid punishments. Our framework offers a principled foundation for understanding how environmental structure shapes the human sense of control, paving the way towards an integrative science of agency.

articles.title: Activities, Motivational Congruence, and Well-Being:  Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Evidence
articles.authors: Taylor G. Hill
articles.abstract: A consistent observation across positive psychology is that similar activities do not benefit everyone equally, yet it remains unclear whether well-being depends more on activity content or on motivational congruence. Two preregistered studies examined associations between activities, motivational variables, personality, and well-being using cross-sectional (N = 392; 1,179 personally meaningful activities) and longitudinal (N = 350; 1,012 orientation–experience observations) data. In Study 1, behavioural activity categories showed little association with well-being, whereas hedonic and eudaimonic orientations showed consistent positive associations across outcomes. Motivational motives showed smaller but generally positive associations, and interaction effects between motives and orientations were limited, suggesting that these components contributed relatively independently rather than through strong cross-sectional congruence effects. Personality moderation effects were selective and modest. In Study 2, greater orientation–experience congruence most consistently predicted subsequent life worthwhileness, whereas evidence for life satisfaction was weaker. Congruence was associated primarily with competence need satisfaction, with little evidence of associations with autonomy or relatedness. Hedonic and eudaimonic experiences each showed independent positive associations with well-being, although their interaction was negative rather than synergistic. Across both studies, the findings suggest that activity categories alone provide limited insight into well-being, whereas motivational variables (and particularly within-person orientation–experience congruence) show more consistent associations with well-being.

articles.title: The crossword effect: A recall advantage for words encoded in alignment with their spatial associations
articles.authors: Christoph Scheepers; Ricarda Senger
articles.abstract: Across two preregistered experiments, we demonstrate that free word recall improves when words are encoded in alignment with their spatial associations. Experiment 1 compared words with a strong horizontal association (e.g., railway) to words with a strong vertical association (e.g., rocket) and established that the latter were more likely to be recalled when presented vertically rather than horizontally during encoding. No such benefit was observed for horizontally associated words.
