Experiment 2 extended these findings by showing a vertical encoding advantage also for spatially neutral words (e.g., foam), which was smaller than for the vertically associated words but larger than for the horizontally associated words in Experiment 1. Beyond suggesting a general vertical encoding advantage in free word recall, the results support Barsalou's (1999) Perceptual Symbol Hypothesis, which posits that word meanings are grounded in perception and action. Our findings demonstrate that access to word concepts in short term memory is modulated by sensorimotor processes during encoding, specifically horizontal versus vertical reading.

articles.title: Stability and Change of Spirituality following Childbirth: Longitudinal Evidence Swiss Household Panel Data Using Multiple Propensity Score Matching Analyses
articles.authors: Friedemann Trutzenberg; Michael Eid
articles.abstract:
Introduction: The birth of a child typically transcends parents’ daily lives and is frequently described as a spiritual experience. Yet, little is known about medium- or long-term effects of becoming parents on individuals’ spirituality. Spirituality is commonly conceptualised more broadly than religiosity and can refer to an ori- entation towards something divine, no matter whether this is a religious being or a non-religious entity. Its lifespan development and responsiveness to life events are not yet systematically understood, and existing evidence often does not allow for causal conclusions. Addressing this research gap, our study seeks to provide robust causal insights on the medium-term stability and change of spirituality following childbirth.

Methods: Using longitudinal pre- and post-birth spirituality data from the Swiss Household Panel (SHP), we compared participants who had become parents for the first time between 2015 and 2018 with propensity score (PS)-matched child- less and multiparous parent controls.

Results: Across multiple robustness conditions regarding covariate selection, manifest and structural equation modelling analyses suggested a high average medium-term stability in spirituality (r ≥ 0.87; ρ ≥ 0.95) and no average spiritual change following childbirth among the first-time parents (N = 138) compared to the matched controls.

Discussion: Given this high average stability, future research should focus on differential trajectories rather than average effects to better understand which individual and situational characteristics influence the development of spirituality following life events.

articles.title: Detecting political misinformation: A boosting intervention tested on Donald Trump’s statements
articles.authors: Lucca Pfruender; Ewout Meijer; Merijn Volmer; Leonie Hannah Shoshana Loewy; Bruno Verschuere
articles.abstract:
Misinformation has become an unavoidable part of political reality, eroding institutional
trust. We tested whether a simple booster intervention can improve misinformation detection
compared to intuitive judgments. The booster conditions instructed people to focus on the
level of detail in a politician's message while allowing them to weigh in factual knowledge.
Americans (n = 588) judged the veracity of statements made by Donald Trump, which were
fact-checked as true or false. False statements were judged less detailed than true statements,
and the booster interventions increased misinformation-detection accuracy by 4 to 6
percentage points over intuitive judgments. Political statements as short as one sentence
differed in detail depending on whether they were true or false, and this could be used to
boost voters’ ability to detect misinformation, at least in Donald Trump’s statements.

articles.title: How Prompting and Editing Shape Psychological Ownership in AI-Assisted Creative Writing
articles.authors: Niki Pennanen; Pyry Kanerva; Christian Guckelsberger
articles.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as writing partners, but their use complicates whether writers experience the resulting text as genuinely their own. Such psychological ownership is especially relevant in AI-assisted writing because it contributes to the immediate and extended experience of AI use, and users may sign, share, revise, or be held accountable for texts whose content was partly generated by AI. Prior work shows that greater human input can increase ownership, but it remains unclear how ownership is shaped by two common forms of involvement: steering generation through prompting, directly revising generated text, and their combination. We report a preregistered mixed factorial experiment (N=273) in which online participants wrote short stories either without AI assistance or with AI assistance under one of two prompting styles (single-prompt vs. iterative), crossed with editing or not editing the AI-generated text. Editing increased ownership, especially for single-prompt generation. Iterative prompting increased ownership when editing was unavailable, but not when editing was available. These findings suggest that iterative prompting and post-generation editing are partially substitutable routes to psychological ownership, each providing opportunities for control and self-investment at different phases of the writing process. Fully manual writing nevertheless produced substantially higher ownership than all AI-assisted conditions, a gap that persisted in exploratory covariate analyses adjusting for effort, perceived story quality, and intrinsic motivation. The results suggest that AI writing tools should avoid one-shot delegation workflows when ownership matters, and instead support users in both steering and directly revising co-created text.

articles.title: Growth Trajectory Profiles of Self-concept of Abilities, Intrinsic Value, Utility Value, and Emotional Cost in Math Across Grades 4 to 8
articles.authors: Mathilda Sandman; Anna Widlund; Jaana Viljaranta; Rebecca Lazarides; Wendy Symes; Johan Korhonen
articles.abstract:
Background: Previous research has consistently shown that students’ math motivation declines across the school years. However, less is known about individual differences in these developmental trajectories. 
Aim: This study investigated the development of students’ math self-concept of abilities, intrinsic value, utility value and emotional cost from Grades 4 to 8 at the average level and by identifying distinct growth trajectory profiles. Profile membership was further related to gender and performance. 
Sample: The sample comprised 875 Finnish students (53 % girls) from Grades 4 to 8 using an accelerated longitudinal design. 
Method: Latent growth curve models and growth mixture modeling were utilized. Gender differences were analyzed using the 3-step approach and differences in math performance were examined using the BCH method.
Results: On average, self-concept of abilities, intrinsic value, and utility value declined whereas emotional cost increased over time. Three trajectory profiles were identified: Positive declining reflected the normative developmental pattern, while students in the Struggling profile showed lower initial motivation, increasing emotional cost, and the lowest math performance. Further, students in the Fading interest profile, predominantly boys, maintained high self-concept and performance despite low/moderate utility value and steeply declining intrinsic value. 
Conclusion: The average developmental trends concealed individual differences in students’ motivational development. While most students followed the expected decline, distinct profiles showed that motivation can develop differently across students and have different implications for academic performance.

articles.title: The Role of Individual Differences in the Effects of PC and VR Simulations on Elementary School Students’ Learning and Curiosity
articles.authors: Valdemar Aksel Stenberdt; Géraldine Fauville; Cecilie Fenja Strandsbjerg; Adéla Plechatá; Ingo Zettler; Guido Makransky
articles.abstract: Curiosity is related to important academic outcomes. Yet, current research suggests that children’s curiosity decreases during formal schooling, and research exploring theory-informed interventions to increase curiosity remains limited. Building on a synthesis of prior research, the SIM-Curious framework is introduced, identifying pathways to support curiosity-driven learning with simulations. Then, results of a pre-registered, randomized field trial (N = 217, Mage = 13.22 years, SD = 0.94) are presented, examining the overall effects of simulations and the relative effects of media (Virtual Reality vs PCs) in promoting curiosity and knowledge. Students’ specific state curiosity and knowledge increased, but there were no significant main effects of media. Higher prior specific state curiosity indirectly influenced follow-up knowledge through question-asking during the simulation. Individual differences in trait curiosity, prior knowledge, in-simulation question-asking, and post-simulation specific state curiosity influenced post-intervention information-seeking. The results are discussed in light of the SIM-Curious framework and illustrate its promise.

articles.title: A scoping review of the sexual health and wellbeing of LGBTQIA+ people affected by cancer.
articles.authors: Daniel Brown; Pierre Roscher; Karina Rune
articles.abstract:
Background
Sexual health and wellbeing are critical components of quality of life following cancer, yet they remain under-addressed in care. LGBTQIA+ people affected by cancer face additional challenges due to heteronormative healthcare systems, minority stress, and limited access to inclusive, culturally responsive services.
Aims
This scoping review aimed to map the extent, nature, and characteristics of research on the sexual health and wellbeing and sexual healthcare experiences of LGBTQIA+ people affected by cancer.
Methods
Databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and CINAHL) were searched up to September 2024. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed research on LGBTQIA+ individuals affected by cancer. Data were charted using both manual and AI-assisted extraction, and analysed thematically.
Results
Forty-nine reports representing 29 studies were included, involving approximately 3,800 participants. Research was dominated by cisgender sexual minority men with prostate cancer. Seven key themes were identified: sexual function and adaptation, healthcare heteronormativity, psychosocial wellbeing, chosen family, interventions, measurement, and intersectional disparities. Sexual dysfunction was common but experienced differently across groups, often requiring adaptation rather than restoration. Heteronormative care limited inclusive communication and tailored support. LGBTQIA+ individuals reported higher psychological distress, with social and chosen family support playing a key role in adjustment. There was a lack of tailored interventions and inclusive measurement tools, and limited representation of diverse subgroups.
Conclusions
Significant gaps exist in understanding and addressing the sexual health needs of LGBTQIA+ cancer survivors. Inclusive, queer-informed frameworks, improved measurement tools, and targeted interventions are needed to support equitable and person-centred care.

articles.title: A Test of the 2 × 2 Model of Perfectionism in Predicting Distress among Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles.abstract: Perfectionism has been consistently linked to psychological distress, yet most evidence in the Philippine context relies on cross-sectional designs, limiting temporal conclusions. Licensure examinations in the Philippines, such as the Psychometrician Licensure Examination mandated by Republic Act No. 10029 (2009), represent a high-stakes evaluative context that may amplify perfectionistic tendencies. The present study tested the 2 × 2 model of perfectionism among 315 licensure examination reviewees, examining how Evaluative Concerns Perfectionism (ECP) and Personal Standards Perfectionism (PSP) predicted Time 2 overall distress, anxiety, and depression after a one-month interval. ECP was a significant positive predictor of all three outcomes, whereas PSP was not. Consistent with the 2 × 2 model, Pure PSP did not differ from Non-perfectionism, while Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism are associated significantly greater distress, anxiety, and depression than Non-perfectionism and Pure PSP. Notably, Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism did not significantly differ, lending support to the aggravating factor hypothesis. These findings underscore that ECP, rather than PSP, drive psychological distress in high-stakes evaluative contexts.

articles.title: Unique and common qualifiers in the lexical differentiation of blue and brown in American English: Corpus evidence at the vision–language interface
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell; Anke Marit Albers; Sean Isamu Johnson; Galina Paramei
articles.abstract:
While humans perceive color as a nearly continuous spectrum, most languages categorize hues using a small set of basic color terms (BCTs). Several languages (e.g., Russian, Greek, Italian) lexicalize two or more basic ‘blue’ categories, distinguishing light from dark blue, a distinction English is usually said to lack. No basic split for English blue has been found, yet speakers may differentiate blue shades in everyday usage by attaching modifiers such as “light” and “dark” to blue more than to other color terms. Using the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA; ~560 million words, five genres), we extracted the 11 English BCTs with their most frequent preceding collocates and quantified chromatic specification, correcting for non-chromatic uses of the color words and their qualifiers. Although light blue and dark blue do not function as separate basic categories, blue attracts chromatic specifiers more often, and a far wider variety of unique ones (navy, cobalt, cerulean), than any other BCT, a lead we link to its communicative prominence and chromatic richness. Brown is the other heavily qualified term, but its qualification runs through common, largely achromatic modifiers rather than unique specifiers, a pattern we link to its status as a constitutively dark, lightness-defined color whose subcategories are largely lightness variants. The central contrast replicates on the current, larger COCA release (~993 million words, eight genres) using an independently constructed classification of qualifiers. We argue that color-term basicness is gradient rather than discrete, and that corpus structure offers a naturalistic window onto the vision–language interface.
Keywords: color categorization; basic color terms; color names; blue; brown; corpus linguistics; COCA; vision-language interface

articles.title: The Positively Reconstructed Self-Voice: The Mental Representation of One’s Own Voice is Brighter and Clearer than Recorded Voice
articles.authors: Yusuke Suzuki; Naoki Kuroda; Masayoshi Nagai
articles.abstract: People experience discomfort hearing their recorded voices due to the discrepancy with their internal representation. While attributed to bone-conduction amplifying low frequencies, simulating this hypothesis has yielded inconsistent results. Challenging this view, we explored the self-voice mental representation using psychophysical reverse correlation, a data-driven approach without prior assumptions. Across two experiments, Japanese adults (Study 1: n = 24; Study 2: n = 54) selected one of two randomly spectral amplitude-modulated voices that sounded more like their own. Voices reconstructed from these judgments yielded significantly higher own-voice likeness ratings than recordings or bone-conduction simulations. Acoustic analyses revealed these representations contradicted bone-conduction predictions (“lower and deeper”), emerging as “brighter and clearer” (increased spectral centroid and F1 frequency) and emphasizing “individual identity” (selectively amplified formants). Although limited to the sustained vowel /a:/, a generalized filter approximated the self-voice for novel speakers, suggesting a common mechanism underlying self-voice representations across individuals.

articles.title: Time to Divest?: Perceived Inconsistencies between universities’ environmental policy and actions reduce staff and students’ intentions to engage in pro-environmental behaviours
articles.authors: Alice M Davis; Paulina Schenk; Hiu Laam Tse; Sabine Topf; Jeremy I Skipper
articles.abstract: Many universities have environmental policy statements that are decidedly pro-environmental. However, some of their past actions may be perceived as inconsistent with these commitments. For example, one university previously invested £21 million in companies and intermediaries that produce fossil fuels, which are known to contribute to environmental devastation and global warming. In line with its policy statement, the university also promoted initiatives to encourage staff and students to adopt pro-environmental behaviours (PEBs). How might the perception of inconsistency between environmental policy and actual practice affect the efforts of members of the university community to enact individual PEBs? To address this question, in two studies we tested the hypothesis that university community members would be less likely to engage in PEBs if they were made aware of inconsistencies between environmental policy and actions. Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that staff and students were less likely to say they intend to adopt PEBs in the coming week when told about inconsistencies, compared to a group told that university environmental policy and actions are consistent. Furthermore, there were a number of interactions with attitudes, knowledge, and situational factors in both studies, mostly showing fewer PEBs when policy was inconsistent. These results imply that perceived inconsistencies between environmental policy and actions could lead university staff and students to engage in fewer PEBs. Interpretation of statistical interactions further suggests that when individual attitudes are not strong, community members—especially students—reference the university’s inconsistency and decide to perform fewer PEBs than they might otherwise. Given increasing global awareness of environmental problems, this interpretation leads to the suggestion that universities should either consider adding caveats to their environmental policy statements or bring their actions in line with those policies (e.g., by divesting fossil fuel holdings—as this university ultimately did).

articles.title: A Single-Arm Longitudinal Pilot Study of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu as a Mental Health Intervention for Combat Veterans with Military-Connected Disabilities
articles.authors: Jack Ryan Kaufman; Wyatt R. Evans; Robert W. Haley; C. Munro Cullum
articles.abstract: Combat veterans experience increased incidences of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, along with challenges when adjusting to life post-discharge, but have been under-served using traditional mental health treatments. Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu has emerged as potentially therapeutic for combat veterans, although empirical support is lacking. A single-arm pre-post pilot study was used to evaluate seven psychosocial outcomes among participants from the We Defy Foundation program (n = 40; 87.5% male; Mage = 41.1, SD = 5.8). The primary outcomes measured were post-traumatic stress severity (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5; PCL-5), depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7; GAD-7), and Military-Civilian Transition Quality (M2CQ). Secondary outcomes included Self-Efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale; GSE), Functional Disability (World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule; WHODAS 2.0), and Life Satisfaction (Satisfaction with Life Scale; SWLS). Assessments were completed at baseline (T0), 3 months (T3; n = 34), and 6 months (T6; n = 23, final). Results revealed significant improvements in the four primary outcomes, which demonstrated high symptom severity scores at baseline, at both T3 (Cohen’s dz = .52-.63) and T6 (dz = .84-1.04) after applying the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. Two of the three secondary outcomes achieved statistical significance at T3 (GSE and SWLS) and WHODAS became statistically significant at T6. These preliminary findings indicate BJJ participation resulted in positive accumulative mental health improvements for this veteran population and provides a promising therapeutic target for future studies.

articles.title: Resolving Phonological Uncertainty in Reading: Orthography-to-Phonology Computations in Hebrew
articles.authors: Naama Schwartz; Golan Ankory-Shaked; Ram Frost; Noam Siegelman
articles.abstract: How do readers resolve phonological uncertainty in their writing system? Are there universal principles governing this process? We address these questions by examining how phonological uncertainty of orthographic units at different grain sizes shape visual word recognition. Our target language was Hebrew, a Semitic writing system characterized by particularly high uncertainty in letter-to-sound correspondences. We employed information-theoretic measures of surprisal and entropy computed at the letter level, together with a measure of orthographic-phonological (O-P) consistency that captures print-speech regularities at larger grain sizes. This allowed us to test to what extent reading behavior in Hebrew is driven by sublexical O-P mappings, and to identify the preferred unit size of these computations. Analyses of naming and lexical decision performance from the large Hebrew Lexicon Project (HeLP) revealed robust effects of sublexical O-P regularities on word recognition despite the substantial phonological uncertainty of Hebrew letters. Large grain-size O-P regularities generally produced stronger effects than letter-level surprisal measures, suggesting that readers compensate for the uncertainty at the single-letter level by relying on larger orthographic-phonological units. These findings demonstrate how sublexical O-P computations play a central role in reading, even when they provide ambiguous phonological information, and show how readers exploit different orthographic unit sizes given the characteristics of their writing system.

articles.title: The Sensitivity of Rasch Tree DIF Detection to Model Misspecification
articles.authors: Andrew Krist; Sanford R Student; Stefanie Wind
articles.abstract: The Rasch Tree model for differential item functioning (DIF) detection is a useful tool that uses exploratory yet interpretable methods to investigate intersectional DIF. Recent research has explored Rasch Tree performance under specific data conditions. The present research expands upon this by examining the effect of Rasch model misspecifications (i.e., misfit) on Rasch Tree estimation performance. Using a Monte Carlo simulation, we test the effects of including discrimination and pseudo-guessing parameters in the data generation process on DIF detection accuracy, DIF magnitude estimates, and resulting Rasch Tree structure. Results indicate that imposing the Rasch model on data that contain varied item discriminations and guessing behavior leads to a decrease in DIF detection accuracy and stability. In addition, we also assess these effects under different sample sizes and test lengths and examine the Rasch Tree’s ability to distinguish between person ability differences and item level DIF under various conditions.  We discuss implications and future directions from this research.

articles.title: Identifying Acoustic Characteristics for Disgust-Related Musical Stimuli
articles.authors: Jorge Alvarado; Oscar Andrés Hernández Salgar; Pablo Alexander Reyes; Britney Carolina Robayo; Juan Diego Rodríguez-Romero; Angelica María Ospina Cardona
articles.abstract: Disgust remains one of the least studied emotions in music psychology, largely because music is typically regarded as an aesthetic medium and because disgust is phylogenetically rooted in chemical and tactile rather than auditory senses. This study addresses the absence of standardized musical stimuli for disgust through two sequential experiments involving the affective evaluation of 36 musical clips (20 s each) composed to represent three categories: disgust, positive, and neutral. In Experiment 1 (n = 125), participants rated the clips on valence, arousal, and a disgust–fear continuum. Disgust clips occupied the low-valence, high-arousal quadrant but were not consistently differentiated from fear. Seven clips were revised by removing low-register pedals, increasing the salience of sounds semantically associated with contamination, and reducing rhythmic regularity. In Experiment 2 (n = 62), the revised clips achieved significant differentiation from fear on the continuum. Results suggest that musical expression of disgust requires not merely abstract structural codes but the integration of indexical sounds associated with contamination experiences within non-tonal musical environments. These findings provide a methodological foundation for constructing disgust-related auditory stimuli applicable to research on music-evoked emotions and their interaction with moral and political judgment.

articles.title: Assessing Parent and Youth Perceptions of Attachment:  Validation of the Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI)
articles.authors: Jason W. Payne; Sebastian Dys; Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles.abstract: The Adolescent Attachment Anxiety and Avoidance Inventory (AAAAI) is a 16-item measure of youth attachment in caregiving relationships. Modelled after the original anxiety and avoidance subscales of the Experiences in Close Relationships questionnaire (ECR; Brennan et al., 1998), which assesses these dimensions in adult romantic relationships, the AAAAI includes parallel youth and parent report formats, providing options for comparative psychometric evaluation. This study examined the factor structure and validity of the AAAAI across four independent parent samples (N = 490, 400, 228, 551) and one youth sample (N = 499). Confirmatory factor analyses supported a two-factor structure, with improved fit after select model relaxations. Differential associations with youth internalizing and externalizing problems supported the discriminant validity of each subscale. Additionally, multi-method analyses confirmed that anxiety and avoidance were distinguishable across informants, while modest parent-youth convergence suggested complementary rather than interchangeable perspectives. This study provides robust psychometric support for the significance of differentiating attachment anxiety and avoidance dimensions in parent and youth-reports of attachment and supports the use of AAAAI for this purpose.

articles.title: Bayesian Evidence Synthesis: Aggregating Evidence from Partially Overlapping Hypotheses
articles.authors: Florian Metwaly; Björn Alfons Edmar; Duco Veen; Irene Klugkist
articles.abstract: Bayesian Evidence Synthesis (BES) provides a framework for aggregating evidence across studies that evaluate the same hypothesis but differ in design, precluding traditional data pooling or meta-analysis approaches. We investigate a novel application of BES in which individual studies assess only part of an overarching informative hypothesis. Using a comprehensive simulation study inspired by an applied research setting, we compare evidence aggregated through BES with that directly derived from testing a complete hypothesis on pooled data. We consider scenarios in which the overarching hypothesis is correctly specified as well as misspecified, and we evaluate the performance under varying sample sizes, effect sizes, and correlations. Results show that BES can reliably recover support for the correctly specified overarching hypothesis, with convergence to its theoretical limits as information increases. However, under misspecification, BES can come to conclusions that diverge substantially from testing a complete hypothesis on pooled data, particularly when evaluated against the complement hypothesis. These findings are in line with the correct interpretation of BES, as it aggregates evidence on the study level, rather than being pooled evidence. The findings underscore the importance of hypothesis specification and the choice of the alternative hypothesis. We conclude that BES is a valuable tool for synthesizing evidence across heterogeneous studies, but researchers have to be aware of potential misspecifications and the choice of the alternative hypothesis.

articles.title: Cognitive performance in young and middle-aged adults with obesity: a systematic literature review
articles.authors: Camille Sellier; Marie-Claude Brindisi; Léopold Fezeu; Cecilia Samieri; Valentina A. Andreeva; Stéphanie Chambaron
articles.abstract:
Objective
This systematic review synthesizes longitudinal evidence on associations between obesity and cognitive performance in early or middle adulthood aged 18 to 64. 
Methods
A comprehensive search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science identified prospective studies comparing adults with obesity to those of normal weight and assessing cognitive performance, using validated cognitive tests. Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-E, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results
Among a total of 4,871 studies, 4 met the inclusion criteria. Three studies evaluated global cognitive performance in middle-aged adults. Two studies reported poorer cognitive performance in individuals with midlife obesity and a more rapid decline in cognitive performance over 10 years in those who were metabolically unhealthy. One study found no association. Long-term obesity was also associated with lower overall cognitive performance in middle age. Executive performance appeared to be associated with obesity. Research on memory was mixed, as two studies found a negative association with obesity, while two found no association. Methodological weaknesses included imprecise exposure measurements and inadequate adjustment for confounding factors.
Conclusions
The available evidence is too sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically uncertain to establish a clinically meaningful independent association between obesity and cognitive performance before age 65. Future prospective studies should include cognitive assessment at baseline and repeated follow-up, report standardized effect estimates, use domain-specific cognitive outcomes, address confounding a priori, and assess central adiposity and metabolic health alongside BMI, particularly in younger adults.
PROSPERO registration: CRD42024573250
Keywords: Adults, Cognitive functions, Cohort studies, Executive functions, Obesity

articles.title: A stakeholder-informed approach to the development and implementation of national digital registry for psychosis: findings from the EPICare platform
articles.authors: Rachel Upthegrove; Melanie Lafanechere; Megan A. Pope; India Francis-Crossley; John Ainsworth; Sophie Allan; Tumelo Bogatsu; Niyah Campbell; Richard Drake; Sonia Johnson
articles.abstract:
Introduction
Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) services reduce the burden of psychotic disorders, yet significant inequities persist across England in access to NICE‑recommended treatments, provision of psychological therapies, and long‑term outcomes. These disparities are compounded by fragmented electronic health record (EHR) systems, inconsistent data capture, and limited interoperability, preventing routine real‑time evaluation of care quality and effectiveness. The Early Psychosis Informatics into Care (EPICare) programme aims to develop a national learning healthcare system incorporating a standardised core dataset and clinician dashboard to support equitable, data‑driven psychosis care. 

Methods
Our stakeholder co-design approach comprised three interlinked work packages delivered between 2021 and 2022. Using a participatory co‑design approach, four multi‑stakeholder workshops and preparatory lived‑experience sessions were conducted to identify essential data elements, refine content, and develop dashboard requirements. Stakeholders included people with lived experience, carers, clinicians, informaticians, academics, and policymakers. Parallel informatics work examined EHR systems across five NHS Mental Health Trusts to assess technical feasibility, data maturity, and harmonisation requirements. Implementation research—via interviews and workshop observations—evaluated anticipated barriers and facilitators to future adoption. 

Results
Consensus was achieved on a core EPICare dataset including sociodemographic variables, NICE psychosis standard measures, PROMs (DIALOG, GBO, ReQOL), CROMs (HoNOS, symptoms), and longitudinal symptom data. Stakeholders defined key dashboard features such as outcome notifications, treatment reminders, and performance indicators, prioritising usability and alignment with clinical workflow. Substantial variation in Trust‑level data infrastructure informed a flexible technical architecture to mitigate implementation risk. 

Discussion
Our EPICare stakeholder engagement delivered a co‑designed, technically feasible and nationally scalable specification for a psychosis learning health system, enabling progression to platform development and piloting across five NHS demonstrator Trusts.

articles.title: Silent Scars: Psychopathology Networks Across Cumulative Childhood Trauma Exposure and the Role of Shame About Eating
articles.authors: Emanuele Fino; Simona Popusoi; Cherie Armour; Leah Browne; Andrei Corneliu Holman
articles.abstract: Background: Childhood trauma is associated with eating disorder (ED) psychopathology and broader transdiagnostic symptoms, yet the role of shame about eating remains overlooked. This study examined psychopathology networks across cumulative childhood trauma exposure, focusing on internal and external shame about eating. Methods: A sample of 624 Romanian adults from the community completed self-report measures of childhood trauma, EDs, shame about eating, mentalisation, alexithymia, post-traumatic stress, depression, anxiety, insomnia, dissociative experiences, and psychotic-like experiences. Participants were grouped according to whether they reported no moderate-to-severe trauma, one trauma domain, or multiple trauma domains. Networks were estimated using Spearman correlations and EBICglasso regularisation. Community structure, expected influence, bridge expected influence, and network comparison analyses were conducted. Results: Across groups, shame about eating was embedded within ED psychopathology. Internal shame was most central in the multiple-domain trauma network, where it showed the highest expected influence and was more central than in the no-trauma network. Interoceptive deficits, PTSD, personal alienation, depression, and alexithymia also showed high centrality and bridge centrality. The multiple-domain network showed a distinct dissociative and psychotic-like experiences community. Conclusion: Shame about eating represents an important but under-recognised component of ED psychopathology, particularly in the context of cumulative childhood trauma exposure, where it shows a distinctive pattern of associations with ED behaviours and other mental health symptoms.

articles.title: Bodily experiences shape spatial-size associations: Links between hand dominance and physical stimulus size
articles.authors: Christian Seegelke; Peter Wühr
articles.abstract: Participants respond faster to physically smaller stimuli with their left hand and faster to larger stimuli with their right hand as compared to the reversed assignment, constituting the SSARC (spatial-size association of response codes) effect. In the present study, we tested the hypothesis that the mapping between space and size (the SSARC effect) might originate from manual asymmetries (i.e., handedness). Right-handed and left-handed participants performed reaching movements in the horizontal plane with their left and right hand to centrally presented target positions of different size (small or large). Regardless of arm posture (parallel or crossed) and handedness, participants initiated their movements faster with their non-dominant hand in response to small stimuli and faster with their dominant hand in response to large stimuli compared to the reversed assignment. These findings thus document a strong influence of anatomically- or body-based coding on the SSARC effect and provide evidence that it originates from bodily experiences related to manual asymmetries.

articles.title: Some psycholinguistic effect sizes are larger in the lab than on web-based platforms
articles.authors: Grusha Prasad; Emily Morgan
articles.abstract: The increasing use of web-based platforms for evaluating quantitative predictions in psycholinguistics raises an important methodological question: are effect sizes estimated on these platforms comparable to those obtained in laboratory settings? To address this question, we replicated an existing self-paced reading study designed to measure garden-path and syntactic adaptation effects across four platforms: SONA-lab, SONA-online, Prolific, and MTurk. We found that garden-path effects were consistently larger in the laboratory than on all three web-based platforms. Exploratory analyses of filler items revealed a similar attenuation of word frequency and word position effects in the web-based platforms. Together, these findings suggest that testing platform can systematically influence estimated effect sizes and should therefore be considered when evaluating quantitative predictions in psycholinguistics.

articles.title: Illusion of control, gambler’s fallacy, or neither? Testing key models of gambling psychology by extending Langer and Roth (1975)
articles.authors: Charlotte Eben; Ty Hayes; Zhang Chen; Philip Newall
articles.abstract: Cognitive biases about randomness, such as the illusion of control and the gambler’s fallacy, are central to the widely-used cognitive models of disordered gambling. In a highly-cited foundational paper, Langer and Roth (1975) found that participants thought they were better at predicting coin-flips when they were randomised to receive more wins at the start rather than the end of a 30-flip sequence. This replicable effect, which has been attributed to the illusion of control, could also be driven by biases that do not involve active involvement, such as the gambler’s fallacy. We therefore designed a large-scale (N=1,594) online 2x2 experiment, where the sequence manipulation was crossed with a manipulation of active involvement, with “self” participants dictating the coin-flips personally, and “other” participants viewing another participant’s flips and predictions. The original effect of sequence replicated, occurring across both “self” and “other” conditions. However, participants in the “other” condition consistently rated the participants they observed as being better at predicting coin-flips than participants in the “self” condition rated their own abilities, an effect consistent with neither the illusion of control nor the gambler’s fallacy. Furthermore, participants’ Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) scores did not correlate with their ratings of coin-flip predictions. We conclude that while Langer and Roth’s sequence effect is replicable, it is not attributable to the illusion of control or the gambler’s fallacy, and may be a poor analogue of chance-based naturalistic gambling formats due to its lack of association with PGSI scores.

articles.title: Assessing Sensitivity in Youth as a Moderator of Psychopathological Outcomes Across Contexts
articles.authors: Maria Brown; Anne-Laurie Bélec; David P Laplante; Ashley Wazana
articles.abstract: Youth differ in how strongly they respond to environmental influences, with some individuals demonstrating greater sensitivity to both adverse and supportive contexts. Environmental sensitivity (ES) has emerged as a unifying framework encompassing theories such as differential susceptibility, biological sensitivity to context, and vantage sensitivity. This scoping review examined sensitivity as a moderator of the relationship between environmental exposures and mental health outcomes in children and adolescents. The review aimed to (1) identify key markers used to approximate individual differences in sensitivity and (2) examine the methods used to measure these markers across studies. A total of 34 articles representing 37 studies were included. Markers of ES fell into five categories: phenotypic (e.g., temperament, sensitivity), genetic (e.g., 5HTTLPR, DRD4), physiological (e.g., cortisol, vagal tone), biological (e.g., prematurity), and neurobiological (e.g., amygdala activation). Phenotypic markers were most commonly studied, primarily assessed through parent- or youth-report questionnaires. Sensitivity was found to moderate the effects of various environments on mental health, with differential susceptibility emerging as the most consistently supported theoretical model. Assessment approaches varied widely in measurement tools, informants, and analytic methods depending on the marker used. Few studies used multi-informant or longitudinal methods. This review highlights the value of identifying sensitive youth who may be more responsive to both risk and protective factors and highlights the need for more methodologically rigorous research to guide personalized prevention and intervention efforts within an ES framework.

articles.title: Emotional Mirror: A Local Multimodal Generative Framework for Synthetic Memory Reconstruction
articles.authors: Eslam ElShamy; Mohamed W. Fareed; Amir Jahanian Najafabadi
articles.abstract: This research introduces a novel human–AI collaborative framework that establishes the technical foundation for future physiologically informed design in Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). While traditional AI applications treat data as static storage, we explore how machine-learning architectures can facilitate the reconstruction and externalization of fragmented traumatic memories. The proposed framework couples a written narrative, an identity-conditioned webcam image of the human subject, and an optional physical object with a locally deployed diffusion-based generative pipeline, producing visual reconstructions under clinician-adjustable conditioning parameters. The architecture is designed for future integration with real-time autonomic signal processing, enabling physiological markers of arousal to dynamically modulate image generation during graded exposure. In the present work, we establish the underlying multimodal generative and safety infrastructure and evaluate its technical feasibility using healthy volunteers on consumer-grade hardware; no claims regarding clinical efficacy are made. Rather than attempting factual reconstruction, the framework produces an "emotional mirror" that emphasizes subjective emotional experience over objective accuracy. We conclude by discussing the ethical, technical, and translational considerations required for future clinician-supervised deployment and clinical validation.

articles.title: SHAP-Interpretable Random Forest Classification of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder from Resting-State EEG: Comparing Power and Coherence Features
articles.authors: Naderi; Amir Jahanian Najafabadi
articles.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic psychiatric condition for which objective neurophysiological markers remain limited. Resting-state EEG has been proposed as a potential biomarker source, but the relative utility and stability of different EEG feature classes remain unclear. This study compared absolute spectral power and coherence features for classifying OCD patients and healthy controls using a SHAP-interpretable Random Forest framework. Resting-state EEG data from 46 OCD patients and 95 healthy controls were analyzed, with the control group balanced to 46 participants. Separate Random Forest models were trained for absolute power and coherence features using a leakage-free 5-fold cross-validation pipeline in which SHAP-based feature selection was performed exclusively within each training fold. The absolute-power model performed at chance level, whereas the coherence model showed modest classification performance. However, no feature was consistently selected across all folds, indicating substantial instability in the identified predictors. These findings suggest that coherence may contain more discriminative information than absolute power in this dataset, but neither feature class provided clinically reliable classification. More broadly, the results caution against overinterpreting high accuracies reported in small EEG-ML datasets without leakage-free validation, feature-stability analysis, and external replication.

articles.title: Pupil Dynamics Are Associated with Individual Differences in Visual Time-Reproduction Accuracy
articles.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Khaled Bagh; Kayser Christoph
articles.abstract: Accurate temporal reproduction depends on the interaction between sensory encoding, attention, motor production, and bodily state. Visual timing is especially likely to be influenced by oculomotor behavior because the eyes continuously stabilize, interrupt, and resample visual input through pupil-linked arousal changes. The present study tested whether spontaneous pupil fluctuations track moment-to-moment timing or stable individual differences. Eighty healthy adults reproduced visually presented intervals at a fixed viewing distance of 120 cm while pupil size was recorded continuously at 500 Hz. After preprocessing, 4,104 valid participant-trials were available. The primary outcomes were signed relative reproduction error, indexing directional bias, and absolute error, indexing timing precision. Mixed-effects models and participant-level regressions were used to examine within-participant and between-participant associations. Pupil metrics showed weaker trial-level effects, but reduced participant-level pupil models predicted both signed bias and absolute error, suggesting that stable pupil-linked arousal profiles relate to individual timing precision. These findings suggest that the eyes do not merely record visual time-varying events; their stabilization, interruption, and arousal-linked dynamics are embedded in how visual durations are reproduced.

articles.title: Cardiac and Respiratory Dynamics Modulate Temporal Interval Judgments
articles.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi; Khaled Bagh; Kayser Christoph
articles.abstract: Judgments of time intervals are usually studied as decisions made just based on external sensory information. However, various bodily signals continuously provide a rhythmic context in which judgements of time are made. Hence bodily states may bias encoding, maintenance, and decision processes about time. The present study examined whether cardiac and respiratory dynamics predict trial-level performance in temporal interval tasks. Young adult participants completed auditory and visual short/long interval-judgment tasks while electrocardiography (ECG) or respiration was recorded continuously. From the ECG we extracted heart rate, heart-rate variability (RMSSD), cardiac phase, and a binary systole-state around stimulus onset, stimulus offset, and response onset. From the respiration signal we estimated respiratory phase and cycle length. Using Mixed-effects models we tested whether physiological predictors improved the prediction of accuracy and response bias beyond interval duration alone. Cardiac dynamics were associated primarily with response bias: lower heart rate was linked to a greater likelihood of short responses, RMSSD predicted underestimation in an interval-dependent manner, and systole-state models improved fit in time-resolved analyses, especially for shorter intervals. Respiratory phase also predicted temporal decisions, with phase-dependent changes in both short-response bias and accuracy across task-relevant windows. Together, these findings suggest that temporal interval judgments are embedded within dynamic bodily states. Rather than acting as peripheral noise, cardiac and respiratory signals provide physiologically meaningful context for temporal cognition.

articles.title: The Impact of Complexity on Risky Choices: An Evidence Accumulation Account
articles.authors: Maohua Nie; Jörg Rieskamp; Sebastian Olschewski
articles.abstract:
Risky options often differ not only in outcomes and probabilities, but also in the cognitive demands required to evaluate them. Yet most theories of risky choice either ignore complexity or treat it as a static feature of the option, modeled as a utility discount or with heteroscedastic errors. We propose a process-level framework that explains how complexity shapes both choice and response time within an evidence-accumulation architecture. The framework assumes that complexity reduces the signal-to-noise ratio of evidence accumulation, making evaluation slower and choices less consistent, and that decision makers partly adapt to these processing constraints by adjusting their decision strategies. These mechanisms can explain how complexity reduces choice consistency and how it shifts preferences toward simpler options.
We evaluated this framework in three preregistered experiments that manipulated complexity in structurally distinct ways: through the number of outcomes, arithmetic expressions of outcomes, and compound probabilities. Across studies, complexity made choices slower and less consistent. When both options were complex, these effects were best explained by reduced signal-to-noise ratios and partially compensatory increases in decision thresholds. When options differed in complexity, preferences for simpler options were best explained by an initial bias toward simplicity combined with a drift-rate adjustment during accumulation. The compound-probability manipulation, however, marked a boundary condition: different forms of complexity can change the representations that evidence accumulation operates on. Together, these findings advance a dynamic account of risky choice in which complexity shapes preference construction by changing both the rate at which decision evidence accumulates and the strategies used to evaluate the options.

articles.title: When Is Complexity Avoided in Risky Choice? A Domain Comparison of Gains and Losses
articles.authors: Maohua Nie; Jörg Rieskamp; Sebastian Olschewski
articles.abstract: Risky options often differ not only in expected value and risk but also in complexity. Although complexity aversion is well documented in the gain domain, it remains unclear whether this aversion extends to losses. We contrast two theoretical accounts that make diverging predictions: if complex options are avoided because processing them requires cognitive effort, complexity aversion should be similar for gains and losses; if complexity instead induces cognitive uncertainty, whose evaluation depends on domain-specific risk preferences, complexity aversion should be weaker for losses than for gains. We tested these predictions in two preregistered experiments (N = 138 and 135) using gambles that vary outcome complexity, separately for the gain and loss domain: Study 1 examined choices between two risky options, and Study 2 contrasted a risky with a sure option. In both studies, participants chose complex options significantly less often in the gain than in the loss domain; specifically, they were complexity averse for gains but complexity neutral for losses. Response times showed a converging asymmetry, significant in Study 2. Subjective ratings of cognitive uncertainty predicted complexity aversion in the gain but not in the loss domain. These results favor the cognitive-uncertainty account over the effort account: complexity increases cognitive uncertainty, whose behavioral consequences depend on the outcome domain.

articles.title: Modeling Individual Differences in Working Memory: Subject-Level Parameter Recovery within the Memory Measurement Model Framework (M³)
articles.authors: Jan; Gidon T. Frischkorn; Klaus Oberauer; Simon B. Schaefer; Anna-Lena Schubert
articles.abstract: The memory measurement model (M3) is a flexible modeling framework designed to measure parameters associated with different processes in working memory. It assumes that memory representations receive different levels of activation at retrieval, which arise from the sum of the strengths of item and binding memory. Transforming the activation of representations in different response categories into their respective recall probabilities then allows estimating the contributions of different memory processes to working memory performance. So far, parameter recovery has been reported only for group-level parameters of the M3. In contrast to experimental research, individual differences research focuses on variation in subject-level parameters. Adequate recovery of subject-level parameters is therefore a requirement for their valid measurement. To address this gap, we ran a parameter recovery simulation to assess subject-level parameter recovery as function of different experimental design choices. Our Bayesian hierarchical M3 implementation recovers subject parameters acceptably to very well, as demonstrated both through simulations and empirical parameter recovery using a complex span dataset. Based on the results, we recommend that researchers ensure that participants select not-presented lures (i.e., items not in the memory set) at least sometimes ( ≥ 2%) and collect a minimum of 200 retrieval responses per subject (40 trials at set size 5). When these conditions are met, the simple and complex span models specified in the M3 framework exhibit robust parameter recovery, well-calibrated posteriors, and satisfactory reliability. These challenges primarily arose from the substantial amount of data required to achieve sufficiently precise parameter estimates. In contrast, M3 parameters modeling free-time effects such as extended encoding and removal processes could not be recovered with sufficient precision and showed poor reliability. Posteriors of the M3-CS-EE model were well calibrated, while the M3-MU model showed systematic miscalibration of the subject-level parameters.

articles.title: Audioaufnahmen von Entscheidungsgesprächen in der Geburtsplanung bei Beckenendlage – Evaluation von Akzeptanz, Relevanz und Umsetzbarkeit einer perso-nenzentrierten Intervention
articles.authors: Anja Lindig; Mirja Baumgart
articles.abstract:
In around five percent of pregnancies, the baby is in breech presentation at term, meaning that the buttocks or feet are positioned downward instead of the head. In Germany, a cesare-an section is performed in 87% of these cases. Many of these procedures are planned, alt-hough there is not always a clear medical indication. At the same time, many pregnant wom-en wish to receive comprehensive and understandable counseling in order to make an in-formed decision together with their healthcare professionals about whether to attempt an ex-ternal cephalic version before birth or about the mode of birth itself (vaginal birth or cesarean section). These decisions are considered “preference-sensitive” because personal wishes, fears, experiences, and life circumstances play an important role. 
The PregAUDIO pilot project, led by Dr. Anja Lindig, examined the attitudes of 23 pregnant women and 5 gynecologists toward a person-centered intervention – namely, audio record-ings of birth planning consultations at BEL. Only 7 participants listened to the audio recording at home. In interviews, pregnant women and gynecologists expressed support for audio re-cordings as part of birth planning. However, the pregnant women found the recording to be of little relevance to their own decision, as they remembered the content of the conversation well, their partner was present during the conversation, or the decision had already been made during the conversation. When the recording was listened to, it mostly served to con-firm a decision that had already been made. Gynecologists expressed concern regarding possible legal consequences of recorded counseling sessions. 
The Decisional Conflict Scale used showed that the pregnant women’s decision conflict de-creased significantly between t0 and t1 and continued to decrease slightly to t2. Pregnant women rated PEF as very high during the counseling session. However, the objectively measured extent of PEF (measured using the Observer OPTION 5 TM observation instrument) indicated low implementation of PEF, particularly regarding “supporting a collaborative coun-seling process.” The interviews with pregnant women revealed that consultations at the clinic and the experiences shared by others were particularly influential in their decision-making. Participants expressed a desire for better access to evidence-based information, particularly from private practice gynecologists, as well as for their ambivalent feelings to be addressed during counseling sessions.
The findings from PregAUDIO can help develop interventions for pregnant women and gyne-cologists, and, through structural changes, empower pregnant women, improve the quality of care, and thereby facilitate more patient-centered obstetric care.

articles.title: Losing Focus Behind the Wheel: Psychometric Adaptation of the Attention‑Related Driving Errors Scale in Türkiye
articles.authors: Ibrahim Ozturk; Betül Akçakoca; Melike Kahraman; Alperen Orhan; Bahar Öz
articles.abstract: Understanding the psychosocial factors influencing driving behaviours is of significant importance due to its potential impact on enhancing road safety. A specific category of driving behaviours, attention-related driving errors, represents a critical yet understudied aspect of everyday road safety in Türkiye. To address this gap, this study aimed to (1) adapt the Attention-Related Driving Errors Scale (ARDES) for the Turkish context, (2) examine gender and in-vehicle interface differences in attention-related driving errors, and (3) investigate associations between attentional control, driving skills, and attention-related driving errors. A total of 420 licensed drivers (aged 18–62 years) participated in an online survey that included the ARDES, Attentional Control Scale, Driving Skills Inventory, and demographic measures. The sample was randomly divided for principal component analysis (PCA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Group differences were examined using the Kruskal–Wallis test, and the relationships between other factors and attention-related driving errors were tested via hierarchical regression. EFA supported a single-factor structure for the ARDES, explaining 32% of the variance, while CFA indicated an acceptable model fit. Female drivers reported significantly more attention-related errors than males, whereas males reported higher perceptual-motor skills. Interface type was associated only with attentional shifting, with drivers of combined interfaces scoring lower than those using touch- or button-based systems. Younger age, touch-based interface use, poorer attentional focus, and lower perceptual-motor and safety skills are associated with higher rates of attention-related driving errors. The results demonstrated that the ARDES-TR is a reliable and valid measure for assessing attention-related driving errors in Türkiye. These errors are significantly associated with attentional control and driving skills. These findings underscore the importance of considering both cognitive capacities and driving skills in interventions.

articles.title: Intra-decisional Dynamics Shape the Influence of Attributes on Value-based Choice
articles.authors: Douglas G. Lee; Fadong Chen; Youqi Quan
articles.abstract: Managers, marketers, and policymakers increasingly shape decisions by arranging when and how option attributes are presented, yet we lack a process-level account of why such interventions work. Do people apply well-defined preferences when making value-based decisions, or do they construct preferences on the spot in ways that depend on how information is acquired and evaluated over the course of a decision? Resolving this question is central to understanding and influencing decisions in households, organizations, and markets. Here, we investigate how the temporal dynamics of the choice process shape consumption decisions in two studies using response times and time manipulations. In each study, participants made binary choices between snack foods with and without time constraints. Using regression analysis and drift-diffusion modeling, we found that moving from time pressure to free response to time delay increases the importance of pleasure and decreases the importance of nutrition for pleasure-seeking participants, whereas the pattern reverses for nutrition-seeking participants. These results indicate that people preferentially process either pleasure or nutrition early in the choice process (relative to the other attribute) and that the time afforded by a choice environment systematically reweights these attributes. Because these intra-decisional dynamics are governed by when attributes enter processing, they identify a concrete lever – the ordering, salience, and timing of attribute information – through which managers and policymakers can steer consumption and other economic decisions.

articles.title: Anatomical Reorganisation Channels the Emergence of the Infant Vocal Repertoire
articles.authors: Christopher Martin Mikkelsen Cox; Axel G. Ekström
articles.abstract: Why do infants the world over begin their vocal lives with growls, grunts, squeals, and creaky phonation? And why does this pattern hold across radically different languages and caregiving environments? We propose that the mechanical geometry of the vocal tract at each developmental stage acts as a continuously changing constraint on what infant vocal exploration can discover. Beyond limiting what sounds are possible, this geometry actively generates certain acoustic events as the natural consequence of ordinary exploratory activity. In the neonatal larynx, tissue properties lower the thresholds for phonatory regime transitions; in the tongue, fibre geometry confines early exploration to a single axis until hyoid descent and palatal deepening open new dimensions; in the anterior articulators, independently available components, such as lip closure and jaw oscillation, await the reorientation of suprahyoid muscles that makes their coupling discoverable. Drawing on the motor development literature and neuropsychology of learning, we argue that vocal repertoire emerges through the same discover-stabilise-differentiate logic that governs early limb control: the body generates variation before any intent exists, sensory consequences draw the infant back to the patterns that produced them, and stabilised motor-auditory mappings gradually become communicative resources. The sequence of vocal development can thus be understood as the natural output of exploration within a continuously reorganising anatomy, where each new configuration, through its own mechanical properties, redefines the acoustic possibilities that undirected exploration will discover.

articles.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
articles.authors: Brian W. L. Wong; Arthur G. Samuel; Efthymia C Kapnoula
articles.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

articles.title: The Impact of Social Learning on Learning Traps
articles.authors: Yanjun Liu; Alisha Shaikh; Ben R Newell; Andrew Perfors; Brett Hayes
articles.abstract: People often fall into learning traps where a false belief about the structure of the environment leads to under-exploration of rewarding options. Five studies (N = 1342) examined whether observation of decisions made by another learner facilitated escape from a trap or increased trap prevalence. In studies of horizontal social learning (Experiments 1a, 1b, 2), participants first had private experience with a task where approach of different category members could lead to gains or losses. We identified whether participants had learned an optimal two-dimensional categorization rule or fallen into the trap of using a one-dimensional rule. Participants then observed the approach decisions of another learner using the same or a different category rule. A substantial proportion of those who had initially fallen into the trap shifted to the optimal rule after observing use of an alternate rule. This escape from a learning trap was found following observation of both optimal (Experiment 1a) and sub-optimal rules (Experiment 1b, 2). In vertical social learning (Experiments 3, 4), social observation of approach decisions took place before private learning. Such observation led to reduced trap prevalence when the social demonstrator modeled an optimal rule but increased trap prevalence when they modeled a one-dimensional rule. These effects generalized to a learning environment with the same underlying feature structure but different feature-category mappings. These results both offer a novel approach to remediating learning traps as well as highlighting how poorly coordinated social learning can intensify traps.

articles.title: Gradual delays do not affect the tolerability of a smartphone friction intervention
articles.authors: Sabrina Fay Norwood; David Joachim Grüning; Frederik Riedel; Malte Elson
articles.abstract: Friction-based digital interventions reduce unwanted smartphone behaviour by interrupting automatic app-opening sequences, but substantial attrition rates limit their real-world impact. One proposed strategy for improving retention is to gradually increase intervention intensity, allowing users to adapt before encountering the full intervention dose. We tested this in a preregistered six-week field experiment (N = 1,641) in which new users of the smartphone friction app one sec were randomly assigned to one of four delay escalation schedules ranging from immediate full-dose exposure (10 seconds throughout) to gradual escalation (3 → 6 → 10 seconds). Retention was low and relatively similar across conditions (65–70% dropout), with no significant difference between any of three escalation schedules and the standard full-dose condition. Exploratory analyses likewise found no association between delay duration and weekly dropout. However, among participants who remained engaged, longer delays were associated with higher rates of dismissed app opening attempts, suggesting that delay duration influenced behaviour without improving retention. These findings do not support gradual intensity escalation as a retention strategy and instead suggest that intervention characteristics may optimise different outcomes. While delay duration appears useful for shaping behaviour among retained users, retention itself may depend more on the introduction of interruption than its precise duration.

articles.title: Training the power: Physical size guides the processing of exponential expressions
articles.authors: Bar Salman; Ami Feder; Serena Mingolo; Nadav Neumann; Mariya Lozin; Michal Pinhas
articles.abstract: This study examined how training and the physical size of base and power components affect the processing of exponential expressions. Research has shown that exponential expressions are cognitively challenging and that physical attributes, such as component size, can influence their processing. In the present study, we aimed to improve the comprehension of exponential expressions by training participants (N = 32) to learn the mathematical roles of bases and powers across standard and non-standard displays, where the latter featured a physically larger power than the base. Over five training sessions, participants practiced matching exponential expressions with their multiplication decompositions. In a subsequent test phase, we assessed both automatic processing (via a physical comparison task) and intentional processing (via a numerical comparison task) of the trained exponential expressions, as well as untrained expressions. Training improved response speed for familiar expressions, although automatic processing was limited; participants continued to focus on the physically larger component rather than the mathematically more important one. In the numerical comparison task, training improved the understanding of the power’s role for familiar expressions, but this understanding did not generalize to new expressions. Additionally, performance on the exponent knowledge test improved significantly following training, with reduced underestimation errors. The findings suggest that while training can enhance the intentional processing of exponential expressions, automatic processing of exponential syntax remains limited, highlighting the need for refined instructional approaches to exponential expressions.

articles.title: Recycling Rivalry: Social Identity Appeals Increase Recycling When Combined with Intergroup Comparison
articles.authors: Hege Landsvik; Jareef Martuza; Sveinung Jørgensen; Lars Jacob Pedersen; Siv Skard
articles.abstract: While many people recycle at home, they are less likely to do so in public, where high waste production meets a diffusion of individual responsibility. We examine whether social identity can close this gap. Across two preregistered season-long field experiments at a Norwegian Premier Division football stadium, we test the separate and combined effects of ingroup identity appeals and intergroup comparison on the recycling behavior of football supporters. In Study 1 (N = 5,712), an ingroup identity appeal did not increase recycling relative to an outgroup appeal, suggesting that standalone identity appeals are insufficient to shift behavior. When the ingroup appeal was combined with a ranking of clubs by their recycling rate, recycling rates were more than two times higher than in any other condition. Study 2 (N = 6,598) replicated this effect against a no-intervention control. Study 3 (N = 761), a post-game survey among Study 2’s participants, showed that supporters exposed to the combined intervention reported greater motivation to recycle and greater perceived importance of contributing to the ingroup’s success. These findings extend social identity theory by showing that identity appeals increase recycling when group performance is tied to a concrete metric of success, which an intergroup comparison can supply, making the behavior a way to pursue positive group distinctiveness.

articles.title: No Single Model Fits All: Conflict Decision-Making Models Vary More Across Datasets Than Across Tasks
articles.authors: Wanke Pan; Jia-Shun Wang; Klaus Oberauer; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles.abstract: Conflict variants of evidence accumulation models are widely used to explain human cognitive control. However, the generalizability of these models is largely unknown because of the lack of systematic comparisons across multiple conflict tasks and multiple datasets. Here, using a unified amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) framework, we compare the standard DDM and three conflict-specific variants across a benchmark database comprising eight independent studies (N = 1,375). We validate the ABI as a common framework for model comparison, fit DDM, DMC, DSTP, and SSP to each participant, and find that DSTP is the most frequently selected best-fitting model, but its superiority varies more across datasets than across tasks. Exploratory analyses show the 22 parameters cluster into four latent dimensions; the Inhibitory Process factor, of greatest theoretical interest in cognitive control, is unstable. Achieving cross-dataset generality of conflict diffusion models remains a major challenge.

articles.title: Depression symptom network reorganization under internet-based emotion regulation intervention: Evidence from a large real-world cohort
articles.authors: Jianjie Xu; Sihan Liu; Hanyi Zhang; lu Chen; Lv Xiangxi; Mengyu Miranda Gao; Yueqin Hu; Shaozheng Qin; Mark S. Chen; Rachel Han
articles.abstract: Depression can be conceptualized as a network of interacting symptoms. Although internet-based interventions are widely used, their associations with changes in symptom network structure remain unclear. Here, in a real-world observational cohort of 26,643 adults completing an internet-based emotion regulation intervention, we examined pre–post differences in depressive symptom network structure, global connectedness, and symptom centrality, stratified by reduction status. Analyses indicated that the two core depressive symptoms (i.e., depressed mood and anhedonia) showed reduced centrality after the intervention, whereas several non-core symptoms either increased or remained unchanged. The “symptom reduction” and “symptom non-reduction” subgroups showed largely comparable network characteristics at baseline. After the intervention, the “symptom reduction” subgroup displayed lower global network strength, a reorganized network topology, and reduced centrality of the core symptoms, whereas the “symptom non-reduction” subgroup showed no significant network alteration. Further analyses using residualized symptom change scores showed a similar pattern: among individuals with comparable baseline depressive symptom severity, those with better-than-expected outcomes showed lower post-intervention network connectivity than those with poorer-than-expected outcomes. Clinically anchored improvement analyses further indicated that reduced centrality of depressed mood was observed across alternative definitions of improvement. Although causal inference is precluded by the observational design, this study provides large-scale descriptive real-world evidence on how depressive symptom networks change alongside symptom reduction during routine use of a digital intervention.

articles.title: Empirically derived phenotypes can reduce diagnostic heterogeneity
articles.authors: Miriam K. Forbes; John F. Buss; Daniel P. Moriarity; Eiko I Fried; Holly Frances Levin-Aspenson; Lorenzo Lorenzo-Luaces; Kasey Stanton; Ashley L. Watts; Gregory W. Forbes
articles.abstract: Diagnostic heterogeneity is a longstanding challenge for the classification of mental illness because people who receive the same diagnosis can differ markedly in their symptom presentations as well as in the mechanisms underlying those symptoms. High heterogeneity undermines both the clinical utility of diagnostic labels and the scientific accuracy of research that treats disorders as coherent constructs. In this study, we examined heterogeneity across six internalizing disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD], major depressive disorder [MDD], and posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD]) using three complementary approaches to quantifying heterogeneity: 1) descriptive heterogeneity (how many symptom profiles can theoretically satisfy the diagnostic criteria, and how many are observed in practice), 2) person-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels capture people with similar symptom presentations), and 3) construct-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels group symptoms with similar patterns of association with external validators). Analyses drew on subsamples from a large convenience sample with elevated psychopathology, predominantly from Australia and the USA (n = 14,762, mean [SD] age = 38.0 [18.0]; 55% women). Results showed that specific phobia was consistently the least heterogeneous; social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and GAD had mixed results; and MDD and PTSD were highly heterogeneous across all metrics. Notably, empirically derived phenotypes nested within each disorder substantively reduced heterogeneity relative to the DSM diagnoses. The study provides both a systematic multi-method approach to characterising different types of diagnostic heterogeneity, and a practical path toward more precise and informative constructs that can be implemented by rescoring existing data.

articles.title: Bilingualism and Cognitive Aging in Ethnically Diverse Older Adults: Cross-sectional and Longitudinal Evidence from HABS-HD
articles.authors: Lihua Xia; Kang Ren; Ina Demetriou; Kshipra Gurunandan; Karin Meeker; Didac Vidal Pineiro; Richard Henson
articles.abstract:
Objectives
Identifying modifiable factors that shape cognitive aging trajectories is a central goal in aging research. This study examined whether bilingualism is associated with dementia status and longitudinal cognitive decline, and whether associations vary by ethnicity or gender.
Methods
We analyzed Wave 7 data from the Health and Aging Brain Study—Health Disparities (HABS-HD), a longitudinal US cohort of adults aged ≥50 years. Bilingualism was defined by self-reported use of a second language. Cross-sectional analyses included 4,140 participants (1,013 bilinguals); longitudinal analyses included 1,760 participants (522 bilinguals) followed for up to four visits at approximately 2-year intervals. Outcomes were baseline dementia status and latent factor scores for executive function and episodic memory derived from 11 neuropsychological tests. Regression and linear mixed-effects models assessed associations, adjusting for age, education, gender, ethnicity and practice effects.
Results
Results indicated that bilingualism was not associated with baseline dementia status or conversion to probable dementia. Cross-sectionally, associations varied by ethnicity: Hispanic bilinguals showed higher executive function and episodic memory scores. No advantage was seen in White participants; conversely, Black bilinguals had lower episodic memory scores. Longitudinally, bilingualism was associated with slower episodic memory decline independent of sociodemographic factors; no longitudinal association was observed for executive function. Discussion
These findings suggest that bilingualism may confer domain-specific benefits for memory trajectories in later life, while cross-sectional differences appear shaped by sociocultural context. The results underscore the importance of considering ethnic diversity and language history when evaluating experiential influences on cognitive aging.

articles.title: ‘It is my life don’t take that choice from me’: Autistic young adults’ experiences, preferences and needs regarding autistic peer support
articles.authors: Tohid Zarei; Caelan Farr; Maxx Fischer; Summer Marchiori; KJ Hepworth; Caroline Ellison; Tobias Loetscher
