We also find heterogeneity across technologies in consumers' sensitivity to subsidies and that attitudinal predictors (and especially beliefs about cost, health, and safety benefits) dominate sociodemographic predictors. These results have direct implications for active policy design. Information campaigns designed to shift beliefs about health and safety play an important complementary role alongside cost-focused messages. Our geographically fine-grained estimates of future adoption at the census tract level provide rich local data for policy-makers, researchers, and practitioners designing incentive programs and planning grid infrastructure as California households continue to electrify.

articles.title: Risks and possibilities in sharing preprints during the doctorate
articles.authors: Margaret K. Merga
articles.abstract: During doctoral candidature, students may seek to publish journal articles, which they may incorporate in their thesis if their institutional policy permits. They may consider sharing pre-prints of these texts either pre- or post-publication to promote open access and knowledge mobilisation. There is very little extant research that explores doctoral students’ knowledge of the risks and possibilities involved in sharing their work in this form, and this chapter seeks to identify those that they could encounter. It offers immediate value for informing doctoral education and a useful foundation for future research that is specific to the doctoral student experience.

articles.title: What Does Frontier Access Buy? Benchmarking LLM Access Tiers and the Reproducibility Case for Open Weights in Survey Coding
articles.authors: Chris Soria
articles.abstract: Social scientists coding open-ended survey responses with large language models (LLMs) face a tradeoff between proprietary frontier systems, cheaper commercial alternatives, and open-weight models that can be audited and self-hosted. This study benchmarks eighteen LLMs across four access tiers, from proprietary flagships to open-weight models small enough to run on a laptop, zero-shot against a human consensus on three open-ended questions from a probability-sampled U.S. panel. External validation adds a British Election Study task and an online-comment emotion task (GoEmotions), spanning five tasks in three contexts. The flagship proprietary models' average margin over their cheaper counterparts is statistically indistinguishable from zero, despite stronger general-benchmark performance. Pricing tells the same story: frontier models cost 1.3–6× more per token, yet for most of them some cheaper model is also more accurate, and the field's second-best macro F1 comes from its cheapest closed model. Open-weight models have largely caught up. The largest ones match both proprietary tiers on cell-level agreement, while on the stricter macro F1 they trail by about two points on average. They reach this at no per-call cost, with the reproducibility and data-privacy advantages of self-hosting. Both patterns hold out of domain. The leading models, closed and open alike, agree with a trained human coder about as well as the two coders agree with each other. Failure is patterned. Errors concentrate on interpretive categories where the human coders themselves disagreed, and on longer responses, penalties from which frontier prices buy little relief. The caveat is scale. Laptop-scale models show strong cell-level agreement but trail further on macro F1, so fully local deployment carries a modest, task-dependent accuracy cost. Hardware scale and question difficulty, not price or license, are the binding constraints on these tasks.

articles.title: International Migration: A Barrier towards Help Seeking for IPV among South Asian Immigrant Women in the US
articles.authors: Tasneem Moshiour
articles.abstract: The literature review explores the way international migration works as the barrier in seeking help by South Asian immigrant women in the U.S. Significant number of women from these countries experience IPV and suffers from asking for help or support due to different aspects of South Asian culture. This review examines the structural barriers faced by these populations and also, looked into the theoretical perspective of fundamental cause theory. Finally, the review addressed the future scope of study and need for culturally driven services targeted toward these women.

articles.title: Request routing services undermine the reproducibility of open weight LLMs
articles.authors: Joe Higton; Joshua A Tucker; Christopher Barrie
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard tool for classifying text in social science. To make these classifications reproducible, researchers are often advised to use open weight models and to set the sampling temperature to zero. We show that this advice is insufficient when models are accessed through a request-routing service, in which queries are sent to different hosting providers through a single API. Using a popular request-routing service, OpenRouter, we classify British manifesto sentences for ideology 100 times per sentence across eight models and 33 hosting providers, alongside five model configurations served on our own hardware, generating approximately 1m classification draws. When using the request-routing service, open weight models consistently fail to return deterministic outputs. Depending on the model, only 26% to 92% of sentences receive the same label in all repeated classifications. This variation is not solely due to different providers fielding queries: for five of the eight models, the majority of classification variance arises within providers. On our own hardware, the same task is perfectly reproducible at temperature=0. We conclude that reproducibility depends on the entire model hosting environment, and recommend that researchers report the fullest available metadata and raw responses when using LLMs.

articles.title: Same Facts, Different Meanings: Factual Information, Interpretation, and Attitude Change
articles.authors: Martín Opertti
articles.abstract:
A key puzzle in the political information literature is why factual information reliably updates citizens’ beliefs about the fact in question but rarely shifts downstream political attitudes. Using two preregistered survey experiments (N ≈ 3,250) covering eleven issues across economic indicators and misstatements by prominent political figures, this paper makes two contributions. First, we test whether the muted effect of factual information on downstream attitudes holds for outcomes that are less entrenched and more proximate to the information than
those tested in prior work—such as economic evaluations and perceptions of politicians’ honesty and competence—and find that even these outcomes respond only modestly. Second, we develop and empirically test a framework of six adjacent belief dimensions—regarding causes,
relevance, and intent—through which factual information may be reinterpreted in ways that reshape its political meaning. We find evidence of adjacent belief updating, although concentrated on specific dimensions rather than widespread. The strongest finding is that individuals
who learn that a favored politician made an inaccurate claim concede the inaccuracy but shift toward viewing the statement as figurative, with sizable effects across two independent studies. Importantly, where adjacent belief adjustment occurs, its direction is contingent on individuals’ predispositions. Uncongenial information triggers adjustment that attenuates the political implications of the fact, while congenial information triggers no such adjustment or small shifts in the opposite direction. Together, the results illustrate how parallel trends in factual accuracy can coexist with divergent trends in how those facts are politically interpreted.

articles.title: Agent-oriented modality in the languages of North America
articles.authors: Jessica K. Ivani; Alexandra Nogina; Taras Zakharko
articles.abstract: This study examines the morphosyntactic and functional encoding of agent-oriented modality in a maximally diverse sample of languages from North America. Focusing on necessity, obligation, ability, and desire, we show that agent-oriented modality is expressed through a wide range of construction types, including tense-aspect-mood morphology, modal verbs, non-verbal formatives, and complex clauses. We show that clustering the constructions by their formal properties yields three groups that align closely with the modal functions of necessity, ability, and desire. We further show that the constructions encoding different modal functions tend to differ in their morphosyntactic profiles, with strong necessity and obligation in particular showing systematic associations with tense marking, and weak and strong necessity with mood marking, respectively. These findings suggest that agent-oriented modality is not a uniform grammatical category, but a structured functional domain whose subtypes recruit material from different areas of grammar. The study contributes to a typological understanding of modality by combining constructional detail and an autotypologizing approach to cross-linguistic comparison.

articles.title: Measuring Perceptions of Extreme Weather Events and  Climate Change
articles.authors: Clara Brügge; Patrick Kraft; Franziska Quoß
articles.abstract: As climate change increases the frequency and severity of extreme weather events (EWEs), people worldwide are beginning to experience these impacts firsthand. While a growing body of research has explored how this direct experience of EWEs affects public perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors, findings remain inconclusive. A central challenge in this literature is the large researcher degrees of freedom in operationalizing EWEs. This inconsistency partly stems from a lack of theoretical and empirical clarity regarding what the public actually perceives as an EWE. Previous work has shown a low correspondence between subjective perceptions and objective meteorological data, highlighting a disconnect between scientific definitions and the experience of laypeople. To address this gap, we investigate how average citizens conceptualize EWEs using a high-quality panel survey conducted in Switzerland. We field an open-ended survey question with experimental variation in its wording and use large language models (LLMs) to classify the content of responses across multiple dimensions – including the type of event, its regional focus, and its relation to climate change. Validating the classification against human coding and benchmarking it against fine-grained objective weather data, we find that respondents draw on a wide range of considerations, that question wording – especially a local cue – strongly shapes responses while explicit climate-change priming does not, and that open-ended responses correspond at least as closely to objective weather data as a targeted closed-ended item. We discuss the promise and limitations of LLM-based measurement for research on climate and extreme weather perceptions.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: When the Well-Off Feel Left Behind: Income Misperception and Populist Attitudes
articles.authors: Thilo N.H. Albers; Daniel Bischof; Felix Kersting; Fabian Kosse
articles.abstract: Why do materially secure citizens embrace populist attitudes? Research on the populist right has focused primarily on economically vulnerable voters and left-behind places, leaving unclear why support extends to citizens who are objectively well off. We argue that a belief-based source of grievance helps explain this puzzle: citizens may underestimate their relative economic standing and feel deprived despite material security. Using a survey module embedded in the Innovation Sample of the German Socio-Economic Panel, we show that pessimistic income-rank misperceptions predict stronger populist attitudes conditional on actual rank. Instrumental-variable and within-household analyses strengthen a causal interpretation. A preregistered survey experiment randomly provides personalized information about respondents' actual income percentile. The control arm replicates the observational pattern; the treatment corrects beliefs and shifts income satisfaction, but does not reduce populist attitudes. Economic grievance can therefore travel upward through perceived status, while becoming politically resistant once organized by populist narratives.

articles.title: Embodied Knowledge: The Case of Sociology
articles.authors: Ruben Gowricharn
articles.abstract:
Spontaneous Community Research (SCR)—research that draws on experiences accumulated over years or decades of community participation before research questions are formulated—generates valuable sociological knowledge from insider perspectives. Yet current ethical frameworks and journal data requirements often exclude this approach. This article demonstrates that standard expectations—such as prospective research design, informed consent, tangible data deposits, and reproducibility—are incompatible with SCR's distinctive characteristics because its data are embodied: stored in the researcher's memory, inseparable from lived experience, and not amenable to conventional documentation. Rather than excluding SCR from academic discourse, the article argues for epistemic pluralism by recognising multiple legitimate forms of social knowledge production, each requiring ethical standards that are appropriate to its methodology rather than uniformly applied. To this end, it proposes alternative validation strategies that emphasise contextual transparency, collective corroboration, and reflexive acknowledgement of the evolution of the researcher's positionality.

Keywords: embodied knowledge, insider research, autoethnography, positionality, data repositories, research ethics

articles.title: Digital Infrastructures and Contemporary Governance in Times of Conflict
articles.authors: Ahmad Agha
articles.abstract: Scholarship on internet shutdowns and digital authoritarianism tends to treat digital infrastructure as an instrument of repression, while research on wartime digital government treats it as an instrument of resilience. This article argues that the two are not separable: in conditions of acute interstate war, the same architecture can simultaneously secure a regime’s continuity and restrict the visibility of its population. Drawing on Michael Mann’s concept of infrastructural power and using the 2026 U.S.–Israel–Iran war as a revealing single case, it examines connectivity control, command decentralization, cyber pressure on critical systems, and the management of online narratives as one governing logic rather than discrete tactics. A central claim is that wartime decentralization mattered politically as well as militarily: it helped preserve authority after leadership losses and communications disruption, while the same distributed architecture widened the scope for miscalculation and escalation. The article’s contribution is to specify a mechanism the two literatures have tended to treat separately — the co-location of resilience and repression in a single infrastructure, and the double-edged character of the decentralization that sustains continuity.

articles.title: Economic Constitutionalism: Legitimate Authority and the Democratic Governance of Institutional Purpose
articles.authors: Anton Oleynov
articles.abstract: Formally accountable regulation can remain inadequate when its objectives are privately, technically, or distributionally insulated from democratic authorization. This article introduces economic constitutionalism as a second-order framework that extends regulatory legitimacy analysis from the conduct of regulators to the authority to define what regulation is for. The analysis reconstructs authorization assumptions across regulatory legitimacy, capture, public-purpose, and quantification literatures and derives three mechanisms of regulatory-purpose displacement and four design properties for purpose-responsive regulation. Applications to artificial intelligence, platform labor, education, care, and public information demonstrate the framework's comparative diagnostic reach. The argument shifts the regulatory design agenda from procedural compliance alone to the authorization and revision of regulatory purpose.

articles.title: Digital Green Signaling: Dual Pathways to Conspicuous Green Consumption and eWOM
articles.authors: Senyo Obed Amponsah
articles.abstract: Social media has become a key space where consumers encounter green claims, watch others perform sustainable lifestyles, and decide whether green products are credible, desirable, and worth sharing. Yet green consumption research still tends to treat online green communication as a single influence and often stops at purchase intention. This conceptual paper develops a dual-pathway model explaining how engagement with online green content may lead to green conspicuous consumption intention and green electronic word-of-mouth intention. The firm-generated pathway argues that brand-controlled green content builds perceived green brand authenticity and green trust, especially when green claims are transparent, specific, and verifiable. The user/influencer-generated pathway argues that peer and influencer green content activates informational and normative social influence, especially when social proof is visible through likes, comments, reviews, shares, and public endorsement. Green trust and anticipated social approval then converge to shape consumers’ willingness to display green consumption, which subsequently encourages green electronic word-of-mouth. The paper makes three contributions. First, it separates firm-controlled and socially embedded green content as distinct routes to consumer response. Second, it positions conspicuous green consumption as a meaningful sustainability outcome in social media contexts. Third, it explains green electronic word-of-mouth as a digital extension of visible green identity, rather than merely a post-purchase communication behavior. Future empirical directions, theoretical implications, and practical implications for sustainable marketing are also discussed.

articles.title: BLACK LGBTI+ PENTECOSTAL FAMILIES AND AFFECT OF RESISTANCE: DECOLONIAL PERSPECTIVES FROM THE BRAZILIAN PERIPHERY
articles.authors: Átila Augusto dos Santos
articles.abstract: This paper presents key results from doctoral research in Religious Studies on Black LGBTI+ Pentecostal families in Brazil, conceptualized herein as quilombo families (famílias aquilombadas), viewed as ethical-affective expressions of resistance within the religious field. Utilizing an intersectional, decolonial, and affective framework, engaging critical scholars such as Joe Coyle, E. Patrick Johnson, and Beatriz Nascimento, the study deploys the metaphor of the Pentecostal quilombo to analyze inclusive churches as urban territories of affection, freedom, and the restoration of social bonds. Grounded in semi-structured qualitative interviews with 33 Black LGBTI+ individuals and families across inclusive congregations, the findings reveal how these family units challenge traditional Christian heterocisnormative dogmas and articulate a counter-hegemonic spirituality. This framework demonstrates both the transformative potential of affective-political reconstruction and the structural limits of inclusion when racial, moral, and gender hierarchies remain unbroken.

articles.title: LABRASHURIAS: THE PRETOGAYS LANGUAGE OF PENTECOSTAL INCLUSIVE CHURCHES
articles.authors: Átila Augusto dos Santos
articles.abstract: The "pretogays" language (Santos, 2022) represents a linguistic manifestation resulting from the intersection of the epistemic category "pretoguês" (Gonzalez, 1988), the vernacular "pajubá" (Lima, 2017), a "dialect" of "resistance" utilized by transvestites and transgender individuals, and "glossolalia" (Sullivan, 2020), the characteristic and mystical speech of Pentecostals. These three communicative modes converge among LGBTI+ individuals within inclusive Pentecostal churches in Brazil, faith communities that do not condemn dissident sexualities but reframe them as divine gifts. Utilizing an intersectional framework (Crenshaw, 2002), further enriched by E. Patrick Johnson's Quare theory, Ashon Crawley's Blackpentecostal Breath, and Black sociolinguistics (Smitherman; Alim), this study demonstrates how race, class, gender, linguistics, and religion intersect to reveal how words and speech acts function as performative signs intrinsically linked to Black, gay, and Pentecostal embodiment.

articles.title: Designing engagement: A Research through Design approach to cultivating relational motivation for community-supported agriculture
articles.authors: Sota Takagi; Maoko Fujisaki; Mitsuyo Toyoda; Takumi Ohashi
articles.abstract: Global challenges such as climate change and food insecurity are closely linked to the unsustainable structures of dominant food systems. These systems are reinforced by entrenched mental models that treat consumers as passive buyers and agriculture as mere market transaction. Community-Supported Agriculture (CSA) offers a locally grounded model in which producers and consumers share the risks and benefits of production, holding potential to challenge these structures and foster new relationships and behaviors that contribute to systemic food system change. However, CSA remains underdeveloped in Japan, and how participation motivations are relationally generated through design remains poorly understood. This study examines how design interventions can cultivate relational motivation: forms of engagement arising through social connection and shared values rather than individual preference alone. A Research through Design (RtD) approach was employed to examine a collaborative design intervention in Isumi, Chiba, Japan (October 2025). It followed five phases: (1) educational sessions on CSA and natural farming, (2) a chef-curated meal featuring locally grown produce, (3) a farm field tour, (4) a facilitated Philosophy for Children (p4c) dialogue, and (5) a co-creation workshop. Eleven participants attended, supported by eight collaborators including a producer, a chef, local staff, and researchers. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires (seven-point Likert scales) and thematic analysis of dialogue and workshop data were used for analysis. Quantitative analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) showed a significant increase in participants’ ethical food-selection intention (p = .046, r = .63), and eight of ten reported increased willingness to join CSA despite half having had no prior awareness. Thematic analysis identified three themes: deepened understanding of natural farming, intergenerational responsibility for food culture, and critical reflection on production structures. These themes were translated into concrete CSA visions in the co-creation workshop. Through RtD, the study derived design principles for an entry-point intervention to cultivate participation intentions toward CSA: (1) sequential integration of learning, experience, and reflection; (2) cross-domain intermediary collaboration as social infrastructure; and (3) embodied and relational ethics that translate abstract values into situated action. These principles offer actionable guidance for designers, educators, and policymakers seeking to lower barriers to CSA participation within local communities.

articles.title: Dual Momentum: Cash Flows and Discount Rates
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: Observed continuation in abnormal returns is best understood not as a primitive phenomenon, but as the combined effect of two channels: cash-flow momentum and discount-rate momentum. This two-channel view follows directly from the identity that decomposes abnormal returns into cash-flow news and discount-rate news. We show that these channels imply distinct patterns in the joint behavior of raw returns and normal returns, extending the analysis beyond the canonical facts of momentum. These patterns provide a diagnostic for assessing whether momentum profits are driven more by cash-flow momentum or by discount-rate momentum.

articles.title: Intertemporal Dynamics of Asset Prices
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: A basic intuition in asset pricing is that higher perceived risk is associated with higher expected return. Yet this intuition alone does not fully explain how expected return is translated into realized return. An important link is therefore still missing. To address that gap, this study moves beyond the static risk-return tradeoff and focuses on three intertemporal elements: information processing, repricing in response to revisions in perceived risk, and hedging against future reinvestment risk. By bringing these elements together, the study explains how asset prices evolve over time and how returns take shape over time.

articles.title: Speculation-Based Asset Pricing
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study proposes speculation-based asset pricing, in which valuation is driven by speculative beliefs and return forecasts rather than by risk-based dividend discounting. This shift matters because the theory does not require a dividend stream and therefore applies to non-dividend-paying assets. The key object is a speculative baseline return, defined as the return level investors believe the asset can eventually deliver. This baseline determines the explosive growth rate of the bubble component, which identifies the speculative part of the asset price. The analysis then shows a dynamic implication: faster convergence to this growth potential requires a greater near-term return cost.

articles.title: Long-run political change after the Great Recession
articles.authors: Vincent Heddesheimer; Hanno Hilbig
articles.abstract: What are the long-run political consequences of economic crises? We study the Great Recession in the United States, exploiting geographic variation in unemployment shocks. Harder-hit counties shifted toward Democratic candidates. House gains persisted through 2022, after the shock's employment effects had dissipated, while presidential gains attenuated after 2016. House gains did not track local recovery or Republican incumbency, which weighs against simple retrospective voting accounts. Harder-hit places also showed no shift toward right-wing populist candidates or movements. Instead, survey and ballot measure evidence points to economic scarring and demand for protection: residents of harder-hit places remained pessimistic about their economic prospects, even as personal finances recovered, and became more supportive of social protection. Taken together, the findings suggest that a crisis can durably reshape what affected communities demand from government after acute local labor market distress has subsided.

articles.title: Institutions and the future African fertility decline
articles.authors: Tom Austin Moultrie; Ian M Timæus
articles.abstract: Africa will account for nearly all global population growth in the 21st century, driven by persistently high fertility rates and substantial demographic momentum. This paper argues that, while many of the distal factors that affect fertility (for example, education, urbanisation, and contraceptive access) are well-understood as important determinants of fertility patterns and levels, demographers have tended to focus on these at the expense of considering the less-quantifiable institutional aspects which mediate the impact of those factors on the pace and timing of fertility declines. Drawing on McNicoll's foundational framework, we argue that weak, contested, or unstable institutions render high fertility a rational household strategy. Without deliberate institution-building — analogous to East Asia's developmental states — a demographic-institutional trap is likely to perpetuate Africa's elevated fertility well into the 21st century.

articles.title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
articles.authors: Mihai Alexandru Bîclea
articles.abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

articles.title: Stable Contexts Are Not Static Causes: A Latent Variable Approach to Time-Varying Consequences of Stable Unobserved Heterogeneity
articles.authors: Baeksan Yu
articles.abstract: Urban-health studies increasingly examine environmental co-occurrences, but longitudinal analyses often rely on fixed-effects (FE) models whose assumptions about stable unobserved heterogeneity are left implicit. This article uses a structural equation modeling (SEM) representation of FE to clarify a narrow but important point: stable, time-invariant, unobserved heterogeneity is controlled by conventional FE only when its contribution to repeated outcomes is also constant across waves. When stable histories of segregation, infrastructure, or governance have changing consequences as environmental co-occurrence configurations are reorganized, conventional FE models may leave residual confounding. I review the classical fixed-effects structural equation modeling (FE-SEM) representation, then present two diagnostic extensions: time-varying-loading FE-SEM (TVL-FE-SEM), a single-latent-dimension model with wave-specific loadings, and constant-and-deviation-loading FE-SEM (CDL-FE-SEM), a two-latent-dimension model that adapts the intercept/slope logic of latent growth modeling to separate common and deviation-loading profiles. A compact Monte Carlo simulation shows that classical FE-SEM recovers the true effect only when stable unobserved heterogeneity enters repeated outcomes with constant loadings, TVL-FE-SEM performs well when the same single latent source has changing loadings, and CDL-FE-SEM helps diagnose whether stable heterogeneity operates through more than one loading profile under a fixed-effects specification, though with finite-sample instability. An empirical illustration using Korean community-health data from 2021–2024 demonstrates the sequence as a diagnostic workflow.

articles.title: Consumer Protection Governance in Gendered Markets: Appearance Pressure, Consumer Awareness, and Gender-Differentiated Pricing in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula Tricity, India
articles.authors: Vishal Thakur
articles.abstract: Gender-differentiated pricing, commonly termed the "Pink Tax," describes situations in which comparable products or services are priced differently by gender. While prior research has documented such price differences, less is known about the behavioral mechanisms shaping how consumers experience them. Drawing on the Political Economy of Beauty and consumer protection governance frameworks, this study examines how appearance pressure, gendered consumption behavior, and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior relate to experienced gender-differentiated pricing among 151 consumers surveyed in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula tricity, India. Using exploratory factor analysis, correlation, and multiple regression, the results indicate that appearance pressure (β = .407, p < .001) and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior (β = .320, p < .001) significantly predicted experienced gender-differentiated pricing, while gendered consumption behavior did not (β = .128, p = .120), together explaining 44.6% of the variance. These findings suggest that consumers' experiences of differential pricing are shaped more by social expectations around appearance and price awareness than by purchasing behavior alone. Robustness checks (Harman's single-factor test, variance inflation factors, and bootstrapped confidence intervals) support the stability of these results. Given the study's convenience sample and cross-sectional design, findings are presented as exploratory rather than generalizable, with implications framed as hypotheses for future regulatory attention rather than settled policy prescriptions. The study contributes an interdisciplinary behavioral perspective to consumer protection governance research in the Indian context.

articles.title: Dealing with Factor Mismeasurement
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: Empirical implementation of asset pricing models faces a fundamental constraint. The true pricing factors implied by theory are unobservable, so researchers must rely on observable empirical factors. Because these factors are only proxies, they may contain measurement errors that distort estimated factor exposures, risk premia, and assessments of model performance. This study examines factor measurement errors and develops a methodology for assessing their empirical consequences. The methodology allows researchers to evaluate the reliability of asset pricing tests more carefully and draw more credible conclusions from empirical evidence.

articles.title: Shifting toward a Micro ICAPM
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: Intertemporal asset pricing models typically begin with the market factor and introduce additional state variables to capture changes in investment opportunities over time. Empirically, these state variables have traditionally been proxied by macroeconomic variables because they reflect broad shifts in economic conditions affecting the aggregate opportunity set. These proxies are useful at the aggregate level, but less suited to representing variation in investment opportunities across individual assets. This study therefore develops a micro-level approach that replaces macroeconomic proxies with asset-specific variables. The central idea is that a broad set of such variables can more fully represent individual, time-varying investment opportunities.

articles.title: Out of the APT Shadow
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: In empirical asset pricing, researchers often evaluate a pricing theory through its empirical factor model. This practice is widespread, but rests on a strong premise: the factor model must be a valid empirical proxy for the theory it claims to implement. In most applications, this premise is assumed rather than verified. Good performance alone is not decisive, because a factor model may reflect equilibrium pricing, arbitrage pricing, or both. This study addresses this ambiguity by separating risks arising solely from arbitrage considerations from those relevant to equilibrium pricing. It then tests whether a factor model truly represents equilibrium pricing theory.

articles.title: Operationalizing Qualitative Multimedia Content Analysis for Short-Form Video: A Methods and Data Study of Grooming Precursors Masked as Relationship Advice
articles.authors: Heath Landress
articles.abstract:
Objective: This methods and data article operationalizes qualitative multimedia content analysis (QMCA) for short-form video posts on TikTok and Instagram Reels, focusing on the method's execution and the frequency structure of observable grooming-precursor cues masked as relationship advice.
Method: A purposive corpus of 100 public short-form videos, evenly split between TikTok and Instagram, was archived, de-identified, and coded using MAXQDA 24 for time-segment coding and Excel for the codebook, audit trail, and thresholds. A five-pass routine separated visual features, audio features, on-screen text, and relational/boundary cues. Category development relied on same-document co-occurrence, with recurrence requiring five or more distinct posts.
Results: The final codebook contained 289 codes and produced 1,233 post-level feature hits. Recurrence concentrated in presentation-layer categories: Parasocial Proximity and Platform Normalization appeared in all 100 posts, and Intimate Setting Cues in 80. Covert precursor categories recurred less often: Power Imbalance Normalization in 30 posts, Coercive Reframing in 15, Boundary Erosion in 14, and Isolation and Secrecy in 10.
Conclusions: QMCA provides an auditable method for documenting how short-form advice content packages relational scripts through camera, voice, setting, captioning, and platform conventions. The taxonomy supports prevention-oriented screening without inferring creator intent or labeling any post as grooming.

articles.title: Lessons from Tanzania’s Ujamaa for Smart Settlements in Nepal: Social Justice and Economic Development
articles.authors: Keshav Bhattarai; Ambika P. Adhikari
articles.abstract:
This article examines lessons Nepal can draw from Tanzania’s experience with Ujamaa, the African socialist development model initiated by President Nyerere in 1967. Using comparative policy analysis, published research, official documents, and exploratory field observations from selected Tanzanian locations, including the capital and villages in the Iringa Region, the study evaluates Ujamaa’s achievements and limitations. It assesses their relevance for Nepal’s landless populations and smart-settlement initiatives. The analysis focuses primarily on rural and peri-urban development and does not examine urban squatter housing and rural-to-urban migration.

The comparison demonstrates that some lessons from Tanzania can be considered for Nepal’s own program. Ujamaa contributed to national integration, a shared linguistic identity, literacy, primary education, and rural services. However, it also reduced household autonomy, disrupted existing livelihood systems, and failed to achieve sustained agricultural productivity, employment generation, and income growth. 

The article also briefly discusses Nepal’s own Go to the Village Campaign of 1967, which had mixed success, and Korea’s generally successful 1970 Saemaul Undong movement for a comparative perspective of village-oriented national programs.

The article proposes a Smart Settlement Framework for Nepal based on verified beneficiary identification, differentiated tenure and housing options, voluntary participation, livelihood-oriented site selection, serviced land, cooperative enterprise, accountable local governance, and measurable pathways from social protection to economic mobility.

articles.title: The missing quadrant: perceived voluntariness, option sets and the acceptance of green digital tools
articles.authors: Maha Jehanzeb; Talha Murtaza; Rida Safdar
articles.abstract: Technology acceptance research measures voluntariness as a perception and, in its consumer flagship, assumes it outright, while parallel stream studies explicitly mandate use. It is between the perception and the mandate that a state lies which neither can classify: a use that is formally optional and reported as chosen while the adopter’s set of viable alternatives has been closed off by conditions beyond their control. This paper names that state foreclosed adoption, where the voluntariness assumption of acceptance research is adapted through the lens of the self-determination theory, whose definition of autonomy as endorsement rather than independence entails that the experience of free adoption cannot certify that alternatives existed. The paper goes on to develop a typology of adoption states (volitional, foreclosed, mandated), three foreclosure mechanisms (economic, architectural, relational) with distinct sources and visibilities, an account of leadership style as the mechanism converting foreclosure into internalisation or bare compliance, and eight propositions with an operationalisation agenda. Green digital technology is argued to be the domain where the resulting misclassification costs most, because foreclosed green adoptions are counted twice over, as voluntary and as value driven, inflating estimates of environmental motivation in research and in organisational sustainability metrics.

articles.title: Humanity after the peak: long-run population and human-capital pathways for global environmental change
articles.authors: Samir KC
articles.abstract: Population and human-capital pathways are central to global environmental change research, yet most widely used demographic projections end in 2100. This creates a time-horizon problem for slow-moving environmental processes, including sea-level rise, land-use change, long-lived infrastructure, food-system transformation and adaptation across generations. We extend Shared Socioeconomic Pathways population and human-capital scenarios to 2300 and examine how peak population gives way to long-run demographic decline, aging and regional redistribution. In the middle-of-the-road pathway, the global population declines to about 4.2 billion by 2300. In the sustainability pathway, it approaches 1 billion. These are not extinction scenarios, but they describe a profound change in the social and demographic setting in which environmental demand, exposure, adaptation and policy operate. The results show that the post-2100 period cannot be treated as a simple continuation of twentieth-century population growth. A smaller, older and more educated world may reduce some overall pressures while intensifying others, especially around labor, care, migration and uneven regional change. Long-run environmental analysis, therefore, needs population pathways that extend beyond 2100 and include not only population size, but also age, education, spatial distribution and demographic momentum.

articles.title: Bringing public attention to disease into global health priority-setting
articles.authors: Wenceslao Arroyo-Machado; Ismael Rafols; Adrian A. Díaz-Faes
articles.abstract:
Background: A central concern in global health priority-setting is whether the supply of scientific knowledge aligns with health needs and demands. This alignment is usually assessed by comparing research effort with disease burden, overlooking other type of “social demand” of disease, in particular whether diseases are socially visible and generate public attention. We develop an analytical framework that treats public attention and epidemiological burden as complementary dimensions of health demand and examines their alignment with knowledge supply.
Methods: We combine data on publications indexed in OpenAlex, disability-adjusted life years from the Global Burden of Disease, and Wikipedia pageviews for 2016 to 2023, as indicators of research effort, disease burden, and public attention, respectively. We map 19 disease groups and 138 specific diseases across these three dimensions. Ternary plots are used to position diseases according to their relative balance across dimensions and to identify diseases that are over- or under-represented in research effort relative to epidemiological burden and public attention. We compare Global North-South patterns using German, Persian, Swahili, and Vietnamese language areas to assess how these relationships vary across territories.
Results: The three dimensions show limited alignment. At the disease group level, cardiovascular diseases account for the largest share of disease burden, mental disorders attract the largest share of public attention, and neoplasms concentrate the largest share of research effort. Public attention and disease burden are weakly correlated at both group and specific disease levels, indicating that Wikipedia pageviews and DALYs capture distinct dimensions of health demand. Ternary plots reveal different forms of misalignment, with some diseases showing plots dominated by burden, others by research effort, and others by public attention. Territorial analyses add a further layer by showing that diseases follow disparate patterns of supply-demand (mis)alignment across different linguistic territories.
Conclusions: Public attention provides a complementary dimension for mapping global health needs and demands. Our approach identifies where scientific knowledge supply fails to match epidemiological and/or public attention, supporting more nuanced global health analysis that may be useful for priority-setting.

articles.title: Seguros complementarios y gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección de Fonasa: ¿riesgo moral o sesgo de selección? Análisis con microdatos administrativos, Chile, 2022 a 2025
articles.authors: Matias Goyenechea; Alberto Aylwin
articles.abstract:
Introducción. La crisis del sistema de Isapres, la migración de cotizantes hacia el seguro público y la expansión de la oferta de seguros complementarios han modificado los incentivos de gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección de Fonasa. No es claro si el mayor gasto de los beneficiarios asegurados refleja riesgo moral o sesgo de selección.
Objetivos. Estimar, desde la perspectiva del asegurador público, el gasto adicional en la Modalidad de Libre Elección atribuible a la tenencia de un seguro complementario, y descomponerlo en sesgo de selección y riesgo moral, entre 2022 y 2025.
Métodos. Estudio observacional analítico sobre microdatos administrativos individuales (enero 2022 a mayo 2025).El aseguramiento se identificó a partir de su uso efectivo. Se construyó un contrafactual mediante emparejamiento[MG1.1] de vecino más cercano (k = 1, sin reemplazo) sobre covariables observables y se corrigió el error de clasificación con un modelo no lineal de decaimiento por tamaño del hogar. El resultado fue la diferencia porcentual de gasto FAM en la Modalidad de Libre Elección por beneficiario, en unidades reajustables por inflación (unidades de fomento).
Resultados. La brecha bruta de gasto per cápita fue 57,6% mayor en los asegurados; se redujo a 44,2% tras el emparejamiento y convergió a un efecto promedio sobre los tratados de 30,2% (28,8 a 31,3% anual) tras corregir el error de clasificación. 
Conclusiones. El mayor gasto asociado a seguros complementarios combina selección de riesgo y riesgo moral; al menos unos 13 puntos porcentuales corresponden a diferencias de composición de la población que contrata seguros complementarios. Los seguros complementarios se asocian a un aumento del gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección del orden de 30% una vez controlados los sesgos observables y de clasificación.

articles.title: Social spending and democratic institutions in Southeast Asia: A comparative study between Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines
articles.authors: FADILLAH PUTRA
articles.abstract:
Purpose
This paper aims to analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries. Furthermore, this essay will also challenge the theory that the government system (majoritarian versus consensus democracy) influences the magnitude of social spending and welfare commitment, especially in Southeast Asian democracies, namely, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines.

Design/methodology/approach
This research uses descriptive statistics and qualitative data to match social spending with the development of democratisation in four cases.

Findings
The main argument is whether the presence of democratic institutions encourages the government to be more open, citizen-oriented and responsive or whether the inclusive political conditions will create more open public participation in the policymaking process. Thus, in the context of developing countries, public participation will be more likely to demand social policies.

Research limitations/implications
It has not been able to undertake a more detailed impact evaluation assessment of the development and change of democratic institutions towards policy outcomes within a shorter temporal scope. In addition, this thesis does not also provide details or explanations about the interaction process between particular democratic institutions and specific social policy sectors.

Practical implications
The process of interactions between particular electoral systems. For instance, the contribution to the emergence of policy in the health services sector or conducting research in normative democratic institutions such as public awareness of the importance of public participation in shaping and directing the implementation of poverty reduction policies could be studied, by using the historical institutionalism approach.

Originality/value
The impact of certain political institutions on public policy has become a very important discussion in the new institutionalism perspective. Social policy (social spending) as a manifestation of government’s commitment towards welfare is the result of institutional arrangement. In the context of developing countries, where social policy is needed to fulfill the basic needs of citizens, it is important to identify what kind of institutional formations are conducive to the development of social policy. This essay will analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries.

articles.title: Social norms solve coordination problems paradoxically created by shared interests
articles.authors: Minhua Yan; Yuanmei Li; Zhizhong Li; Robert Boyd; Sarah Mathew
articles.abstract: Human cooperation is motivated both by shared interests arising from kinship and friendship and by social norms, but whether these mechanisms substitute for or complement one another remains debated. Cooperative farming among Derung horticulturalists offers an ideal study context, because most cofarming occurs among kin or friends, and a norm prescribes equal harvest division by household regardless of contributions. We show that this norm solves two problems that shared interests cannot solve, or may even exacerbate. First, shared interests expand the range of acceptable divisions, making coordination harder. By specifying a salient division, the norm resolves this problem. Second, cofarmers often misperceive how much their partner benefits. By prescribing a division independent of cost-benefit assessments, the norm prevents these differences from unraveling cooperation. The complementary action of norms and shared interests may explain why humans cooperate with kin and friends more than other animals.

articles.title: The Harder the State Hits: Coercive Intensity, Protest Repression, and Terrorist Backlash
articles.authors: Ana Cristancho
articles.abstract:
Why does repression sometimes deter dissent but at other times generate terrorist backlash? Existing theories emphasise political opportunity, grievances, legitimacy and strategic interaction, but they do not fully explain when repression against dissent escalates into terrorist violence. I argue that backlash depends on the coercive mode through which state force is organised and interpreted. Coercion is more likely to deter when it remains proportionate, fair and predictable. Backlash becomes more likely when coercion creates two interconnected expectation gaps. The first is instrumental: compliance no longer appears sufficient to guarantee safety. The second is normative: the state violates its own claim to exercise force within bounded limits, signalling the exclusion of some groups rather than their protection. Under these conditions, excessive, arbitrary, indiscriminate or visibly disproportionate coercion weakens deterrence while intensifying grievance. It changes the moral ecology through which dissent is interpreted, making terrorist retaliation appear more strategically plausible or morally defensible.

I test this argument using country-quarter event data from ACLED and GTD for 2018–2021. The results show that coercive military involvement in domestic security is associated with higher subsequent terrorist activity. The association follows a coercion-intensity gradient: excessive force and military protest repression are more strongly associated with subsequent terrorism than lower-intensity intervention or police-led repression. These findings hold across alternative controls, temporal diagnostics and balancing checks, but remain observational. They suggest that repression backfires not simply because it is forceful, but because some forms of coercion undermine the legitimacy and predictability on which deterrence depends.

articles.title: What Is Coercion?
articles.authors: J Onwuka
articles.abstract: A brief monograph investigating the subject of coercion, comparing the perspectives of Sarah Conly's "Seduction, Rape, and Coercion", Patrick Bratton's "When Is Coercion Successful?: And Why Can’t We Agree on It?", and H.J. McCloskey's "Coercion: Its Nature and Significance". It is concluded that coercion is separate from persuasion by its method of action in that coercion threatens identity and persuasion does not. There is also a distinction between legitimate and illegitimate coercion.

articles.title: Fuzzy Cross-Database Record Matching for Missing and Unidentified Person Cases: Design and Retrospective Validation of the CAIRN Engine
articles.authors: Laura Innis
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Missing-person (MP) and unidentified-person (UID) records in the United States are fragmented across federal,
state, county, and volunteer-maintained systems, and the matching applied within those systems is
predominantly exact-field or manual. This paper describes CAIRN (Case Analysis and Intelligent Resolution
Network), a hypothesis-generation engine that scores MP-UID candidate pairs using seven weighted, error-
tolerant signals (fuzzy name similarity, distinguishing marks, temporal compatibility, geographic distance, age
fit, height/weight, and race with subset tolerance), applies two hard filters that eliminate a pair outright rather
than scoring it (biological sex, and chronological impossibility), and attaches an explicit confidence tier
reflecting how many identity-grade signals supported each score.
The engine was validated retrospectively on forty-eight confirmed-solved case pairs assembled from Internet
Archive snapshots of Doe Network case pages, current NamUs records, official press materials, and recovered
snapshots of NamUs records deleted after resolution. In a ranking benchmark on six solved pairs that took four
to forty-two years to resolve in reality - decades combined - the engine ranked the true match first in six of six
cases in a matter of seconds. Forty-two additional pairs spanning records-strong, minimal-data, recovered-
record, and movement and concealment classes scored between 0.463 and 1.000, each consistent with its
evidentiary class.
Of the twelve pairs scoring above 0.92, ten required more than a year of human review to connect and five
required more than a decade, with a median of approximately three years; the two exceptions, resolved in
roughly one month and roughly nine months respectively, are the two most recent cases in the benchmark.
Two confirmed matches are eliminated outright by hard filters: one by an incorrectly recorded biological sex,
and one by a missing-person report date standing in for a last-contact date, placing the recovery twenty years
before the reported disappearance.
A separate prospective field test cross-scored 2,508 Florida MP and 869 Florida UID summary records,
measuring behaviour under summary-level data rather than match accuracy. It demonstrated that summary-
level data alone produces high-scoring but low-confidence false positives; all three top-ranked candidates were
disproven under human review, and the failures directly motivated three engine corrections now incorporated.
All output is framed as leads for human verification through official channels, never as conclusions.

articles.title: A Rejoinder to 'Still Instrumentally Inclusive' (Turnbull-Dugarte & López Ortega)
articles.authors: Daniel de Kadt
articles.abstract: Turnbull-Dugarte and López Ortega's "Still Instrumentally Inclusive" (the Response) answers my replication (the Comment) of their 2024 American Political Science Review paper (the Article) with, among other things, a multiverse of 2,970 analyses based on eighteen different weighting schemes, randomization inference, and a trichotomous moderator. As I show in this rejoinder, each is undermined by bona fide errors in their code, their writing, and their interpretation. First, the multiverse is just many correlated variants of the same test. This is in large part due to the weighting schemes which suffer multiple problems (some due to code errors, some intrinsic), and are largely correlated variations on one weighting scheme. Second, due to code errors the randomization inference compares a weighted statistic against an unweighted null and, in the two heterogeneity tests, permutes the interaction column rather than treatment assignment column. Every permutation p-value the Response reports is therefore computed against the wrong reference distribution; when they are recomputed correctly, two of the five it reports as significant are no longer so, and they are the two the Response emphasizes. Third, the trichotomous moderator is erroneously described as terciles, but it is in fact based on non-tercile cutpoints. The key subgroup effect reported in the Response thus rests on comparing just thirty high-weight control respondents against thirty-one high-weight treated respondents, and ends up reaffirming my original point that the heterogeneity in study 2 is with respect to weights, and not immigration sentiment as their theory predicts. I close by documenting seven claims in the Response that are untrue or misleading.

articles.title: THE FORMATION OF THE U.S. HEGEMONIC REVOLUTIONARY BLOC
articles.authors: Aleksandar Korolija
articles.abstract: This article examines the formation and transformation of the revolutionary hegemonic bloc in colonial America during the period 1763-1776. Drawing on Antonio Gramsci's theory of hegemony, the analysis conceptualizes the American Revolution as a process of formation of class alliances among heterogeneous social classes under conditions of crisis. The article argues that revolutionary unity did not emerge spontaneously nor through elite manipulation alone, but through a prolonged and conflictual process in which merchants, large landowners, and lawyers articulated a hegemonic project capable of incorporating artisans and yeomen, while simultaneously containing popular radicalism. Using a structural-historical approach, the article distinguishes between two phases of the revolutionary crisis: an initial phase characterized by a fragmented and decentralized bloc organized around negative unity and resistance to British taxation (1763-1774), and a second phase marked by the institutionalization of the hegemonic bloc through the Continental Congress, provincial conventions, and committees of safety (1774-1776). The analysis highlights the central role of institutional mediation, the relative autonomy of political and ideological processes, and the strategic sacrifice of short-term economic interests by leading classes in order to sustain bloc cohesion. By demonstrating how hegemony can be constructed and exercised in the absence of a consolidated state, the article contributes to historical sociology and offers a theoretically grounded reinterpretation of the American Revolution as a case of pre-state hegemonic formation.

articles.title: Consumer Protection Governance in Gendered Markets: Appearance Pressure, Consumer Awareness, and Gender-Differentiated Pricing in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula Tricity, India
articles.authors: Vishal Thakur
articles.abstract: Gender-differentiated pricing, commonly termed the "Pink Tax," describes situations in which comparable products or services are priced differently by gender. While prior research has documented such price differences, less is known about the behavioral mechanisms shaping how consumers experience them. Drawing on the Political Economy of Beauty and consumer protection governance frameworks, this study examines how appearance pressure, gendered consumption behavior, and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior relate to experienced gender-differentiated pricing among 151 consumers surveyed in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula tricity, India. Using exploratory factor analysis, correlation, and multiple regression, the results indicate that appearance pressure (β = .407, p < .001) and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior (β = .320, p < .001) significantly predicted experienced gender-differentiated pricing, while gendered consumption behavior did not (β = .128, p = .120), together explaining 44.6% of the variance. These findings suggest that consumers' experiences of differential pricing are shaped more by social expectations around appearance and price awareness than by purchasing behavior alone. Robustness checks (Harman's single-factor test, variance inflation factors, and bootstrapped confidence intervals) support the stability of these results. Given the study's convenience sample and cross-sectional design, findings are presented as exploratory rather than generalizable, with implications framed as hypotheses for future regulatory attention rather than settled policy prescriptions. The study contributes an interdisciplinary behavioral perspective to consumer protection governance research in the Indian context.

articles.title: Designing engagement: A Research through Design approach to cultivating relational motivation for community-supported agriculture
articles.authors: Sota Takagi; Maoko Fujisaki; Takumi Ohashi; Mitsuyo Toyoda
articles.abstract: Global challenges such as climate change and food insecurity are closely linked to the unsustainable structures of dominant food systems. These systems are reinforced by entrenched mental models that treat consumers as passive buyers and agriculture as mere market transaction. Community-Supported Agriculture (CSA) offers a locally grounded model in which producers and consumers share the risks and benefits of production, holding potential to challenge these structures and foster new relationships and behaviors that contribute to systemic food system change. However, CSA remains underdeveloped in Japan, and how participation motivations are relationally generated through design remains poorly understood. This study examines how design interventions can cultivate relational motivation: forms of engagement arising through social connection and shared values rather than individual preference alone. A Research through Design (RtD) approach was employed to examine a collaborative design intervention in Isumi, Chiba, Japan (October 2025). It followed five phases: (1) educational sessions on CSA and natural farming, (2) a chef-curated meal featuring locally grown produce, (3) a farm field tour, (4) a facilitated Philosophy for Children (p4c) dialogue, and (5) a co-creation workshop. Eleven participants attended, supported by eight collaborators including a producer, a chef, local staff, and researchers. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires (seven-point Likert scales) and thematic analysis of dialogue and workshop data were used for analysis. Quantitative analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) showed a significant increase in participants’ ethical food-selection intention (p = .046, r = .63), and eight of ten reported increased willingness to join CSA despite half having had no prior awareness. Thematic analysis identified three themes: deepened understanding of natural farming, intergenerational responsibility for food culture, and critical reflection on production structures. These themes were translated into concrete CSA visions in the co-creation workshop. Through RtD, the study derived design principles for an entry-point intervention to cultivate participation intentions toward CSA: (1) sequential integration of learning, experience, and reflection; (2) cross-domain intermediary collaboration as social infrastructure; and (3) embodied and relational ethics that translate abstract values into situated action. These principles offer actionable guidance for designers, educators, and policymakers seeking to lower barriers to CSA participation within local communities.

articles.title: Evaluating the Youth Outcomes and Change Pathways of “Walk With Me”, a Peer Support Programme for Youths With or at Risk of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury in Singapore
articles.authors: Lyon Koh; Gerard Chung; Elizabeth Yee Min Chia; Anusha Agarwal; Sophie Cheng
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is common among youth and often serves social functions, yet most young people avoid formal services and turn to peers first. Walk With Me (WWM), a journey-based peer support programme in Singapore, pairs trained volunteers with youths who have or are at risk of NSSI. This study evaluated youth outcomes. 
Methods: Using a mixed-method, single-group, pre–post design, 36 youths (aged 15–25; 72% female) completed surveys before and after the programme. Eight outcomes spanning interpersonal and emotion-regulation domains were assessed, four theory-of-change pathways were tested and open-ended responses were analysed qualitatively. 
Results: All outcomes improved significantly from pre- to post-test, with medium to large effects; the largest gains were in emotion regulation and coping, and younger participants showed greater resilience gains. The four hypothesised change pathways were supported or partially supported; notably, encouragement to reach out predicted increased support-seeking. Youths rated their peer-supporter relationship highly, and qualitative accounts echoed these gains. 
Conclusion: WWM is linked to meaningful improvements in youths' social skills, support-seeking, communication, and emotion regulation, appearing to operate through a gradual peer relationship. As one of the first studies to test these mechanisms, it offers a promising foundation for rigorous evaluation.

articles.title: Dynamics of Skill Mismatch in the Workplace: Longitudinal Evidence from a Medium-Sized Japanese Company
articles.authors: Tomotaka Hirao
articles.abstract: Although skill mismatch in the labor market is an important topic of discussion and research worldwide, that phenomenon in the Japanese labor market or organizations remains to be fully elucidated, despite the fact that Japan has a distinctive employment system. Therefore, using newly available data, such as longitudinal personnel data and employee satisfaction survey data, this study investigates the existence and determinants of vertical skill mismatch in a typical medium-sized Japanese company in order to address the dearth of similar literature in Japan. As a result, this study shows the vertical skill mismatch of frequent occurrence. Additionally, empirical results reveal: 1) job autonomy decreases the likelihood of vertical skill mismatch; 2) supervisors’ precise advice related to business activities for their subordinates reduces the likelihood of vertical skill mismatch; and 3) communication among employees in the workplace increases accessibility to skill matched roles. Career development in the Japanese company may not reflect a linear progression from easy work to more difficult work, but may rather be more of a mixed change involving under- and over-skilled mismatching.
